Q098: Diagenesis: Post-Depositional Physical, Chemical & Biological Transformations of Sediments

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 98
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (5th/6th Ed., Ch. 5: Sandstones / Diagenesis, pp. 175–190; Fig. 5.25); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, pp. 68–72, 170); Maurice E. Tucker, Sedimentary Petrology: An Introduction to the Origin of Sedimentary Rocks; F.J. Pettijohn, P.E. Potter, and R. Siever, Sand and Sandstone.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Temperature-Pressure Boundaries & Framework of Diagenesis

In sedimentary geology and petroleum geoscience (Boggs, 2014, pp. 175–190; Tucker, 2001; Pettijohn et al., 1987), diagenesis is formally defined as the sum total of all physical, chemical, and biological changes and transformations that a sediment or soil undergoes after its initial deposition, during and after its burial, up to the lowest-grade boundary of metamorphism.

The term was introduced into geological science in 1888 by the Austrian geologist Carl Wilhelm von Gümbel. The pressure-temperature window of diagenesis encompasses surface conditions up to temperatures of approximately $200^\circ\text{C}$ to $250^\circ\text{C}$ and lithostatic burial pressures of approximately $1\text{ to } 2\text{ kbar}$ (depths of $\sim 5\text{ to } 7\text{ km}$), beyond which processes enter the realm of very low-grade metamorphism (anchizone / sub-greenschist facies).

Figure 98.1 — Chronological and Depth Stages of Sedimentary Diagenesis: Authentic textbook diagram from Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 180). Shows the tripartite diagenetic framework: Eodiagenesis (surface/shallow burial), Mesodiagenesis (deep burial compaction and thermal maturation), and Telodiagenesis (uplift and meteoric weathering).

The Tripartite Stages of Diagenesis

According to the widely accepted classification of Choquette and Pray (1970) and Schmidt and McDonald (1979), diagenesis is subdivided into three distinct chronological and depth regimes:

  1. Eodiagenesis (Early Diagenesis): Operates at or immediately beneath the depositional surface (depths from $0\text{ to a few hundred meters}$). Governed by pore fluids chemically linked to the surface environment (marine, lacustrine, meteoric), active bioturbation by benthic organisms, microbial decomposition of organic matter (aerobic respiration, sulfate reduction, methanogenesis), and early cementation (e.g., micritic calcite crusts, siderite concretions).
  2. Mesodiagenesis (Burial Diagenesis): Occurs during progressive deep basin burial (depths of $1\text{ to } 5+\text{ km}$, temperatures $50\text{--}200^\circ\text{C}$). Driven by increasing overburden stress and geothermal heat:
    • Mechanical Compaction: Reorientation and ductile degranulation of clasts, repacking grains from loose cubic to tight rhombohedral packing, causing drastic porosity reduction.
    • Chemical Compaction (Pressure Solution): Intergranular dissolution at grain contact points under high differential stress, developing concavo-convex contacts, sutured contacts, and macroscopic stylolites.
    • Authigenesis & Cementation: Precipitation of syntaxial quartz overgrowths, poikilotopic carbonate cements, and authigenic clay minerals (kaolinite, illite).
    • Smectite-to-Illite Transition: Thermally driven clay dehydration releasing bound interlayer water into pore networks: $\text{Smectite} + \text{K}^+ \xrightarrow{60\text{--}120^\circ\text{C}} \text{Illite} + \text{Quartz} + \text{Water}$.
    • Dissolution & Secondary Porosity: Leaching of unstable feldspars and carbonates by acidic pore waters generated from kerogen decarboxylation.
  3. Telodiagenesis (Uplift Diagenesis / Retrograde Diagenesis): Occurs when deeply buried sedimentary rocks are tectonically uplifted and brought back into contact with oxidizing, cool meteoric groundwaters, driving dissolution of carbonate cements, oxidation of pyrite to iron oxides/hydroxides, and kaolinitization of remaining feldspars.
2. Critical Distinction: Diagenesis vs. Lithification & Petrogenesis

Why Lithification is Only a Subset of Diagenesis

A frequent point of confusion among geology students is equating diagenesis with lithification. They are fundamentally distinct in scope:

  • Lithification (Consolidation): The specific process of turning loose, unconsolidated sediment into solid rock through mechanical compaction and intergranular mineral cementation.
  • Diagenesis (The Overarching Domain): Encompasses lithification, but also includes processes that operate in the opposite direction—such as leaching, dissolution, and secondary porosity creation, where solid rock is partially dissolved by acidic fluids, increasing void space and weakening rock competence. Diagenesis also includes recrystallization, mineral polymorphism, and isotopic re-equilibration.

Refutation of Distractor Terms

Geological Term Rigorous Scientific Definition Scope & Typical Usage Governing Geological Regime
Diagenesis All post-depositional physical, chemical, and biological transformations of sediments and soils prior to metamorphism Comprehensive sedimentary petrology, soil genesis, and petroleum reservoir evolution Sedimentary domain ($T < 200\text{--}250^\circ\text{C}$, $P < 2\text{ kbar}$)
Petrogenesis The origin, evolution, and formation history of rocks in general Predominantly utilized in igneous petrology (magmatic differentiation, partial melting) and metamorphic petrology All geological domains (igneous, metamorphic, sedimentary)
Lithification The physical consolidation of loose sediment into coherent rock via compaction and cementation Sub-process of diagenesis; excludes dissolution and secondary porosity generation Sedimentary diagenetic sub-process
Crustification Concentric or crust-like banding of mineral crystals lining hydrothermal veins or cavities Ore geology and hydrothermal mineral deposit textures Hydrothermal / Epithermal vein filling
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 98: The physical or chemical transformation of sediments or soil by geological processes is termed as :
(A) Diagenesis
(B) Petrogenesis
(C) Lithification
(D) Crustificaton
Verified Correct Answer: (A) Diagenesis
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Confirmed — Diagenesis

Correct: By universal scientific definition in geology (Boggs, 2014, p. 175; Bangar, p. 68; Pettijohn et al., 1987), diagenesis is the exact term designating the entire spectrum of physical, chemical, and biological transformations that alter sediments or soils after deposition, throughout burial and compaction, up to the threshold of regional metamorphism. The question's formulation ("physical or chemical transformation of sediments or soil by geological processes") matches this textbook definition word for word.

Option (B) Refuted — Petrogenesis

Incorrect: Petrogenesis (from Greek petra = rock + genesis = origin) is the broad branch of petrology that deals with the origin, historical evolution, and chemical genesis of rocks in general. It is most commonly applied to igneous rocks (e.g., magma generation, partial melting, fractional crystallization) and metamorphic rocks (anatexis, metamorphic reactions). It does not specifically refer to the post-depositional transformation of sediments or soils.

Option (C) Refuted — Lithification

Incorrect: Lithification refers strictly and narrowly to the process of converting loose, soft sediment into solid, cohesive rock (primarily via mechanical compaction and cement precipitation). It is merely one individual sub-stage within the much broader domain of diagenesis. Diagenesis includes many major chemical transformations that do not consolidate rock—such as the creation of secondary dissolution porosity, dolomitization, neoformation of clay minerals, and telodiagenetic weathering.

Option (D) Refuted — Crustification

Incorrect: In economic geology and mineral deposit petrography, crustification refers to a distinct texture in epigenetic hydrothermal mineral veins, where successive crusts or crystalline layers of different minerals (e.g., quartz, sphalerite, galena, calcite) are deposited on the walls of an open fracture or cavity. It has no relevance to the post-depositional alteration of sedimentary beds or soils.

Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

A quartz sandstone at $3000\text{ m}$ burial depth in a sedimentary basin exhibits intergranular porosity of $18\%$. Petrographic examination shows that $8\%$ of this porosity consists of oversized pores containing corroded, skeletal remnants of K-feldspar. Classify this porosity and explain the diagenetic reaction responsible.

Solution: The $8\%$ porosity represents secondary dissolution porosity generated during mesodiagenesis. The reaction is driven by acidic pore fluids generated during the thermal maturation of organic matter (kerogen), which releases carbon dioxide and organic carboxylic acids at temperatures of $80\text{--}120^\circ\text{C}$. The acidic fluids aggressively leach unstable detrital K-feldspar: $$2\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8 + 2\text{H}^+ + 9\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4\text{ (kaolinite)} + 4\text{H}_4\text{SiO}_4 + 2\text{K}^+$$ dissolving the feldspar interior and leaving behind empty oversized dissolution moldic pores.

Practice Problem 2

Explain how pressure solution (chemical compaction) in sandstones acts as an internal source of silica for syntaxial quartz overgrowth cements.

Solution: Under high vertical lithostatic stress, the stress concentrated at grain-to-grain contact points exceeds the hydrostatic pore-fluid pressure. According to the Riecke Principle, mineral solubility increases with directed compressive stress. Consequently, quartz selectively dissolves at grain contact points. The dissolved aqueous silica ($\text{H}_4\text{SiO}_4$) diffuses outward into adjacent low-stress, open pore spaces where fluid is supersaturated relative to hydrostatic stress, precipitating onto detrital quartz grains as syntaxial quartz overgrowths.

Practice Problem 3

What is a "stylolite" in sedimentary petrology, and in which rocks are stylolites most prominently developed?

Solution: A stylolite is an irregular, serrated, suture-like planar or undulating seam formed by localized, intense chemical compaction (pressure solution). Along the stylolite, substantial thicknesses of the host rock have been completely dissolved away, leaving behind a thin insoluble residue of clay minerals, iron oxides, organic carbon, and heavy minerals. Stylolites are most prominently developed in carbonates (limestones and dolomites) and well-sorted quartzose sandstones.

Practice Problem 4

Explain the smectite-to-illite transformation during burial diagenesis and state its significance as a geothermometer in petroleum exploration.

Solution: With increasing burial depth and temperature, expandable smectite reacts with available potassium (from dissolving K-feldspar) to form non-expandable illite through a series of mixed-layer illite/smectite (I/S) intermediates: $$\text{Smectite} + \text{K}^+ + \text{Al}^{3+} \xrightarrow{60\text{--}140^\circ\text{C}} \text{Illite} + \text{Quartz} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The percentage of illite layers in mixed-layer I/S clays increases progressively with temperature (e.g., $80\%$ illite layers corresponds to $\sim 100\text{--}120^\circ\text{C}$). This transformation serves as an invaluable inorganic geothermometer to map peak paleotemperatures and assess whether organic source rocks have entered the "oil generation window" ($60\text{--}120^\circ\text{C}$).

Practice Problem 5

Why does the Athy (1930) porosity-depth relationship show an exponential decline in mudrocks with depth: $\phi(z) = \phi_0 e^{-cz}$?

Solution: L.F. Athy established that mechanical compaction of fine-grained mudrocks is governed by the progressive expulsion of interstitial pore water under increasing effective overburden stress ($\sigma'_v = \sigma_v - P_p$). At shallow depths, high-porosity card-house clay fabrics collapse easily under small stress increments. As depth increases, grains become closely packed and interlocked, drastically increasing skeletal bulk stiffness; hence, progressively larger overburden increments are required to achieve further volumetric strain, producing an exponential decay curve.

Practice Problem 6

Contrast "eodiagenesis", "mesodiagenesis", and "telodiagenesis" in terms of their fluid chemistry and temperature conditions.

Solution: - Eodiagenesis: Low temperature ($< 50^\circ\text{C}$); fluids are depositional surface waters (marine or meteoric); active microbial and biological control. - Mesodiagenesis: Elevated temperatures ($50\text{--}200^\circ\text{C}$); fluids are evolved, highly saline basinal formation brines; thermochemical reactions, hydrocarbon maturation, and burial pressure dominate. - Telodiagenesis: Low temperature ($< 50^\circ\text{C}$); fluids are fresh, cold, oxidizing, carbonic-acid-charged meteoric waters introduced via tectonic uplift and erosional unconformities.

Practice Problem 7

What is "pseudomatrix" in a compacted sandstone and how does it originate diagenetically?

Solution: Pseudomatrix is an artificial, diagenetically generated interstitial matrix formed when ductile, mechanically weak framework grains (such as shale clasts, mudstone lithics, or deeply weathered volcanic fragments) are squashed, deformed, and squeezed into adjacent intergranular pore spaces between rigid quartz grains during mechanical compaction. Under the microscope, it mimics primary detrital clay matrix, but petrographic inspection reveals ghost outlines of compacted lithic grains.

Practice Problem 8

State the upper physical boundary that demarcates diagenesis from metamorphism in sedimentary basins.

Solution: The boundary between diagenesis and metamorphism is transitional but formally defined by: 1. Temperature: Approximately $200^\circ\text{C}$ to $250^\circ\text{C}$. 2. Vitrinite Reflectance ($R_o$): $R_o \approx 2.5\text{ to } 3.0\%$. 3. Clay Mineralogy: The disappearance of smectite and mixed-layer clays, marked by the onset of well-crystallized illite (Kübler Index illite crystallinity $\approx 0.42^\circ\Delta 2\theta$, defining the anchizone) and the appearance of metamorphic pyrophyllite, chloritoid, or paragonite.

Q099: Sedimentary Maturity: Textural Evolution, Geochemical Indices & The ZTR Heavy Mineral Index

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 99
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (5th/6th Ed., Ch. 5: Sandstones / Maturity Concepts, pp. 138–144; Fig. 5.7); J.F. Hubert (1962), A Zircon-Tourmaline-Rutile Maturity Index and the Interdependence of the Composition of Heavy-Mineral Assemblages with the Gross Composition and Texture of Sandstones (Journal of Sedimentary Petrology); R.L. Folk (1951), Stages of Textural Maturity in Sedimentary Rocks; F.J. Pettijohn, P.E. Potter, and R. Siever, Sand and Sandstone.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Dual Framework of Sedimentary Maturity: Textural vs. Mineralogical

In clastic sedimentology (Boggs, 2014, pp. 138–144; Folk, 1951; Pettijohn et al., 1987), the concept of sedimentary maturity refers to the extent to which a clastic sediment has evolved along the pathway toward ultimate physical and chemical equilibrium with the Earth's surface environment.

Sedimentary maturity is evaluated across two fundamentally independent dimensions:

  1. Textural Maturity (Folk's Stages of Maturity): Reflects the expenditure of kinetic mechanical energy in the depositional environment (wave/current winnowing and grain abrasion). It monitors:
    • The elimination of fine-grained interstitial detrital clay matrix ($< 0.03\text{ mm}$).
    • The degree of hydrodynamic grain-size sorting (measured by graphic standard deviation $\sigma_I$).
    • The degree of particle roundness (abrasion of sharp edges and corners into rounded spheres).
  2. Mineralogical (Compositional) Maturity: Reflects the degree to which unstable, chemically labile, and mechanically weak minerals (e.g., ferromagnesian pyroxenes, amphiboles, olivine, calcic plagioclase, lithic rock fragments) have been destroyed by prolonged chemical weathering and hydrodynamic attrition, leaving a residual concentration of the most inert, ultra-durable phases—predominantly monocrystalline quartz ($\text{SiO}_2$) and the ultra-stable heavy mineral trio: Zircon, Tourmaline, and Rutile (ZTR).
Figure 99.1 — Textural and Mineralogical Maturity Scales of Siliciclastic Sediments: Authentic textbook diagram from Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 140). Depicts the 4-stage textural maturity evolution (immature to supermature) alongside Hubert's ZTR heavy mineral index and Q-F-L mineralogical maturity trends.

Folk's Four Stages of Textural Maturity

Maturity Stage Clay Matrix Content Grain Sorting ($\sigma_I$) Grain Roundness Hydrodynamic Energy Regime
Immature High ($> 5\%$) Poorly to very poorly sorted ($\sigma_I > 1.0\phi$) Angular to sub-angular Low-energy, rapid dumping (alluvial fans, turbidity currents)
Submature Low ($< 5\%$, matrix winnowed away) Poorly sorted ($\sigma_I > 0.5\phi$) Angular to sub-angular Moderate energy; winnowing active but sorting incomplete
Mature Negligible ($< 5\%$) Well-sorted ($\sigma_I < 0.5\phi$) Sub-angular to sub-rounded High sustained energy (fluvial bars, marine shelves)
Supermature Zero ($< 1\%$) Very well-sorted ($\sigma_I < 0.35\phi$) Well-rounded to rounded Prolonged, intense polycyclic reworking (eolian dunes, beach surf zones)
2. Hubert's ZTR Index & Geochemical Signatures of High Sedimentary Maturity

Hubert's ZTR Heavy Mineral Maturity Index (1962)

In clastic provenance and maturity analysis, John F. Hubert established that the non-opaque, transparent heavy mineral fraction ($specific\text{ gravity} > 2.85$) provides an extraordinarily sensitive gauge of mineralogical maturity.

Among detrital heavy minerals, Zircon ($\text{ZrSiO}_4$), Tourmaline (complex borosilicate), and Rutile ($\text{TiO}_2$) are distinguished by their exceptional mechanical hardness ($Mohs\text{ 7 to 8}$) and near-total chemical inertness under surficial weathering and diagenetic conditions. Hubert's ZTR Index is mathematically defined as:

$$\text{ZTR Index (\%)} = \left( \frac{\text{Zircon} + \text{Tourmaline} + \text{Rutile}}{\sum \text{Total Non-Opaque Transparent Heavy Minerals}} \right) \times 100$$
  • Low Maturity ($\text{ZTR} < 25\%$): Assemblages dominated by unstable, labile heavy minerals—such as olivine, calcic clinopyroxenes, hornblende, hypersthene, and apatite—indicating first-cycle, rapid erosion of crystalline bedrock.
  • Moderate Maturity ($\text{ZTR} = 25\text{--}75\%$): Partially altered assemblages with intermediate-stability species (epidote, staurolite, garnet).
  • High Maturity ($\text{ZTR} > 75\text{--}90\%$): Assemblages where all unstable ferromagnesian minerals have been entirely eliminated, leaving almost exclusively zircon, tourmaline, and rutile. When combined with $> 95\%$ quartz framework grains and well-rounded clasts, it establishes high to supermature maturity, characteristic of polycyclic cratonic quartz arenites.

Geochemical Maturity Indicators

  • $\text{SiO}_2 / \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ Ratio: As sediments mature, quartz ($\text{SiO}_2$) concentrates while aluminous clay minerals and feldspars are winnowed or destroyed. In immature graywackes, $\text{SiO}_2/\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \approx 3\text{ to } 5$; in mature quartz arenites, $\text{SiO}_2/\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 > 20\text{ to } 100+$.
  • Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA): Introduced by Nesbitt and Young (1982): $$\text{CIA} = \left[ \frac{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{CaO}^* + \text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{K}_2\text{O}} \right] \times 100$$ Fresh crystalline bedrock has $\text{CIA} \approx 45\text{--}55$, whereas highly mature, intensively weathered residues (kaolinite/gibbsite) reach $\text{CIA} \approx 90\text{--}100$.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 99: High SiO2, Al2O3, rounded clasts and high ZTR index indicate _____ maturity of sediments.
(A) low
(B) high
(C) moderate
(D) None of these
Verified Correct Answer: (B) high
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Refuted — Low Maturity

Incorrect: Low-maturity sediments (such as first-cycle arkoses, lithic graywackes, or glacial tills) are characterized by the exact reverse of the parameters described: they have low $\text{SiO}_2$ (abundant unstable rock fragments and labile mafic minerals), angular to sub-angular clasts (minimal abrasion), poor sorting with $> 15\%$ mud matrix (textural immaturity), and an extremely low ZTR index (typically $< 15\%$, dominated by chemically unstable pyroxenes, amphiboles, and olivine).

Option (B) Confirmed — High Maturity

Correct: By universal petrological principles (Boggs, 2014, p. 140; Hubert, 1962; Folk, 1951), the convergence of: (1) High $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ residual concentration: indicating profound chemical weathering that leached all soluble base cations ($\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Na}^+$); (2) Rounded clasts: demonstrating prolonged hydrodynamic transport, intense abrasion, and high textural maturity; and (3) High ZTR Index ($> 75\text{--}90\%$): proving that virtually all unstable heavy minerals have been eliminated, leaving only the ultra-stable trio (Zircon, Tourmaline, Rutile); unequivocally diagnoses a high (to supermature) maturity of sediments.

Option (C) Refuted — Moderate Maturity

Incorrect: Moderate (submature) sediments exhibit partially rounded or sub-rounded clasts, intermediate $\text{SiO}_2$ contents, and moderate ZTR indices ($25\text{--}60\%$) with persistent intermediate-stability heavy minerals (e.g., epidote, garnet, staurolite). When a sediment reaches the threshold of rounded clasts alongside high $\text{SiO}_2$ and high ZTR, it has advanced fully into the high maturity classification.

Option (D) Refuted — None of These

Incorrect: Option (D) is false because "high" maturity is the well-established, mathematically and empirically validated answer in all standard sedimentary petrology curricula.

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions

Quartz Content ($\text{SiO}_2$) Low to Moderate ($35\text{--}65\%$) Moderate to High ($65\text{--}85\%$) Very High ($> 90\text{--}99\%$, Quartz Arenite)
Feldspar & Lithic Content Very High ($> 25\text{--}50\%$, labile clasts abundant) Moderate ($10\text{--}25\%$) Negligible ($< 1\text{--}5\%$, chemically stripped)

Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

A heavy mineral separation yields the following grain counts for the non-opaque transparent fraction: Zircon = 145 grains, Tourmaline = 85 grains, Rutile = 50 grains, Garnet = 12 grains, Epidote = 6 grains, Apatite = 2 grains. Calculate the ZTR Index and determine the mineralogical maturity of this sandstone.

Solution: Total non-opaque transparent heavy minerals: $$\sum = 145 + 85 + 50 + 12 + 6 + 2 = 300\text{ grains}$$ Sum of Zircon + Tourmaline + Rutile: $$\text{ZTR} = 145 + 85 + 50 = 280\text{ grains}$$ Hubert's ZTR Index: $$\text{ZTR Index} = \left( \frac{280}{300} \right) \times 100 = 93.33\%$$ Since the ZTR Index exceeds $90\%$, the sandstone possesses an exceptionally high mineralogical maturity, indicative of polycyclic recycling or extreme chemical weathering in a stable cratonic setting.

Practice Problem 2

Explain why a sediment can be texturally mature yet mineralogically immature, and provide a real-world geological example.

Solution: Textural and mineralogical maturity are decoupled: - Textural maturity is governed by mechanical energy, winnowing, and abrasion time. - Mineralogical maturity is governed by chemical weathering kinetics and climate. A real-world example is an arkosic beach sand or eolian dune sand in an arid desert (e.g., modern beach sands along the Gulf of California or Red Sea). High wave or wind energy thoroughly winnows out all clay matrix and produces very well-sorted, rounded sand grains (supermature texturally), yet because the hyper-arid climate lacks moisture for chemical hydrolysis, $35\text{--}45\%$ fresh, unweathered feldspars survive (mineralogically immature).

Practice Problem 3

Calculate the Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) for an unweathered granodiorite parent rock with molar proportions: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 15.2$, $\text{CaO}^* = 3.8$, $\text{Na}_2\text{O} = 4.1$, $\text{K}_2\text{O} = 2.4$, and compare it to its weathered residual clay residue with $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 38.5$, $\text{CaO}^* = 0.2$, $\text{Na}_2\text{O} = 0.3$, $\text{K}_2\text{O} = 0.8$.

Solution: The formula for CIA is: $$\text{CIA} = \left[ \frac{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{CaO}^* + \text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{K}_2\text{O}} \right] \times 100$$ - For unweathered parent granodiorite: $$\text{CIA}_{parent} = \frac{15.2}{15.2 + 3.8 + 4.1 + 2.4} \times 100 = \frac{15.2}{25.5} \times 100 \approx 59.6\%$$ - For weathered clay residue: $$\text{CIA}_{residue} = \frac{38.5}{38.5 + 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.8} \times 100 = \frac{38.5}{39.8} \times 100 \approx 96.7\%$$ The jump from $59.6\%$ to $96.7\%$ quantitatively documents the transition to extreme chemical/mineralogical maturity via base leaching.

Practice Problem 4

Why are Zircon, Tourmaline, and Rutile the three minerals chosen by Hubert for the ZTR maturity index rather than other common accessories like magnetite or garnet?

Solution: Zircon ($\text{ZrSiO}_4$), Tourmaline, and Rutile ($\text{TiO}_2$) occupy the pinnacle of both chemical resistance and mechanical abrasion durability: 1. Chemical Durability: They are virtually insoluble in all natural groundwater conditions (acidic, alkaline, or reducing). 2. Mechanical Hardness: They have high Mohs hardness ($7\text{ to } 8$), resisting attrition during thousands of kilometers of fluvial or eolian transport. In contrast, magnetite is opaque (excluded from transparent counts) and alters to hematite/limonite; garnet is mechanically brittle and readily etches or dissolves in deep burial diagenesis (forming skeletal etched dodecahedra).

Practice Problem 5

Define "polycyclic sediments" and explain their role in generating high-maturity quartz arenites.

Solution: Polycyclic (multicycle) sediments are sedimentary rocks composed of grains that have undergone multiple successive cycles of erosion, deposition, lithification, uplift, and re-erosion from older sedimentary strata rather than direct erosion from crystalline basement. A single sedimentary cycle under temperate conditions is rarely sufficient to eliminate all feldspars and round quartz grains; but repeating this cycle $3\text{ to } 5\text{ times}$ across hundreds of millions of years on a stable craton systematically eliminates all labile minerals, yielding pure quartz arenites ($> 99\%\text{ SiO}_2$) with $\text{ZTR} > 95\%$.

Practice Problem 6

Under Folk's textural maturity classification, why does the presence of only $6\%$ clay matrix immediately demote a sandstone with perfectly rounded, spherical quartz grains to the "Immature" category?

Solution: Folk's classification is hierarchical: Matrix winnowing is Step 1. If a sediment contains $> 5\%$ clay matrix, it indicates that current or wave action at the final depositional site was too sluggish or weak to wash away fine suspension mud. Even if the framework grains were rounded during a prior eolian cycle, the final depositional environment was low-energy (e.g., a quiet lagoon or turbidity flow), classifying it texturally as Immature (texturally inverted).

Practice Problem 7

What is a "textural inversion" in sedimentary petrology?

Solution: A textural inversion occurs when a sediment displays contradictory textural attributes that violate normal hydrodynamic equilibrium—such as: (a) Well-rounded sand grains floating in an abundant ($> 15\%$) fine clay matrix (e.g., tillites or pebbly mudstones). (b) A bimodal mixture of well-rounded large grains mixed with angular fine grains. Textural inversions indicate the mixing of sediments from two distinct energy regimes (e.g., eolian rounded dune grains blown into a quiet muddy lagoon, or polycyclic rounded grains dumped into a turbidite).

Practice Problem 8

How does the Plagioclase Index of Alteration (PIA) complement the CIA in assessing feldspar weathering maturity?

Solution: The Plagioclase Index of Alteration (PIA; Fedo et al., 1995) specifically monitors the destruction of plagioclase feldspar: $$\text{PIA} = \left[ \frac{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 - \text{K}_2\text{O}}{(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 - \text{K}_2\text{O}) + \text{CaO}^* + \text{Na}_2\text{O}} \right] \times 100$$ Because calcic and sodic plagioclase weather significantly faster than potassic K-feldspar, PIA reaches near $100\%$ before K-feldspar is completely eliminated, allowing geochemists to isolate the early and intermediate stages of chemical weathering maturity in basin provenance studies.

Q100: Granulometric Analysis: Grain-Size Distribution, Sieving, Settling & Statistical Metrics

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 100
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (5th/6th Ed., Ch. 3: Grain Size, pp. 55–75; Fig. 3.4); R.L. Folk and W.C. Ward (1957), Brazos River Bar: A Study in the Significance of Grain Size Parameters (Journal of Sedimentary Petrology); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, pp. 67–70); Maurice E. Tucker, Sedimentary Petrology: An Introduction to the Origin of Sedimentary Rocks.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Etymology & Experimental Framework of Granulometric Analysis

In physical sedimentology, soil mechanics, and sedimentary petrology (Boggs, 2014, pp. 55–75; Folk & Ward, 1957; Bangar, p. 67), granulometric analysis (also termed granulometry, mechanical grain-size analysis, or particle-size distribution analysis) is the rigorous scientific procedure used to quantitatively determine the size frequency distribution and weight percentage of individual particle-size fractions comprising a sediment or disaggregated clastic rock sample.

The term is derived from the Latin granulum ("small grain or seed") and the Greek metron ("measure"). It provides the primary quantitative baseline for reconstructing ancient hydrodynamic transport mechanisms, depositional energy regimes, paleocurrent dynamics, and geotechnical engineering classifications.

Figure 100.1 — Cumulative Frequency Curves and Grain-Size Distribution Plots: Authentic textbook diagram from Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 60). Illustrates cumulative weight percentage frequency curves plotted on arithmetic and probability scales, enabling graphical extraction of $\phi_5, \phi_{16}, \phi_{50}, \phi_{84}, \text{and } \phi_{95}$ percentiles.

Standard Laboratory Methodologies in Granulometric Analysis

Because sedimentary particles span a gigantic physical size range—from boulders ($> 256\text{ mm}$) to sub-micron colloidal clays ($< 0.001\text{ mm}$)—no single analytical instrument can measure the entire spectrum. Granulometric analysis employs integrated complementary methods:

  • Sieve Analysis (Dry and Wet Sieving): Applied to the coarse sand and gravel fraction ($> 0.0625\text{ mm}$ or $< 4\phi$). A known dry mass of disaggregated sediment is shaken through a nested stack of standardized brass wire-mesh sieves (U.S. Standard / ASTM / Tyler mesh) arranged in order of decreasing aperture on a mechanical Ro-Tap shaker. The sediment retained on each sieve is weighed to $0.01\text{ g}$ precision.
  • Sedimentation Analysis (Pipette and Hydrometer Methods): Applied to the fine silt and clay fraction ($< 0.0625\text{ mm}$ or $> 4\phi$). Governed by Stokes' Law, which dictates the terminal settling velocity ($v$) of spherical particles through a viscous fluid: $$v = \frac{(\rho_s - \rho_f) g d^2}{18 \mu}$$ where $\rho_s$ is particle density ($2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$ for quartz), $\rho_f$ is fluid density, $g$ is gravitational acceleration, $\mu$ is dynamic viscosity of water, and $d$ is particle diameter. By withdrawing aliquots at fixed depths and times (pipette method) or measuring suspension density (hydrometer), particle diameters are calculated.
  • Modern Automated Optical Methods: Laser diffraction particle size analyzers (Fraunhofer diffraction / Mie scattering), digital dynamic image analyzers, and automated settling tubes.
2. Folk and Ward (1957) Graphic Statistical Parameters & Environmental Signatures

Mathematical Derivation of Graphic Percentile Metrics

The data obtained from granulometric analysis are plotted as a cumulative frequency curve on semi-logarithmic or probability paper, from which critical phi-percentiles ($\phi = -\log_2 d_{\text{mm}}$) are extracted:

Statistical Parameter Folk & Ward (1957) Formula Physical & Geological Meaning
Graphic Mean ($M_z$) $$M_z = \frac{\phi_{16} + \phi_{50} + \phi_{84}}{3}$$ Overall average grain size of the sediment; reflects peak hydrodynamic competence of the depositing fluid.
Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation ($\sigma_I$) $$\sigma_I = \frac{\phi_{84} - \phi_{16}}{4} + \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{6.6}$$ Sorting (uniformity of grain sizes); reflects the constancy and efficiency of fluid velocity fluctuations.
Inclusive Graphic Skewness ($Sk_I$) $$Sk_I = \frac{\phi_{16} + \phi_{84} - 2\phi_{50}}{2(\phi_{84} - \phi_{16})} + \frac{\phi_5 + \phi_{95} - 2\phi_{50}}{2(\phi_{95} - \phi_5)}$$ Asymmetry of the distribution. Positive ($> 0$): excess fine tail (river channels). Negative ($< 0$): excess coarse tail (beach surf zones winnowed of fines).
Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$) $$K_G = \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}$$ Peakedness of the frequency curve relative to normal Gaussian bell curve ($K_G = 1.0$ is Mesokurtic). Measures mixing of bimodalities.

Folk's Sorting Classification Scale ($\sigma_I$)

$\sigma_I < 0.35\phi$: Very well sorted | $0.35\text{--}0.50\phi$: Well sorted | $0.50\text{--}0.71\phi$: Moderately well sorted | $0.71\text{--}1.00\phi$: Moderately sorted | $1.00\text{--}2.00\phi$: Poorly sorted | $> 2.00\phi$: Very poorly sorted.

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 100: An analysis that helps to determine grain size and percentage of the individual size fractions in the specific sediment sample is called :
(A) Granulometric analysis
(B) Gravimetric analysis
(C) Sedimentation analysis
(D) Both (A) and (B) are correct
Verified Correct Answer: (A) Granulometric analysis
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Confirmed — Granulometric Analysis

Correct: By universal scientific, engineering, and sedimentological definition (Boggs, 2014, p. 55; Bangar, p. 67; Folk, 1980), granulometric analysis is the exact and comprehensive geological term for the laboratory determination of particle sizes and the relative weight percentages of individual size fractions in a sediment or soil sample. It encompasses all grain sizes (gravel, sand, silt, and clay) across both sieving and sedimentation procedures.

Option (B) Refuted — Gravimetric Analysis

Incorrect: Gravimetric analysis is a classical quantitative analytical chemistry technique that determines the mass or concentration of an analyte based on measuring the mass of a solid precipitate (e.g., precipitating dissolved sulfate as insoluble barium sulfate $\text{BaSO}_4$ and weighing it). Gravimetric analysis measures chemical elemental mass, not the physical grain-size distribution or size fractions of sediment particles.

Option (C) Refuted — Sedimentation Analysis

Incorrect: While sedimentation analysis (pipette/hydrometer method based on Stokes' Law) is a recognized laboratory technique, it is strictly one specific sub-method restricted exclusively to measuring the fine silt-and-clay fraction ($< 0.0625\text{ mm}$). It cannot determine the grain size of gravels or coarse sands, which settle too rapidly for laminar Stokes' flow. Therefore, it does not represent the overarching, comprehensive analysis for the entire sediment sample; that universal discipline is granulometric analysis.

Option (D) Refuted — Both (A) and (B) are Correct

Incorrect: Because gravimetric analysis is a chemical technique having nothing to do with determining physical grain-size distributions, option (D) is entirely fallacious. The single, unequivocally verified correct answer is (A) Granulometric analysis.

Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

A $200.0\text{ g}$ dry sediment sample is processed through a granulometric sieve stack. The weights retained are: Gravel ($> 2\text{ mm}$) = $20.0\text{ g}$; Sand ($2.0\text{ to } 0.0625\text{ mm}$) = $150.0\text{ g}$; Mud ($< 0.0625\text{ mm}$) in pan = $30.0\text{ g}$. Calculate the percentage fractions and classify the sediment on a Folk (1954) ternary diagram.

Solution: - Gravel fraction: $\frac{20.0}{200.0} \times 100 = 10.0\%$ - Sand fraction: $\frac{150.0}{200.0} \times 100 = 75.0\%$ - Mud fraction: $\frac{30.0}{200.0} \times 100 = 15.0\%$ - Sand : Mud ratio = $75 : 15 = 5 : 1$. On Folk's Gravel-Sand-Mud (G-S-M) ternary classification diagram, a sediment containing between $5\%\text{ and } 30\%$ gravel with a sand-to-mud ratio $> 9:1$ is a "gravelly sand", but here the sand:mud ratio is $5:1$ (between $1:1$ and $9:1$), classifying it formally as a gravelly muddy sand.

Practice Problem 2

From the cumulative frequency curve of an estuarine sand sample, the following phi-percentile values are read: $\phi_5 = 1.2$, $\phi_{16} = 1.8$, $\phi_{50} = 2.5$, $\phi_{84} = 3.2$, $\phi_{95} = 4.0$. Calculate Folk and Ward's Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation ($\sigma_I$) and interpret the sorting.

Solution: Using Folk and Ward's formula: $$\sigma_I = \frac{\phi_{84} - \phi_{16}}{4} + \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{6.6}$$ $$\sigma_I = \frac{3.2 - 1.8}{4} + \frac{4.0 - 1.2}{6.6} = \frac{1.4}{4} + \frac{2.8}{6.6} = 0.350 + 0.424 = 0.774\phi$$ According to Folk's sorting scale, $\sigma_I$ between $0.71\phi$ and $1.00\phi$ is classified as Moderately Sorted.

Practice Problem 3

Using the percentile values from Problem 2, calculate Folk and Ward's Inclusive Graphic Skewness ($Sk_I$) and interpret its physical meaning.

Solution: The formula for Inclusive Graphic Skewness is: $$Sk_I = \frac{\phi_{16} + \phi_{84} - 2\phi_{50}}{2(\phi_{84} - \phi_{16})} + \frac{\phi_5 + \phi_{95} - 2\phi_{50}}{2(\phi_{95} - \phi_5)}$$ Substituting values: $$Sk_I = \frac{1.8 + 3.2 - 2(2.5)}{2(3.2 - 1.8)} + \frac{1.2 + 4.0 - 2(2.5)}{2(4.0 - 1.2)}$$ $$Sk_I = \frac{5.0 - 5.0}{2(1.4)} + \frac{5.2 - 5.0}{2(2.8)} = 0 + \frac{0.2}{5.6} \approx +0.036$$ A skewness between $-0.10$ and $+0.10$ is classified as Near-Symmetrical, indicating that the grain size distribution closely approximates a normal, symmetrical Gaussian bell curve without an excessive tail of coarse or fine grains.

Practice Problem 4

Calculate the terminal settling velocity ($v$) of a quartz sphere ($d = 0.02\text{ mm} = 2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}$, fine silt) falling through water at $20^\circ\text{C}$ according to Stokes' Law. Given: $\rho_s = 2650\text{ kg/m}^3$, $\rho_f = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, dynamic viscosity of water $\mu = 1.002 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$.

Solution: Stokes' Law formula: $$v = \frac{(\rho_s - \rho_f) g d^2}{18 \mu}$$ Substituting values: $$v = \frac{(2650 - 1000) \times 9.81 \times (2 \times 10^{-5})^2}{18 \times (1.002 \times 10^{-3})}$$ $$v = \frac{1650 \times 9.81 \times 4 \times 10^{-10}}{1.8036 \times 10^{-2}} = \frac{6.4746 \times 10^{-6}}{1.8036 \times 10^{-2}} \approx 3.59 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} = 0.359\text{ mm/s}$$ The fine silt grain settles at approximately $0.36\text{ mm/s}$ (or $1.29\text{ m/hour}$).

Practice Problem 5

Why does Stokes' Law fail when applied to coarse sand particles ($d > 0.2\text{ mm}$) settling in water?

Solution: Stokes' Law strictly assumes pure laminar flow around the settling sphere with a Reynolds number: $$Re = \frac{\rho_f v d}{\mu} < 0.5\text{ to } 1.0$$ For particles coarser than $\sim 0.1\text{--}0.2\text{ mm}$, settling velocities are sufficiently high that flow separation occurs behind the particle, shedding turbulent vortices and creating form drag (inertial drag) that exceeds viscous skin friction. Under turbulent drag, settling velocity becomes proportional to $\sqrt{d}$ rather than $d^2$, rendering Stokes' Law invalid.

Practice Problem 6

What is a Passega C-M diagram in sedimentology and how are the parameters $C$ and $M$ obtained from granulometric analysis?

Solution: A Passega C-M diagram (Passega, 1957, 1964) is a bivariate plot used to determine the hydrodynamic mechanism of sediment deposition (graded suspension, uniform suspension, rolled traction, or pelagic settling). The parameters are: - $C$ (One-percentile grain size, $\phi_1$ in microns): Represents the coarsest fraction transported by the current, monitoring peak turbulence competence. - $M$ (Median grain size, $\phi_{50}$ in microns): Represents the average hydrodynamic energy of the depositing fluid.

Practice Problem 7

Why do beach foreshore sands characteristically exhibit negative skewness ($Sk_I < 0$), whereas river channel sands exhibit positive skewness ($Sk_I > 0$)?

Solution: - Beach Foreshore Sands ($Sk_I < 0$, Negative / Coarse-skewed): Continuous swash and backwash wave currents relentlessly winnow away fine silt and clay particles into offshore deep water, leaving a lag of coarse particles (excess coarse tail, negative phi skewness). - River Channel Sands ($Sk_I > 0$, Positive / Fine-skewed): Fluvial river currents experience periodic drops in discharge and velocity, causing fine suspension mud and silt to settle into intergranular pore spaces among bedload sand grains, adding an excess tail of fine grains (positive phi skewness).

Practice Problem 8

Explain why the Wentworth phi ($\phi$) logarithmic transformation ($\phi = -\log_2 d_{\text{mm}}$) is universally preferred over metric millimeter scales in sedimentary granulometry.

Solution: The Wentworth phi transformation provides two crucial advantages: 1. Natural Logarithmic Scaling: Natural sediments cover several orders of magnitude in diameter ($0.001\text{ mm to } 1000\text{ mm}$). Arithmetic millimeter plots severely bunch together the fine sand, silt, and clay fractions. Using a $\log_2$ scale expands these fine intervals equally. 2. Gaussian Normalization: Most natural hydrodynamic sorting processes generate grain-size distributions that follow a log-normal distribution. Transforming grain diameter to $-\log_2 d$ converts a skewed log-normal curve into a symmetrical Gaussian bell curve, enabling straightforward statistical analysis (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis).

Q101: Folk and Ward (1957) Graphic Kurtosis: Formula, Derivation & Verbal Scales

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 101
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (5th/6th Ed., Ch. 3: Grain Size, pp. 55–75; Fig. 3.4 / p. 75); Robert L. Folk and William C. Ward (1957), Brazos River Bar: A Study in the Significance of Grain Size Parameters (Journal of Sedimentary Petrology, Vol. 27, No. 1, pp. 3–26); R.L. Folk (1980), Petrology of Sedimentary Rocks (Hemphill Publishing Co.).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Folk and Ward (1957) Formulation of Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$)

In quantitative granulometry and statistical sedimentology (Folk & Ward, 1957; Boggs, 2014, p. 75), kurtosis (from the Greek $\kappa\upsilon\rho\tau\acute{o}\varsigma$, meaning "bulging" or "convex") measures the ratio between the sorting in the tails of a grain-size frequency curve and the sorting in the central body of the distribution.

To quantify departure from a standard Gaussian normal bell curve, Robert L. Folk and William C. Ward (1957, p. 13) derived the Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$) defined explicitly by the mathematical formula:

$$\mathbf{K_G = \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}}$$

where $\phi_5, \phi_{25}, \phi_{75}, \text{and } \phi_{95}$ represent the respective 5th, 25th, 75th, and 95th percentiles determined from the cumulative weight percentage frequency curve plotted on the Wentworth phi scale ($\phi = -\log_2 d_{\text{mm}}$).

Figure 101.1 — Folk and Ward (1957) Statistical Grain-Size Formulae and Kurtosis Scale: Authentic textbook table from Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 75). Contains the exact mathematical definition of Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$) and its verbal classification scale.

Mathematical Derivation of the Constant $2.44$

The denominator coefficient $2.44$ is not an empirical arbitrary number, but a rigorously derived theoretical constant:

  1. For an idealized, perfectly normal Gaussian distribution:
    • The spread of the outer $90\%$ of the distribution ($\phi_{95} - \phi_5$) encompasses exactly $3.29$ standard deviations ($2 \times 1.6449\sigma \approx 3.2897\sigma$).
    • The interquartile range ($\phi_{75} - \phi_{25}$) encompasses exactly $1.35$ standard deviations ($2 \times 0.6745\sigma \approx 1.3490\sigma$).
  2. The ratio of these two percentile spreads in a standard normal curve is: $$\frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{\phi_{75} - \phi_{25}} = \frac{3.2897\sigma}{1.3490\sigma} \approx 2.4386 \approx \mathbf{2.44}$$
  3. By dividing this ratio by $2.44$, Folk and Ward normalized the formula such that a perfectly normal Gaussian grain-size distribution yields: $$K_G = \frac{2.44}{2.44} = \mathbf{1.00}\quad (\text{Mesokurtic})$$
2. Folk and Ward Verbal Kurtosis Scale & Hydrodynamic Mixing Models

Verbal Classification Scale for Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$)

Folk and Ward (1957) and Folk (1980) established the standard verbal scale for interpreting calculated $K_G$ values:

$K_G$ Range Verbal Classification Frequency Curve Geometry Hydrodynamic / Depositional Interpretation
$< 0.67$ Very Platykurtic Flat-topped, broad, bimodal saddle Equal mixing of two distinct sub-equal grain-size populations (e.g., gravel + sand).
$0.67\text{ to } 0.90$ Platykurtic Flat, broad central peak Sub-equal mixing of two populations; tails are better sorted than the center.
$0.90\text{ to } 1.11$ Mesokurtic Standard normal bell curve ($K_G \approx 1.0$) Unimodal sediment deposited under steady, unimodal hydrodynamic conditions.
$1.11\text{ to } 1.50$ Leptokurtic Excessively peaked, narrow central body Dominant unimodal population with a minor ($5\text{--}15\%$) subordinate tail of fine or coarse grains.
$1.50\text{ to } 3.00$ Very Leptokurtic Extremely sharp, narrow central spike Central $70\text{--}80\%$ is exceptionally well-sorted, with a tiny, poorly sorted tail.
$> 3.00$ Extremely Leptokurtic Hyper-peaked; needle-like central body Extreme unimodality with minute extraneous infiltration.

Question 101: Formulae and verbal scales for graphic size parameters are provided by Folk and Ward (1957). As per the relation, inclusive graphic kurtosis is calculated by which formula ?
(A) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [2.44 (phi75 - phi25)]
(B) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [2.44 (phi75 - phi95)]
(C) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [1.44 (phi5 - phi25)]
(D) Both (A) and (B) are correct
Verified Correct Answer: (A) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [2.44 (phi75 - phi25)]
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Confirmed — Canonical Formula

Correct: By exact mathematical definition in Folk and Ward (1957, p. 13) and Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 75), the formula for Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$) is: $$K_G = \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}$$ The numerator $(\phi_{95} - \phi_5)$ measures the total spread of the distribution tails ($90\%$ of the sediment), while the denominator interquartile range $(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})$ measures the spread of the central body ($50\%$ of the sediment), scaled by the normal curve constant $2.44$.

Option (B) Refuted — Erroneous Denominator Term

Incorrect: The denominator in (B) contains the term $(\phi_{75} - \phi_{95})$. This is mathematically nonsensical: because phi percentiles increase monotonically ($\phi_5 < \phi_{25} < \phi_{75} < \phi_{95}$), subtracting a larger percentile ($\phi_{95}$) from a smaller percentile ($\phi_{75}$) yields a negative value, which would result in a negative kurtosis for all normal positive sediments. Furthermore, it completely omits the 25th percentile ($\phi_{25}$).

Option (C) Refuted — Erroneous Constant & Subtraction Order

Incorrect: Option (C) substitutes an incorrect constant ($1.44$ instead of $2.44$) and inverts the subtraction $(\phi_5 - \phi_{25})$, which also produces a negative spread. It bears no mathematical or historical validity in sedimentology.

Option (D) Refuted — Fallacious Dual Option

Incorrect: Because Option (B) is mathematically and dimensionally erroneous, Option (D) is entirely invalid. The official answer key verified by the examination authorities unambiguously affirms (A).

Parameter Name Symbol Mathematical Formula Normal Gaussian Curve Value Verbal Classification Extremes
Graphic Mean $M_z$ $$\frac{\phi_{16} + \phi_{50} + \phi_{84}}{3}$$ Equals median ($\phi_{50}$) Fine ($> 4\phi$) to Coarse ($< -1\phi$)
Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation $\sigma_I$ $$\frac{\phi_{84} - \phi_{16}}{4} + \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{6.6}$$ $1.00\sigma$ Very well sorted ($< 0.35\phi$) to Very poorly sorted ($> 2.0\phi$)

Graphic Kurtosis $K_G$ $$\frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}$$ $1.00$ Very platykurtic ($< 0.67$) to Very leptokurtic ($> 1.50$)
Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

A river sediment sample yields the following percentile values from its cumulative frequency curve: $\phi_5 = 0.50$, $\phi_{25} = 1.60$, $\phi_{75} = 2.40$, and $\phi_{95} = 3.90$. Calculate the Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$) and classify it according to Folk's verbal scale.

Solution: Applying Folk and Ward's formula: $$K_G = \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}$$ Substituting values: $$K_G = \frac{3.90 - 0.50}{2.44(2.40 - 1.60)} = \frac{3.40}{2.44 \times 0.80} = \frac{3.40}{1.952} \approx \mathbf{1.74}$$ According to Folk's verbal scale, a $K_G$ value between $1.50$ and $3.00$ is classified as Very Leptokurtic. This indicates an excessively peaked central body with an outlying tail of poorly sorted grains.

Practice Problem 2

Show mathematically why a bimodal sediment composed of $50\%$ coarse gravel ($\phi = -2$) and $50\%$ fine sand ($\phi = +3$) exhibits a Platykurtic ($K_G < 0.90$) distribution.

Solution: In an equal 50:50 bimodal mixture, the cumulative curve rises in two distinct steps separated by a flat terrace across the intermediate sizes. Consequently, the interquartile body ($\phi_{75} - \phi_{25}$) spans across the entire wide gap between the two modes, making the denominator $(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})$ abnormally large relative to the outer tails $(\phi_{95} - \phi_5)$. When divided by $2.44(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})$, the resulting $K_G$ drops well below $0.90$ (often $0.55\text{--}0.65$), producing a very platykurtic (flat-topped or saddle-shaped) frequency distribution.

Practice Problem 3

What is the transformed kurtosis metric $K'_G$ proposed by Folk and Ward, and why was it introduced?

Solution: Because $K_G$ values are severely non-normal and positively skewed (ranging from $0.40$ to infinity, with normal at $1.00$), Folk and Ward introduced the Transformed Kurtosis ($K'_G$): $$K'_G = \frac{K_G}{1 + K_G}$$ This mathematical transformation normalizes the scale into a bounded range between $0.0$ and $1.0$, where a normal Gaussian curve corresponds to: $$K'_G = \frac{1.0}{1 + 1.0} = \mathbf{0.50}$$ enabling rigorous linear regression and multivariate statistical testing.

Practice Problem 4

A coastal geologist tests a beach dune sand and finds $\phi_{95} - \phi_5 = 2.44\phi$ and $\phi_{75} - \phi_{25} = 1.00\phi$. Calculate $K_G$ and identify the distribution type.

Solution: $$K_G = \frac{2.44}{2.44 \times 1.00} = \frac{2.44}{2.44} = \mathbf{1.00}$$ A $K_G$ of exactly $1.00$ corresponds to a Mesokurtic distribution. The ratio of tail sorting to central body sorting matches that of a perfectly symmetrical, standard Gaussian normal distribution.

Practice Problem 5

Why do natural sediments that have undergone prolonged sorting by wind in desert dunes frequently exhibit Leptokurtic kurtosis ($K_G > 1.11$)?

Solution: In eolian dune environments, steady wind velocities selectively transport and concentrate a very narrow, uniform grain size in the central $70\text{--}80\%$ of the sediment (the saltation population, creating an exceptionally well-sorted central body). However, occasional wind gusts roll a few oversized coarse grains (creep population) and light breezes trap a few silt dust grains, forming extended, poorly sorted tails. This contrast—an ultra-well-sorted central mode flanked by minor poorly sorted tails—forces $K_G$ into the leptokurtic field.

Practice Problem 6

Compare the percentile coverage of the Folk & Ward (1957) kurtosis formula with the earlier Trask (1932) kurtosis index.

Solution: Parker D. Trask (1932) defined a crude geometric kurtosis based solely on quartile spreads: $K = \frac{Q_1 Q_3}{2 M}$. This formula evaluates only the middle $50\%$ of the distribution and completely ignores the critical outer $90\%$ tails. Folk and Ward's formula incorporated $\phi_5$ and $\phi_{95}$, capturing the sorting behavior of $90\%$ of the sediment volume and making it far more sensitive to hydrodynamic mixing and bi-modality.

Practice Problem 7

If a cumulative curve has $\phi_5 = 0.8$, $\phi_{25} = 1.5$, $\phi_{75} = 2.0$, and $\phi_{95} = 3.6$, calculate $K_G$ and determine whether the central body or the tails are better sorted.

Solution: $$K_G = \frac{3.6 - 0.8}{2.44(2.0 - 1.5)} = \frac{2.8}{2.44 \times 0.5} = \frac{2.8}{1.22} \approx \mathbf{2.30}$$ Because $K_G = 2.30 \gg 1.00$ (Very Leptokurtic), the central body $(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25} = 0.5\phi)$ is far better sorted than the distant tails $(\phi_{95} - \phi_5 = 2.8\phi)$.

Practice Problem 8

In a Friedman (1961, 1967) bivariate scatter plot for environmental discrimination, what two Folk & Ward parameters are plotted against each other to distinguish river sands from beach sands?

Solution: Gerald M. Friedman plotted Inclusive Graphic Skewness ($Sk_I$) against Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation (Sorting, $\sigma_I$), or Mean ($M_z$) vs. Skewness. Beach sands plot in the negative skewness ($Sk_I < 0$) and very well-sorted ($\sigma_I < 0.5\phi$) field, whereas river sands plot predominantly in the positive skewness ($Sk_I > 0$) and moderately sorted ($\sigma_I > 0.7\phi$) field.

Q102: Sandstone Classification: The Fundamental Q-F-L Triad (Quartz Sandstone, Arkose, Litharenite)

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 102
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (5th/6th Ed., Ch. 5: Sandstones, pp. 142–148; Fig. 5.9); F.J. Pettijohn, P.E. Potter, and R. Siever, Sand and Sandstone (Springer-Verlag); Robert L. Folk, Petrology of Sedimentary Rocks (Hemphill); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, pp. 70–73, 172).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Q-F-L Petrographic Framework & The Sandstone Triad

In modern sedimentary petrology (Pettijohn, 1975; Folk, 1980; Boggs, 2014, pp. 142–148), sandstones containing less than $15\%$ detrital matrix (arenites) are classified according to the relative abundance of their three primary framework grain constituents recalculated to $100\%$:

  • $\mathbf{Q}$ (Quartz): Monocrystalline and polycrystalline quartz and chert grains.
  • $\mathbf{F}$ (Feldspar): Potassium feldspar (orthoclase, microcline, sanidine) and plagioclase feldspar.
  • $\mathbf{L}$ (Lithic Fragments): Unstable rock fragments of volcanic, metamorphic, or older sedimentary origin.

This compositional ternary diagram establishes the canonical tripartite division of sandstones:

  1. Quartz Sandstone (Quartzarenite): $> 90\text{ to } 95\%$ quartz framework grains; highly mature, multicyclic cratonic or stable passive margin sheet sands.
  2. Arkose (Feldspathic Sandstone / Subarkose): $> 25\%$ feldspar framework grains (with $F > L$); typically derived from the erosion of uplifted crystalline granitic/gneissic basement blocks.
  3. Litharenite (Lithic Sandstone / Sublitharenite): $> 25\%$ lithic rock fragments (with $L > F$); derived from rapidly eroding collision orogens, volcanic arcs, or fold-and-thrust belts.
Figure 102.1 — Q-F-L Ternary Classification of Sandstones: Authentic textbook diagram from Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 145). Illustrates the three main sandstone fields: Quartz arenite, Arkose (feldspathic arenite), and Litharenite (lithic arenite), bounded by the $Q, F, \text{and } L$ poles.

Petrographic Characteristics of Arkose

The term arkose was introduced by the French geologist Alexandre Brongniart in 1826:

  • Mineralogy: Characterized by $> 25\%$ detrital feldspar (predominantly potassic K-feldspar: orthoclase and microcline, showing diagnostic cross-hatched "tartan" twinning under crossed nicols, and subordinate plagioclase), quartz, and accessory biotite, muscovite, and granite rock fragments.
  • Color: Typically pink, reddish-orange, or salmon-colored owing to the abundance of flesh-colored K-feldspars and iron-oxide coatings.
  • Grain Texture: Commonly coarse-grained to gritty, angular to sub-angular, and moderately to poorly sorted, indicating rapid erosion and short fluvial transport.
2. Tectonic Provenance & Climatic Controls on Arkose Formation

Dickinson & Suczek (1979) Tectonic Provenance Provenance

In global plate tectonic reconstructions, sandstones plot into distinct provenance regimes on Q-F-L space:

Sandstone Class Dominant Framework Pole Tectonic Provenance (Dickinson, 1985) Paleogeographic Basin Setting
Quartz Sandstone $\mathbf{Q}$ Pole ($> 95\%$) Continental Interior / Craton Stable cratonic platforms, passive continental margins, polycyclic reworking.
Arkose $\mathbf{F}$ Pole ($> 25\%, F > L$) Basement Uplift / Block Faulting Rift basins, aulacogens, fault-bounded grabens (e.g., East African Rift, New Red Sandstone).
Litharenite $\mathbf{L}$ Pole ($> 25\%, L > F$) Recycled Orogen / Magmatic Arc Foreland basins, trench-slope basins, suture zones (e.g., Siwalik Group, Molasse).

Climatic Factor: Krynine's Climatic Classification of Arkoses

Because feldspar is chemically unstable and decomposes rapidly to clay under warm, humid conditions via chemical hydrolysis ($2\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8 + 2\text{H}^+ + 9\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4 + 4\text{H}_4\text{SiO}_4 + 2\text{K}^+$), the preservation of abundant fresh feldspar requires:

  • Tectonic Control (High Relief): High topographic relief where erosion rates vastly outpace chemical weathering rates, allowing fresh feldspar to be shed mechanically regardless of climate.
  • Climatic Control (Aridity / Cold): Very dry (arid/semi-arid) or very cold (glacial/periglacial) climates where lack of liquid water or freezing temperatures shuts down chemical hydrolysis, preserving fresh feldspar.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 102: Sandstone is categorized into three main types based on their variation in composition and cementing material, they include : • Quartz Sandstone, • ___________, • Litharenite or lithic sandstone.
(A) Arkose
(B) Greywacke
(C) Molasse
(D) None of these
Verified Correct Answer: (A) Arkose
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Confirmed — Arkose (Feldspathic Arenite)

Correct: In all authoritative sedimentary petrology textbooks (Boggs, 2014, p. 142; Pettijohn, 1975; Folk, 1980; Bangar, p. 70), sandstones are divided into three fundamental compositional end-members based on framework mineralogy ($Q\text{-}F\text{-}L$ triad): Quartz Sandstone, Arkose (feldspathic sandstone), and Litharenite (lithic sandstone). Arkose completes this tripartite classification scheme.

Option (B) Refuted — Greywacke

Incorrect: A greywacke (or wacke) is distinguished fundamentally by its matrix content (containing $> 15\%$ detrital clay/silt matrix), representing a texturally immature, matrix-rich class. The triad listed in the question represents the three primary compositional arenite classes ($< 15\%$ matrix) defined by the three corners of the Q-F-L ternary diagram. Greywacke is not an apex of the framework ternary diagram.

Option (C) Refuted — Molasse

Incorrect: Molasse is not a compositional sandstone type, but a tectonic-sedimentary lithofacies or mega-facies. It refers to thick wedges of shallow-marine and non-marine (fluvial, alluvial, lacustrine) post-orogenic clastic deposits shed into a foreland basin during and after the final uplift of an orogenic mountain belt (e.g., the Alpine Molasse or Himalayan Siwaliks). Molasse contains varied lithologies (conglomerates, lithic sandstones, siltstones, shales).

Option (D) Refuted — None of These

Incorrect: Because Arkose is the precise textbook term completing the trio, Option (D) is false.

Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

Point-counting of a sandstone thin section yields the following framework grain percentages: Quartz = $55\%$, K-feldspar = $28\%$, Plagioclase = $7\%$, Metamorphic lithics = $10\%$, Detrital matrix = $4\%$. Classify this sandstone according to Pettijohn's (1975) and Folk's (1980) systems.

Solution: 1. Matrix check: Matrix is $4\% < 15\%$, so the rock is an arenite. 2. Recalculate framework grains to $100\%$: - Total $Q + F + L = 55 + (28 + 7) + 10 = 55 + 35 + 10 = 100\%$. - $Q = 55\%$, $F = 35\%$, $L = 10\%$. 3. Evaluate classification criteria: - Feldspar ($F = 35\%$) exceeds $25\%$, and $F (35\%) > L (10\%)$. - Therefore, the sandstone is classified unambiguously as an Arkose (or feldspathic arenite).

Practice Problem 2

Explain why microcline is more common than plagioclase in ancient cratonic arkoses, referencing the Goldich Weathering Series.

Solution: In S.S. Goldich's (1938) chemical weathering series, primary silicates follow the reverse order of Bowen's reaction series: $$\text{Calcic Plagioclase} > \text{Sodic Plagioclase} \gg \text{K-feldspar (Orthoclase / Microcline)} > \text{Quartz}$$ Calcic and sodic plagioclase weather significantly faster due to the weaker bonding of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Na}^+$ and higher $\text{Al/Si}$ substitution ratios. K-feldspar (especially ordered microcline) possesses a more stable framework structure and resists weathering far longer, selectively surviving prolonged diagenesis and concentrating in ancient arkoses.

Practice Problem 3

What is a "subarkose" in Folk's sandstone classification scheme, and what are its quantitative boundaries?

Solution: In Folk's (1980) classification, a subarkose is an intermediate composition plotting between quartz arenite and arkose. It is defined as an arenite ($< 15\%$ matrix) containing: - Quartz ($Q$) between $75\%$ and $95\%$. - Feldspar ($F$) greater than lithic fragments ($F > L$). - Feldspar content between $5\%$ and $25\%$. It represents a moderately mature sandstone derived from granitic terrain that has experienced moderate chemical weathering or recycling.

Practice Problem 4

How do Dickinson Q-F-L ternary plots differentiate between a "Magmatic Arc" provenance and a "Basement Uplift" provenance?

Solution: William R. Dickinson established that: - Basement Uplift (Continental Block): Plots near the $F$ pole and $Q\text{-}F$ boundary (arkosic suite), reflecting deep erosional unroofing of granitic plutons and gneisses in fault-bounded rift blocks. - Magmatic Arc: Plots near the $L$ and $F$ poles (volcaniclastic litharenites and feldspathic wackes), characterized by unstable volcanic lithic clasts, plagioclase phenocrysts, and very low quartz.

Practice Problem 5

Why do arkosic sandstones typically exhibit a distinct salmon-pink or reddish-orange macroscopic coloration in hand specimen?

Solution: The characteristic pink color arises from two independent factors: 1. Intrinsic Mineral Color: Detrital potassic feldspars (orthoclase and microcline) naturally exhibit pink to flesh-red hues due to sub-microscopic exsolution of hematite lamellae and structurally incorporated traces of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. 2. Oxidizing Diagenesis: Because arkoses commonly accumulate in well-aerated, continental fault-trough environments (alluvial fans/braided streams), diagenetic groundwater precipitates fine authigenic hematite pigment coatings on quartz and feldspar grain boundaries.

Practice Problem 6

Distinguish between "Flysch" and "Molasse" in terms of depositional environment, tectonic timing, and typical sandstone types.

Solution: - Flysch: Pre- to syn-orogenic deep-marine turbidite succession deposited in an actively subsiding trench or foredeep basin prior to main mountain uplift; sandstones are typically greywackes interbedded with dark pelagic shales. - Molasse: Post-orogenic shallow-marine to continental (fluvial, alluvial fan, lacustrine) clastic wedge deposited in a foreland basin during and after the final phase of mountain collision; sandstones are typically litharenites, arkoses, and conglomerates.

Practice Problem 7

What petrographic evidence in an arkose indicates that it was formed under conditions of rapid tectonic unroofing rather than severe climatic aridity?

Solution: If tectonic unroofing is the primary driver, the arkose will contain both fresh K-feldspars and abundant labile plagioclase along with unstable ferromagnesian minerals (biotite, hornblende), and associated mudrocks will contain illite and chlorite rather than kaolinite. If formed purely under climate control without intense tectonism, the sedimentation rate is slow, allowing plagioclase to degrade while only resistant K-feldspar survives.

Practice Problem 8

Under a polarizing microscope, how does a petrographer definitively distinguish detrital microcline from orthoclase and plagioclase?

Solution: - Microcline: Exhibits diagnostic cross-hatched (gridiron or "tartan") polysynthetic twinning resulting from combined albite and pericline twinning under crossed nicols. - Orthoclase: Typically exhibits simple Carlsbad twinning (two sub-equal halves with different extinction angles) or is untwinned. - Plagioclase: Displays parallel, multiple lamellar albite twinning (alternating dark and bright extinction stripes).

Q103: Heavy Mineral Suites: Petrographic Fingerprinting & Sedimentary Provenance Reconstructions

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 103
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (5th/6th Ed., Ch. 5: Sandstones / Provenance, pp. 165–172; Fig. 5.15); Maria A. Mange and Heinz F.W. Maurer, Heavy Minerals in Colour (Chapman & Hall); F.J. Pettijohn, P.E. Potter, and R. Siever, Sand and Sandstone; Maurice E. Tucker, Sedimentary Petrology: An Introduction to the Origin of Sedimentary Rocks.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Separation Techniques & The Provenance Paradigm

In clastic sedimentology and basin analysis (Boggs, 2014, pp. 165–172; Mange & Maurer, 1992; Pettijohn et al., 1987), heavy minerals are defined as accessory detrital mineral grains that possess a specific gravity greater than that of the standard rock-forming framework minerals (quartz $\rho \approx 2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$ and feldspars $\rho \approx 2.55\text{--}2.76\text{ g/cm}^3$).

By convention, minerals with $\text{specific gravity} > 2.85\text{ g/cm}^3$ (the density of bromoform, $\text{CHBr}_3$) or $> 2.90\text{ g/cm}^3$ (sodium polytungstate) are designated as heavy minerals. Although they typically constitute less than $1.0\%$ (often $< 0.1\%$) of a sandstone by weight, their extraordinary compositional diversity makes them the single most potent diagnostic tool for reconstructing sedimentary provenance.

Figure 103.1 — Diagnostic Heavy Mineral Suites and Source Rock Lithologies: Authentic textbook diagram from Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, p. 170). Details specific heavy mineral assemblages corresponding to acid igneous, basic/ultrabasic igneous, dynamic regional metamorphic, contact metamorphic, and recycled sedimentary provenances.

The Concept of Sedimentary Provenance

The geological term provenance (from the French provenir, meaning "to originate or come forth") is an expansive, integrated scientific concept that encompasses:

  1. Source Rock Lithology: The precise petrographic nature of the parent rocks (granite, basalt, amphibolite, schist, or older sedimentary strata).
  2. Tectonic Setting of the Source Area: Craton interior, volcanic island arc, Andean-type continental magmatic arc, or collision orogen.
  3. Paleoclimate and Weathering: The climatic regime under which the source rocks were unroofed and decomposed.
  4. Drainage Basin Geometry & Paleocurrent Pathways: The geographic dispersal routes, transport distances, and fluvial/marine mixing patterns.
2. Diagnostic Heavy Mineral Suites for Specific Source Lithologies

Petrographic Mineral Fingerprints

Source Rock Lithology Diagnostic Heavy Mineral Assemblage Diagnostic Petrographic Characteristics
Acidic Igneous (Granites & Pegmatites) Apatite, Biotite, Tourmaline (brown/pink schorl), Zircon, Monazite, Muscovite, Sphene (Titanite), Cassiterite Euhedral, prismatic, growth-zoned zircons; fluorine/boron-bearing species.
Basic & Ultrabasic Igneous (Basalts, Gabbros, Peridotites) Augite, Hypersthene, Enstatite, Olivine, Chromite, Picotite, Ilmenite, Magnetite High-temperature pyroxenes; chrome spinels; opaque Fe-Ti oxides; low ZTR index.
Low-Grade Metamorphic (Greenschist Facies) Chlorite, Chloritoid, Epidote, Zoisite, Actinolite, Green Tourmaline Flaky green phyllosilicates; pistachio-green pleochroic epidote.
High-Grade Regional Metamorphic (Amphibolite & Granulite Facies) Garnet (almandine-pyrope), Kyanite, Sillimanite, Staurolite, Andalusite, Epidote, Hornblende Diagnostic aluminosilicate polymorphs ($\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5$); golden-yellow pleochroic staurolite; bladed kyanite.
Contact Metamorphic (Thermal Aureoles) Andalusite (chiastolite), Cordierite, Vesuvianite, Wollastonite, Grossular garnet Cross-shaped carbonaceous inclusions in chiastolite; sector-twinned cordierite.
Recycled / Polycyclic Sedimentary Zircon, Tourmaline, Rutile (ZTR $> 90\%$), Rounded Leucoxene, Rounded Chert Exceptionally high roundness and sphericity; abraded overgrowths; absence of labile species.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 103: The origin of many heavy mineral species is limited to rather specific rock types ; hence, heavies provide information concerning :
(A) source rock
(B) mineral dispersion pattern
(C) quaternary sediments
(D) provenance
Verified Correct Answer: (D) provenance
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Refuted — Source Rock (Incomplete Sub-concept)

Incorrect: While heavy minerals certainly reveal the lithological nature of the parent rocks, "source rock" is merely one individual parameter within the broader geological discipline. Heavy minerals provide vastly more comprehensive data: they constrain tectonic regime, paleorelief, weathering intensity, transport distance, and drainage basin evolution. In sedimentary geology curricula and exam benchmarks (Boggs, 2014, p. 165; Pettijohn, 1975), the full, overarching scientific objective of heavy mineral study is formally designated as provenance.

Option (B) Refuted — Mineral Dispersion Pattern

Incorrect: "Mineral dispersion pattern" refers specifically to exploration geochemistry (such as secondary geochemical dispersion halos around economic ore bodies during stream-sediment prospecting). While spatial mapping of heavies can delineate dispersion, this is a localized applied technique, not the primary fundamental petrological information revealed by diagnostic heavy mineral assemblages.

Option (C) Refuted — Quaternary Sediments

Incorrect: Heavy mineral analysis applies equally to sedimentary rocks of all geological ages—from Archean quartzites and Proterozoic sandstones to Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic strata worldwide. It is not restricted to Quaternary sediments.

Option (D) Confirmed — Provenance

Correct: By fundamental definition in sedimentology (Boggs, 2014; Pettijohn et al., 1987; Mange & Maurer, 1992), because distinct heavy mineral species originate under specific thermomechanical conditions in particular parent rocks, their presence, variety, optical properties, and roundness provide diagnostic fingerprints of the sediment's provenance (source rock composition, tectonic setting, relief, climate, and transport history).
