GEO - 2/21 • Engineering Geology & Rock Mechanics

Q121: Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS): The Primary Index Property of Building Stones

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 121
Authoritative References: K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 10: Engineering Properties of Rocks, pp. 186–188); ISRM Suggested Methods for Determining Uniaxial Compressive Strength and Deformability of Rock Materials; ASTM D7012 (Standard Test Methods for Compressive Strength and Elastic Moduli of Intact Rock Core Specimens); Evert Hoek, Practical Rock Engineering (Ch. 5: Rock Mass Properties); Z.T. Bieniawski, Engineering Rock Mass Classifications (RMR System).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Mechanics & Primary Significance of Unconfined Compressive Strength

In engineering geology, rock mechanics, and civil construction, Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS)—also universally designated as Uniaxial Compressive Strength ($\sigma_c$ or $q_u$)—is universally recognized as the single most important index property of building stones and intact rock material (Bangar, p. 186; ISRM, 1979; ASTM D7012).

Physically, UCS represents the maximum axial compressive stress that a right cylindrical rock core specimen can withstand before suffering total mechanical collapse or shear/splitting rupture when subjected to unconfined uniaxial loading (i.e., under zero lateral confining stress: $\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0$).

$$\text{UCS} = \sigma_c = \frac{P_{\text{max}}}{A_0}$$ $$\text{where: } P_{\text{max}} = \text{Peak axial compressive load at failure (N or kN)}, \quad A_0 = \text{Original cross-sectional area of specimen } (\text{m}^2 \text{ or mm}^2)$$
Figure 121.1 — Unconfined Compressive Strength and Crushing Strength Testing: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 186). Explains the standard crushing test procedure, core geometry, and load application mechanics used to evaluate the primary compressive strength of building stones.

Why UCS is the Preeminent Engineering Index Property

Building stones used in heavy civil engineering structures—such as dam abutments, bridge piers, monument foundations, architectural ashlar masonry, and retaining walls—are predominantly subjected to enormous downward compressive stresses caused by gravity and structural superstructures. Intact rock exhibits distinct mechanical asymmetries:

  • Enormous Compressive vs. Weak Tensile Strength: Rocks are natural aggregates of interlocking or cemented minerals. Under compression, mineral grains are forced tightly against one another, mobilizing high frictional and cohesive resistance. In contrast, rocks are extremely weak in tension ($\sigma_t \approx \frac{1}{10} \text{ to } \frac{1}{20} \sigma_c$) and moderate in shear ($\tau \approx \frac{1}{6} \text{ to } \frac{1}{8} \sigma_c$). Because structural stones are purposefully detailed in masonry to bear compressive loads, $\sigma_c$ dictates the ultimate load-bearing capacity.
  • Universal Benchmark in Rock Mass Classification: All major empirical rock engineering rating systems use intact UCS as their fundamental baseline parameter:
    • Bieniawski's Rock Mass Rating (RMR): Up to 15 rating points (out of 100) are assigned directly based on intact rock UCS ($\sigma_c > 250\text{ MPa}$ gets max score).
    • Hoek-Brown Failure Criterion: The non-linear failure criterion for intact and jointed rock masses is formulated directly around intact UCS ($\sigma_{ci}$): $\sigma_1' = \sigma_3' + \sigma_{ci} \left(m_b \frac{\sigma_3'}{\sigma_{ci}} + s\right)^a$.
    • Deere-Miller Engineering Classification: Classifies rock into strength classes A through E based strictly on UCS and modulus ratio ($E_t / \sigma_c$).
2. Standard ISRM & ASTM Testing Protocols: Geometry, Aspect Ratio & Corrections
Figure 121.2 — Mechanical Test Configuration & Stress State: Schematic of a rock cylinder under uniaxial compression ($\sigma_1 = \sigma_c, \sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0$), showing typical shear cone failure geometry and the corresponding single Mohr circle tangent to the shear strength envelope at zero normal confinement.

ISRM / ASTM D7012 Standard Specifications

To ensure reproducible and standardized test results free from frictional platen end-effects, strict testing protocols are enforced:

  • Specimen Shape: Right circular cylinder drilled from intact core (typically $NX$ core size, diameter $D \approx 54\text{ mm}$, or minimum diameter $\ge 47\text{ mm}$ with $D$ at least 10 times the largest mineral grain diameter).
  • Aspect Ratio (Length to Diameter, $L/D$): Must be between $2.0:1$ and $2.5:1$ (typically $L/D = 2.0$). If $L/D < 2.0$, platen friction confines the core ends, artificially increasing measured strength (creating a rigid cone of confinement). If $L/D > 2.5$, Euler column buckling instabilities and lateral deflection can prematurely trigger failure.
  • End Preparation Tolerance: End bearing faces must be ground flat within $0.02\text{ mm}$ and perpendicular to the longitudinal core axis within $0.05^\circ$ ($1\text{ mm}$ per $1\text{ m}$) to avoid eccentric stress concentrations and premature point-loading fractures.
  • Loading Rate: Continuous axial loading applied smoothly at a stress rate between $0.5\text{ to } 1.0\text{ MPa/s}$, ensuring failure occurs within $2\text{ to } 15\text{ minutes}$.
$$\text{ISRM Aspect Ratio Correction: } \sigma_{c(\text{standard}, L/D=2)} = \frac{\sigma_{c(\text{measured})}}{0.778 + 0.222 \left(\frac{D}{L}\right)}$$ $$\text{ASTM / Protodyakonov Formula: } \sigma_{c(L/D=2)} = \sigma_{c(\text{measured})} \times \left(0.88 + 0.24 \frac{D}{L}\right)$$
Figure 121.3 — Engineering Mechanical Properties of Stones: Textbook sheet from K.M. Bangar (p. 187) summarizing crushing compressive strength values, transverse strength, and shear strength ranges across common rock types (Granite, Basalt, Sandstone, Limestone, Quartzite).
3. Geological Spectrum of UCS Values & ISRM Strength Classification

The unconfined compressive strength of rocks spans three orders of magnitude, ranging from $< 1\text{ MPa}$ in poorly consolidated claystones to $> 300\text{ MPa}$ in dense quartzite and dolerite:

ISRM Grade Description UCS Range ($\sigma_c$, MPa) Typical Geological Examples Field Identification Criteria
R6 Extremely Strong $> 250$ Fresh Quartzite, Dense Basalt, Dolerite, Chert Specimen can only be chipped with repeated heavy blows of geological hammer. Rings like steel.
R5 Very Strong $100 - 250$ Fresh Granite, Gabbro, Gneiss, Massive Limestone Requires many blows of geological hammer to break intact core specimen.
R4 Strong $50 - 100$ Hard Sandstone, Marble, Slate, Schist Hand specimen can be broken with a single firm blow of hammer.
R3 Medium Strong $25 - 50$ Siltstone, Porous Sandstone, Chalk, Coal Cannot be scraped or peeled with pocket knife; specimen fractures under firm hammer blow.
R2 Weak $5 - 25$ Claystone, Weathered Shale, Soft Marl Can be peeled with pocket knife with difficulty; shallow indentations made with hammer pick.
R1 / R0 Very Weak / Extremely Weak $< 5$ Heavily altered rock, stiff clay-shale, talc schist Crumbles under firm thumb pressure or easily gouged by thumbnail.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 121
Which type of compressive strength is taken as the most important index property of stones ?
  • (A) Confined
  • (B) Drained
  • (C) Undrained
  • (D) Unconfined
Correct Answer: (D) Unconfined — Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS / $\sigma_c$) is universally recognized in engineering geology and rock mechanics as the primary index property for rock classification, masonry design, and foundation bearing capacity.
Forensic Analysis of Options
Option (A): Confined Compressive Strength — Incorrect

Confined compressive strength refers to the axial compressive strength measured under a non-zero confining pressure ($\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 > 0$) inside a high-pressure triaxial Hoek cell or Karman cell. While triaxial testing is vital for deep underground tunneling, borehole stability, and tectonic modeling, it requires complex, expensive triaxial cells, high-pressure hydraulic pumps, and impervious membrane sleeving. Consequently, confined compressive strength is never used as a routine, rapid index property for classifying building stones in standard engineering practice (IS: 9143; Bangar, p. 186).

Option (B): Drained Compressive Strength — Incorrect

"Drained" strength is a specific test condition taken from geotechnical soil mechanics and porous weak rock testing (such as saturated clay-shale or porous sandstone). In a drained test, pore-water is allowed to escape freely under slow loading rates so that excess pore-water pressure ($\Delta u$) dissipates to zero ($u = 0, \sigma' = \sigma$). In hard, crystalline building stones (granite, basalt, quartzite), permeability is virtually negligible and tests are conducted in ambient dry or naturally moist conditions without pore-pressure drainage control. It is a soil mechanics behavioral state, not an index property of stones.

Option (C): Undrained Compressive Strength — Incorrect

"Undrained" compressive strength ($S_u$ or $c_u$) is another classical soil mechanics parameter, defined for saturated cohesive soils (clays, silts) loaded so rapidly that pore-water cannot escape ($\Delta u \ne 0$). Undrained shear/compressive strength is fundamental for short-term slope and foundation stability in clays, but has no direct application as a fundamental index property for structural building stones.

Option (D): Unconfined Compressive Strength — Fully Verified & Correct

Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS, $\sigma_c$) is determined by applying a uniaxial compressive load to an unjacketed cylinder without any lateral support until failure ($\sigma_3 = 0$). It is universally designated as the most important index property of building stones because:

  1. It directly reflects the stone's capacity to support superincumbent vertical structural loads in masonry pillars, foundations, dam basements, and bridge piers.
  2. It is straightforward, highly standardized (ISRM, ASTM D7012, IS: 9143), and readily reproducible in any basic rock mechanics laboratory.
  3. It serves as the core input parameter for every major engineering classification system (RMR, Q-system, GSI, Hoek-Brown criterion).

8 Advanced Practice Problems & Fully Worked Solutions
Problem 1: Standard UCS Calculation from Peak Failure Load
A standard cylindrical core of fresh charnockite with diameter $D = 54\text{ mm}$ and length $L = 108\text{ mm}$ is tested in uniaxial compression. The peak load recorded by the digital load cell at failure is $412.4\text{ kN}$. Calculate the unconfined compressive strength ($\sigma_c$) in $\text{MPa}$ and classify the rock according to ISRM standards.
Solution:
1. Calculate the cross-sectional area $A_0$: $$A_0 = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 = \frac{\pi}{4} (0.054\text{ m})^2 = 2.2902 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2 = 2290.2\text{ mm}^2$$ 2. Compute the unconfined compressive strength $\sigma_c$: $$\sigma_c = \frac{P_{\text{max}}}{A_0} = \frac{412.4 \times 10^3\text{ N}}{2290.2\text{ mm}^2} = 180.07\text{ N/mm}^2 = 180.1\text{ MPa}$$ 3. Classification: According to ISRM strength grades ($100 - 250\text{ MPa}$), this charnockite belongs to Grade R5: Very Strong Rock.
Problem 2: Aspect Ratio (L/D) Correction
Due to core discing, a sandstone core could only be prepared with diameter $D = 50\text{ mm}$ and length $L = 60\text{ mm}$ (aspect ratio $L/D = 1.20$). When crushed, it sustained a peak load of $157.1\text{ kN}$. Determine: (a) the measured unconfined strength, and (b) the corrected standard UCS ($\sigma_{c(\text{standard})}$ at $L/D = 2.0$) using the ISRM conversion formula.
Solution:
1. Measured strength $\sigma_{c(\text{meas})}$: $$A = \frac{\pi}{4} (50\text{ mm})^2 = 1963.5\text{ mm}^2$$ $$\sigma_{c(\text{meas})} = \frac{157.1 \times 10^3\text{ N}}{1963.5\text{ mm}^2} = 80.01\text{ MPa}$$ 2. Apply ISRM aspect ratio correction formula: $$\sigma_{c(\text{standard})} = \frac{\sigma_{c(\text{meas})}}{0.778 + 0.222 \left(\frac{D}{L}\right)}$$ Here $D/L = 50 / 60 = 0.8333$: $$\text{Denominator} = 0.778 + 0.222 (0.8333) = 0.778 + 0.1850 = 0.9630$$ $$\sigma_{c(\text{standard})} = \frac{80.01}{0.9630} = 83.08\text{ MPa}$$ Notice: Because platen end-confinement artificially increases apparent strength for stubby specimens, standard conversion normalizes the value to the unconfined state.
Problem 3: Indirect UCS Estimation from Point Load Index
A diametral point load test is performed on an $NX$ core of granite ($D = 54\text{ mm}$). The failure load is $P = 18.5\text{ kN}$. Calculate: (a) the uncorrected point load strength $I_s$, (b) the size-corrected point load index $I_{s(50)}$, and (c) the estimated UCS ($\sigma_c$) using the standard Bieniawski correlation factor ($C = 24$).
Solution:
1. Equivalent core diameter $D_e^2 = D^2 = 54^2 = 2916\text{ mm}^2$: $$I_s = \frac{P}{D_e^2} = \frac{18.5 \times 10^3\text{ N}}{2916\text{ mm}^2} = 6.344\text{ MPa}$$ 2. Size correction factor $F = (D_e / 50)^{0.45} = (54 / 50)^{0.45} = (1.08)^{0.45} = 1.0353$: $$I_{s(50)} = F \times I_s = 1.0353 \times 6.344 = 6.568\text{ MPa}$$ 3. Estimated UCS via empirical correlation ($\sigma_c = 24 \times I_{s(50)}$): $$\sigma_c = 24 \times 6.568\text{ MPa} = 157.63\text{ MPa}$$
Problem 4: Masonry Column Allowable Working Stress & Factor of Safety
A monumental ashlar masonry pillar of cross-section $1.2\text{ m} \times 1.2\text{ m}$ is constructed using granite blocks having a laboratory UCS of $\sigma_c = 140\text{ MPa}$. If the building code mandates a safety factor of $\text{FoS} = 15$ against crushing failure (accounting for mortar joints and scale effects), determine: (a) the allowable working compressive stress, and (b) the maximum permissible axial vertical load the pillar can support.
Solution:
1. Allowable working compressive stress $\sigma_{\text{allow}}$: $$\sigma_{\text{allow}} = \frac{\sigma_c}{\text{FoS}} = \frac{140\text{ MPa}}{15} = 9.333\text{ MPa} = 9.333 \times 10^6\text{ N/m}^2$$ 2. Cross-sectional area of pillar: $$A = 1.2\text{ m} \times 1.2\text{ m} = 1.44\text{ m}^2$$ 3. Maximum permissible vertical axial load $P_{\text{perm}}$: $$P_{\text{perm}} = \sigma_{\text{allow}} \times A = (9.333 \times 10^6\text{ N/m}^2) \times 1.44\text{ m}^2 = 1.344 \times 10^7\text{ N} = 13.44\text{ MN} \approx 13,440\text{ kN}$$
Problem 5: Hoek-Brown Failure Envelope for Intact Rock
An intact limestone specimen has an unconfined compressive strength $\sigma_{ci} = 90\text{ MPa}$ and Hoek-Brown intact constant $m_i = 10$. In a triaxial test with a cell confining pressure $\sigma_3 = 15\text{ MPa}$, predict the major principal stress at failure ($\sigma_1$) using the Hoek-Brown intact equation: $\sigma_1 = \sigma_3 + \sigma_{ci} \sqrt{m_i \frac{\sigma_3}{\sigma_{ci}} + 1}$.
Solution:
1. Substitute parameters into the Hoek-Brown intact criterion ($s = 1, a = 0.5$): $$\frac{\sigma_3}{\sigma_{ci}} = \frac{15}{90} = 0.1667$$ 2. Compute the square root term: $$\sqrt{m_i \left(\frac{\sigma_3}{\sigma_{ci}}\right) + 1} = \sqrt{10(0.1667) + 1} = \sqrt{1.6667 + 1} = \sqrt{2.6667} = 1.6330$$ 3. Compute $\sigma_1$: $$\sigma_1 = 15 + 90 \times (1.6330) = 15 + 146.97 = 161.97\text{ MPa}$$ Interpretation: The application of only $15\text{ MPa}$ confining stress increases the rock's compressive capacity from $90\text{ MPa}$ to $162\text{ MPa}$ (an 80% strength increase).
Problem 6: Mohr-Coulomb Cohesion and Friction Angle from UCS and Tensile Strength
Assuming linear Mohr-Coulomb failure for an intact basalt rock with $\sigma_c = 120\text{ MPa}$ and tensile strength $\sigma_t = 10\text{ MPa}$, derive the internal friction angle $\phi$ and cohesion $c$ assuming $\sigma_c = 2 c \frac{\cos\phi}{1 - \sin\phi}$ and $\sigma_t = 2 c \frac{\cos\phi}{1 + \sin\phi}$.
Solution:
1. Take the ratio of compressive to tensile strength: $$\frac{\sigma_c}{\sigma_t} = \frac{1 + \sin\phi}{1 - \sin\phi} = \frac{120}{10} = 12$$ 2. Solve for $\sin\phi$: $$1 + \sin\phi = 12 (1 - \sin\phi) \implies 13 \sin\phi = 11 \implies \sin\phi = \frac{11}{13} \approx 0.84615$$ $$\phi = \arcsin(0.84615) \approx 57.8^\circ$$ 3. Calculate cohesion $c$: $$\cos\phi = \sqrt{1 - 0.84615^2} = \sqrt{1 - 0.7160} = \sqrt{0.2840} \approx 0.5329$$ $$\sigma_c = 2 c \frac{\cos\phi}{1 - \sin\phi} \implies 120 = 2 c \frac{0.5329}{1 - 0.84615} = 2 c \frac{0.5329}{0.15385} = 2 c (3.4638) = 6.9276 c$$ $$c = \frac{120}{6.9276} \approx 17.32\text{ MPa}$$
Problem 7: Scale Effect on UCS (Weibull Size Effect Equation)
A standard laboratory core of diameter $d_1 = 50\text{ mm}$ yields a mean UCS of $\sigma_{c1} = 100\text{ MPa}$. Using the empirical Hoek-Brown / Bieniawski size-effect equation: $$\sigma_c(d) = \sigma_{c(50)} \left(\frac{50}{d}\right)^{0.18}$$ Estimate the expected unconfined compressive strength of a large in-situ rock column of diameter $d = 500\text{ mm}$.
Solution:
1. Compute the diameter ratio: $$\frac{50}{d} = \frac{50}{500} = 0.10$$ 2. Apply the exponent: $$(0.10)^{0.18} = 10^{-0.18} \approx 0.6607$$ 3. Calculate the scaled compressive strength: $$\sigma_c(500) = 100\text{ MPa} \times 0.6607 = 66.07\text{ MPa}$$ Geological Insight: Larger rock volumes contain higher statistical probabilities of microcracks, grain boundary flaws, and veinlets, reducing the effective intact strength by ~34%.
Problem 8: Moisture Degradation Index on Compressive Strength
A limestone sample is tested in oven-dry conditions and gives an unconfined compressive strength $\sigma_{c(\text{dry})} = 110\text{ MPa}$. After 48 hours of full water saturation, another identical specimen tests at $\sigma_{c(\text{sat})} = 71.5\text{ MPa}$. Calculate: (a) the percentage reduction in strength due to water saturation, and (b) the rock's "Softening Coefficient" ($K_s = \sigma_{c(\text{sat})} / \sigma_{c(\text{dry})}$).
Solution:
1. Softening Coefficient ($K_s$): $$K_s = \frac{\sigma_{c(\text{sat})}}{\sigma_{c(\text{dry})}} = \frac{71.5}{110} = 0.65$$ 2. Percentage strength reduction: $$\Delta \sigma_c (\%) = \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{c(\text{sat})}}{\sigma_{c(\text{dry})}}\right) \times 100\% = (1 - 0.65) \times 100\% = 35.0\%$$ Civil Engineering Note: In engineering practice, rocks with $K_s < 0.75$ are considered water-sensitive and unsuitable for hydraulic structures (dams, breakwaters, bridge piers) without specialized waterproofing or grouting.

GEO - 2/21 • Engineering Geology & Rock Mechanics

Q122: Transverse Strength (Modulus of Rupture): Capacity of Building Stones to Withstand Bending Loads

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 122
Authoritative References: K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 10: Engineering Properties of Rocks, pp. 186–188); Bureau of Indian Standards (IS: 9143-1979: Method for Determination of Permissible Stress in Stone Masonry); ASTM C99 (Standard Test Method for Modulus of Rupture of Dimension Stone); ASTM C880 (Standard Test Method for Flexural Strength of Dimension Stone); Timoshenko & Gere, Mechanics of Materials.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Mechanics & Terminology of Transverse Strength

In engineering geology, structural stone design, and rock mechanics, the capacity of a stone beam or slab to withstand bending / flexural loads without rupture is formally designated as its Transverse Strength (Bangar, p. 187; IS: 9143; ASTM C99). In structural mechanics, it is widely referred to as the Modulus of Rupture ($R$ or $\sigma_b$) or Flexural Strength.

When a prismatic stone block is supported at its ends and subjected to a transverse load acting perpendicular to its longitudinal axis, it experiences internal bending moments. The stone acts as a structural beam, generating a coupled stress state:

  • Upper Fibers: Subjected to longitudinal compressive stress.
  • Neutral Axis: Experiences zero bending normal stress.
  • Lower Fibers: Subjected to maximum longitudinal tensile stress ($\sigma_t$).
Figure 122.1 — Three-Point Bending Test Configuration & Stress Distribution: Prismatic stone beam of length $L$, breadth $b$, and depth $d$ under central concentrated load $W$. Illustrates the triangular bending stress distribution: maximum compression at the top surface, zero stress at the neutral axis, and maximum tension at the bottom surface triggering tensile fracture.

Why Transverse Failure is Governed by Tensile Weakness

Intact rocks are exceptionally strong in compression but inherently flawed and weak in tension ($\sigma_t \approx \frac{1}{10} \text{ to } \frac{1}{20} \sigma_c$). Consequently, when a stone beam is bent, failure is never caused by compressive crushing of the top surface; instead, failure initiates suddenly and catastrophically by tensile fracture of the outermost bottom fibers where tensile stress exceeds the tensile strength of the rock material.

Figure 122.2 — Transverse Strength and Modulus of Rupture: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 187). Explains the definition: "The capacity of a stone to withstand bending loads is termed as its transverse strength." Details the three-point loading formula and testing protocol for stone lintels and slabs.
2. Mathematical Formulation: Derivation of the Modulus of Rupture Formula

Derivation from Classical Beam Flexure Theory

According to the Navier-Bernoulli Euler beam bending equation:

$$\frac{M}{I} = \frac{\sigma}{y} = \frac{E}{\rho}$$ $$\implies \sigma = \frac{M y}{I}$$

Consider a prismatic rectangular stone bar of span length $L$ between knife-edge supports, width (breadth) $b$, and depth (thickness) $d$, loaded centrally with a single concentrated load $W$:

  1. Maximum Bending Moment ($M_{\text{max}}$): For a simply supported beam with a central point load $W$: $$M_{\text{max}} = \frac{W L}{4}$$
  2. Section Modulus ($Z$): The moment of inertia of a rectangular cross-section about the neutral axis is $I = \frac{b d^3}{12}$, and the distance to the outermost fiber is $y_{\text{max}} = \frac{d}{2}$: $$Z = \frac{I}{y_{\text{max}}} = \frac{\frac{b d^3}{12}}{\frac{d}{2}} = \frac{b d^2}{6}$$
  3. Modulus of Rupture / Transverse Strength ($R$): $$R = \frac{M_{\text{max}}}{Z} = \frac{\frac{W L}{4}}{\frac{b d^2}{6}} = \frac{3 W L}{2 b d^2}$$
Figure 122.3 — Engineering Mechanical Properties Table: Textbook sheet from K.M. Bangar (p. 187) displaying comparative values of crushing compressive strength, transverse strength, and shear strength for standard Indian building stones.

Standard Testing Specifications (IS: 9143 & ASTM C99)

  • IS: 9143 Protocol: Test specimens are prepared as rectangular prisms of dimensions $200\text{ mm} \times 50\text{ mm} \times 50\text{ mm}$ supported over a span of $L = 150\text{ mm}$ on rounded steel rollers. Load is applied at the center until fracture occurs.
  • ASTM C99 (Three-Point Loading): Specimen size $100\text{ mm} \times 200\text{ mm} \times 57\text{ mm}$ over a span of $178\text{ mm}$.
  • ASTM C880 (Four-Point / Third-Point Loading): Two equal loads applied at one-third points of the span ($L/3$), producing a pure bending moment with zero shear stress across the middle third.
3. Civil Engineering Applications & Structural Significance

Evaluating the transverse strength of stones is crucial whenever structural elements are subjected to flexure or lateral bending rather than direct coaxial compression:

  • Stone Lintels & Beams: Stone blocks bridging doorway and window openings in load-bearing masonry walls act as simply supported beams carrying the dead weight of masonry above. If the stone lacks adequate transverse strength, tensile cracking develops at the lower center face, causing sudden collapse.
  • Pavement Slabs & Flagstones: Paving stones, platform flooring, and pedestrian walkways supported on uneven sub-bases experience heavy wheel or point loads that induce intense flexural stresses. Sandstone and slate flags require high transverse strength.
  • Roof Slates & Cantilevered Corbels: Thin roofing slates spanning battens and cantilevered balcony corbels projecting from historical stone buildings rely entirely on transverse strength to prevent shear-bending snap.
  • Underground Mine Roof Strata: In underground coal and metal mines, immediate roof beds spanning between pillars or roadway supports behave as clamped or simply supported rock beams under gravity and overburden pressure. Flexural tensile failure triggers massive roof falls.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 122
Capacity of a stone to withstand bending loads is termed as :
  • (A) Bending strength
  • (B) Shear strength
  • (C) Transverse strength
  • (D) Lateral strength
Correct Answer: (C) Transverse strength — In engineering geology, Indian Standard specifications (IS: 9143), and standard textbooks (Bangar, p. 187), the capacity of a stone to resist bending loads is formally designated as Transverse Strength (Modulus of Rupture).
Forensic Analysis of Options
Option (A): Bending strength — Partially Descriptive but Non-Standard Terminology

While "bending strength" is a descriptive vernacular phrase describing the physical phenomenon of flexure, it is not the formal engineering term codified in engineering geology textbooks (Bangar, p. 187) or standard Indian testing codes (IS: 9143). Standard specifications explicitly designate this index property as Transverse Strength (or Modulus of Rupture). In professional geotechnical exams, standard codified nomenclature takes strict precedence over colloquial synonyms.

Option (B): Shear strength — Incorrect Mechanics

Shear strength is the capacity of a rock or soil to resist sliding and shear failure along an internal rupture plane under shear stresses ($\tau$). It is governed by the Mohr-Coulomb criterion: $\tau_f = c + \sigma_n \tan\phi$, where $c$ is cohesion and $\phi$ is angle of internal friction. Shear strength measures resistance against parallel shearing forces, not flexural bending moments.

Option (C): Transverse strength — Fully Verified & Correct

Transverse strength is the textbook engineering definition (Bangar, p. 187, Section 10.3): "The capacity of a stone to withstand bending loads is termed as its transverse strength." It is measured by applying a transverse load perpendicular to the axis of a beam supported at both ends until tensile rupture occurs in the outermost fibers ($R = \frac{3 W L}{2 b d^2}$).

Option (D): Lateral strength — Incorrect Concept

"Lateral strength" refers to the resistance of a vertical structural element (such as a retaining wall, foundation pile, or masonry pier) against horizontal/lateral loads (e.g., wind pressure, seismic inertia, or lateral earth pressure). It has no relation to the flexural capacity of a stone specimen under beam bending.

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Comparative Matrix: Strength Properties of Common Indian Building Stones
Stone Type Crushing Strength (UCS, MPa) Transverse Strength ($R$, MPa) Tensile Strength ($\sigma_t$, MPa) Ratio ($R / \text{UCS}$) Structural Suitability
Granite $100 - 250$ $12 - 25$ $7 - 15$ $\approx 0.10$ Heavy pillars, monumental lintels, high-load pier caps.
Basalt $150 - 300$ $15 - 30$ $8 - 18$ $\approx 0.10$ Pavement blocks, foundation rubble, road ballast.
Sandstone (Quartzose) $40 - 100$ $6 - 15$ $3 - 8$ $\approx 0.15$ Architectural lintels, ashlar masonry, flooring flags.
Limestone (Dense) $50 - 120$ $7 - 16$ $4 - 9$ $\approx 0.13$ Window sills, flooring slabs, masonry facings.
Quartzite $150 - 300$ $15 - 28$ $10 - 20$ $\approx 0.10$ Extremely durable aggregate, high-wear paving, retaining walls.

8 Advanced Practice Problems & Fully Worked Solutions
Problem 1: Transverse Strength (Modulus of Rupture) Calculation
In an IS: 9143 standard transverse strength test, a sandstone prism of width $b = 50\text{ mm}$ and depth $d = 50\text{ mm}$ is placed on knife-edge supports spaced $L = 150\text{ mm}$ apart. A central transverse load is applied until the specimen fractures at $W = 6.25\text{ kN}$. Calculate the transverse strength (Modulus of Rupture, $R$) in $\text{MPa}$.
Solution:
1. Apply the 3-point bending formula: $$R = \frac{3 W L}{2 b d^2}$$ 2. Substitute given values ($W = 6250\text{ N}, L = 150\text{ mm}, b = 50\text{ mm}, d = 50\text{ mm}$): $$R = \frac{3 \times 6250 \times 150}{2 \times 50 \times (50)^2} = \frac{2,812,500}{2 \times 50 \times 2500} = \frac{2,812,500}{250,000} = 11.25\text{ N/mm}^2 = 11.25\text{ MPa}$$
Problem 2: Stone Lintel Safe Load Capacity
A granite lintel is used to span an open doorway of clear span $L = 1.8\text{ m}$. The lintel has width $b = 250\text{ mm}$ and depth $d = 200\text{ mm}$. If the transverse strength of the granite is $R = 15\text{ MPa}$ and a safety factor of $\text{FoS} = 5.0$ is required, calculate the maximum safe central point load $W_{\text{safe}}$ that can be placed on the lintel (neglecting lintel self-weight).
Solution:
1. Allowable bending stress $\sigma_{\text{allow}}$: $$\sigma_{\text{allow}} = \frac{R}{\text{FoS}} = \frac{15\text{ MPa}}{5.0} = 3.0\text{ MPa} = 3.0\text{ N/mm}^2$$ 2. Section modulus $Z$: $$Z = \frac{b d^2}{6} = \frac{250 \times (200)^2}{6} = \frac{250 \times 40,000}{6} = \frac{10,000,000}{6} = 1,666,667\text{ mm}^3$$ 3. Maximum allowable bending moment $M_{\text{allow}}$: $$M_{\text{allow}} = \sigma_{\text{allow}} \times Z = 3.0\text{ N/mm}^2 \times 1,666,667\text{ mm}^3 = 5,000,000\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm} = 5.0\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}$$ 4. For a simply supported central point load, $M_{\text{max}} = \frac{W L}{4}$: $$\frac{W_{\text{safe}} \times 1.8\text{ m}}{4} = 5.0\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m} \implies W_{\text{safe}} = \frac{4 \times 5.0}{1.8} = \frac{20.0}{1.8} = 11.11\text{ kN}$$
Problem 3: Minimum Lintel Depth Calculation
A sandstone lintel must span a window opening of span $L = 2.0\text{ m}$ and support a total uniformly distributed load (UDL) of $w = 8\text{ kN/m}$. The lintel width is fixed at $b = 300\text{ mm}$. If the allowable flexural tensile stress of the sandstone is $\sigma_{\text{allow}} = 2.5\text{ MPa}$, calculate the minimum required depth $d$ of the lintel.
Solution:
1. Maximum bending moment for a simply supported beam with UDL: $$M_{\text{max}} = \frac{w L^2}{8} = \frac{8\text{ kN/m} \times (2.0\text{ m})^2}{8} = \frac{32}{8} = 4.0\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m} = 4.0 \times 10^6\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}$$ 2. Equate to flexural capacity: $$\sigma_{\text{allow}} = \frac{M_{\text{max}}}{Z} \implies Z_{\text{req}} = \frac{M_{\text{max}}}{\sigma_{\text{allow}}} = \frac{4.0 \times 10^6\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}}{2.5\text{ N/mm}^2} = 1.6 \times 10^6\text{ mm}^3$$ 3. Solve for required depth $d$ ($Z = \frac{b d^2}{6}$): $$\frac{300 \times d^2}{6} = 1.6 \times 10^6 \implies 50 d^2 = 1,600,000 \implies d^2 = 32,000$$ $$d = \sqrt{32,000} \approx 178.89\text{ mm} \approx 180\text{ mm}$$
Problem 4: Three-Point vs. Four-Point (Third-Point) Bending Comparison
A basalt prism of dimensions $60\text{ mm} \times 60\text{ mm} \times 300\text{ mm}$ is tested over span $L = 240\text{ mm}$. Under three-point loading, a center load of $W_3 = 9.0\text{ kN}$ produces failure. Under four-point loading (loads applied at third points, $L/3 = 80\text{ mm}$ from each support), the total load at failure is $W_4 = 11.25\text{ kN}$. Compare the calculated Modulus of Rupture for both configurations.
Solution:
1. Three-point loading Modulus of Rupture ($R_3$): $$R_3 = \frac{3 W_3 L}{2 b d^2} = \frac{3 \times 9000 \times 240}{2 \times 60 \times (60)^2} = \frac{6,480,000}{432,000} = 15.0\text{ MPa}$$ 2. Four-point loading Modulus of Rupture ($R_4$): For third-point loading with two loads $W_4 / 2$ at distance $a = L/3$, $M_{\text{max}} = \frac{W_4}{2} \times \frac{L}{3} = \frac{W_4 L}{6}$: $$R_4 = \frac{M_{\text{max}}}{Z} = \frac{\frac{W_4 L}{6}}{\frac{b d^2}{6}} = \frac{W_4 L}{b d^2}$$ Substitute values: $$R_4 = \frac{11,250 \times 240}{60 \times (60)^2} = \frac{2,700,000}{216,000} = 12.5\text{ MPa}$$ Insight: Four-point testing stresses the entire middle third volume, encountering a higher probability of critical flaws, and thus yields a slightly lower, more conservative strength ($12.5\text{ MPa}$ vs $15.0\text{ MPa}$).
Problem 5: Flagstone Paving Breaking Under Wheel Point Load
A pedestrian plaza is paved with square sandstone flagstones of size $600\text{ mm} \times 600\text{ mm}$ and thickness $t = 40\text{ mm}$. During maintenance, a utility vehicle wheel delivers a concentrated wheel load of $P = 3.5\text{ kN}$ at the center of a flagstone that is bridge-supported on two edge sleepers spaced $L = 500\text{ mm}$ apart. If the transverse strength of the sandstone is $R = 8.0\text{ MPa}$, determine whether the flagstone will crack.
Solution:
1. Effective beam width $b = 600\text{ mm}$, thickness $d = 40\text{ mm}$, span $L = 500\text{ mm}$: $$Z = \frac{b d^2}{6} = \frac{600 \times (40)^2}{6} = \frac{600 \times 1600}{6} = 160,000\text{ mm}^3$$ 2. Bending moment under wheel load: $$M_{\text{max}} = \frac{P L}{4} = \frac{3500\text{ N} \times 500\text{ mm}}{4} = 437,500\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}$$ 3. Induced tensile bending stress $\sigma_b$: $$\sigma_b = \frac{M_{\text{max}}}{Z} = \frac{437,500}{160,000} = 2.734\text{ MPa}$$ 4. Check against transverse strength: $$\text{Since } \sigma_b = 2.734\text{ MPa} < R = 8.0\text{ MPa}, \quad \text{Factor of Safety } = \frac{8.0}{2.734} = 2.93$$ The flagstone will safely support the wheel load without cracking.
Problem 6: Mine Roof Strata Bending as Clamped Rock Beam
An immediate sandstone roof stratum of thickness $h = 0.8\text{ m}$ spans across a mine roadway of width $B = 4.5\text{ m}$. The rock unit weight is $\gamma = 25\text{ kN/m}^3$. Assuming the roof stratum behaves as a fixed-ended (clamped) beam bending under its own self-weight ($w = \gamma \times h \times 1.0\text{ m}$ per unit advance), calculate: (a) the maximum bending moment at the supports, and (b) the maximum tensile stress induced.
Solution:
1. Self-weight per unit length of $1\text{ m}$ wide strip: $$w = \gamma \times h \times 1.0 = 25\text{ kN/m}^3 \times 0.8\text{ m} \times 1.0\text{ m} = 20\text{ kN/m} = 20\text{ N/mm}$$ 2. Maximum bending moment for a fixed-ended beam occurs at the abutments: $$M_{\text{abutment}} = \frac{w B^2}{12} = \frac{20\text{ kN/m} \times (4.5\text{ m})^2}{12} = \frac{20 \times 20.25}{12} = 33.75\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m} = 33.75 \times 10^6\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}$$ 3. Section modulus of $1\text{ m}$ ($1000\text{ mm}$) wide beam of depth $h = 800\text{ mm}$: $$Z = \frac{b h^2}{6} = \frac{1000 \times (800)^2}{6} = \frac{6.4 \times 10^8}{6} = 1.0667 \times 10^8\text{ mm}^3$$ 4. Maximum tensile stress $\sigma_t$: $$\sigma_t = \frac{M}{Z} = \frac{33.75 \times 10^6\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm}}{1.0667 \times 10^8\text{ mm}^3} = 0.316\text{ MPa}$$ Mining Note: If horizontal tectonic stresses or delamination occurs, tensile bending stress can easily exceed the weak tensile strength of bedding planes ($< 0.5\text{ MPa}$), causing bed separation and roof collapse.
Problem 7: Anisotropy Effect on Transverse Strength in Slate
A metamorphic slate specimen is tested for transverse strength in two orientations: (1) with cleavage planes oriented parallel to the beam length and perpendicular to load (maximum flexural resistance), and (2) with cleavage planes oriented parallel to the load direction. If the measured transverse strength in orientation (1) is $R_1 = 36\text{ MPa}$ and in orientation (2) is $R_2 = 12\text{ MPa}$, calculate the "Anisotropy Ratio of Transverse Strength" ($I_A$) and explain the geological cause.
Solution:
1. Calculate Anisotropy Ratio: $$I_A = \frac{R_{\text{max}}}{R_{\text{min}}} = \frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{36\text{ MPa}}{12\text{ MPa}} = 3.0$$ 2. Geological Cause: Slate possesses strong planar preferred orientation of sheet silicates (muscovite, illite, chlorite). In orientation (2), the tensile stresses acting perpendicular to cleavage readily split the weakly bonded silicate sheets apart, resulting in a three-fold drop in flexural resistance.
Problem 8: Relationship between Modulus of Rupture and Direct Tensile Strength
Laboratory tests on an intact limestone show a direct uniaxial tensile strength (via pull-test) of $\sigma_t = 6.0\text{ MPa}$. When tested under three-point bending, the measured Modulus of Rupture is $R = 10.8\text{ MPa}$. (a) Calculate the ratio $R / \sigma_t$. (b) Explain the two primary mechanical reasons why the Modulus of Rupture is consistently higher than direct uniaxial tensile strength in brittle rocks.
Solution:
1. Ratio: $$\frac{R}{\sigma_t} = \frac{10.8}{6.0} = 1.80$$ 2. Mechanical Reasons:
  • Stress Gradient Effect: In a direct tensile test, the entire cross-section of the specimen is under uniform maximum tensile stress, so failure is initiated by the single worst microscopic flaw in the entire volume. In bending, only a minute skin of rock at the extreme outermost bottom fiber reaches maximum tension, dramatically reducing the statistical probability of a critical flaw coinciding with peak stress.
  • Non-Linear Inelastic Stress Distribution: Classical beam theory assumes linear elastic stress-strain behavior up to rupture. In reality, rock exhibits microcracking and stress-redistribution (plasticity/yielding) near failure at the outer fibers, shifting the neutral axis and making the true maximum fiber stress lower than that calculated by elastic formulas ($R = 1.5 - 2.0 \times \sigma_t$).

Q123: Phase Relations: Void Ratio vs. Porosity in Rock Mechanics and Geotechnics

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 123
Authoritative References: K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 10: Engineering Properties of Rocks, pp. 186–188); Karl Terzaghi, Ralph B. Peck, and Gholamreza Mesri, Soil Mechanics in Engineering Practice (3rd Ed., Ch. 1); ISRM Suggested Methods for Determining Water Content, Porosity, Density and Related Properties (1979); ASTM D7263.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Three-Phase Physical System & Fundamental Volumetric Definitions

In engineering geology, soil mechanics, and rock physics, geological materials (rocks and soils) are idealized as a multi-phase physical system consisting of solid mineral grains and pore spaces (voids). The pore spaces may be partially or completely filled with pore-water and air/gas.

Figure 123.1 — Three-Phase Volumetric Diagram: Representation of a unit element of rock mass divided into solid mineral framework ($V_s$), pore water ($V_w$), and air/gas ($V_a$). Illustrates the critical boundary difference: Void ratio ($e$) is normalized against the solid volume ($V_s$), whereas Porosity ($n$) is normalized against the total composite volume ($V$).

Rigorous Mathematical Definitions

Let the total volume of a rock specimen be $V$, which consists of the volume of solid rock mass / mineral skeleton ($V_s$) and the volume of voids / pore spaces ($V_v$):

$$V = V_s + V_v = V_s + V_w + V_a$$
Figure 123.2 — Porosity and Void Ratio Formulations: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 187). Highlighting the unambiguous distinction: "The ratio of the total volume of pore spaces to the total volume of the solid rock mass is termed as void ratio ($e$)."
  • Void Ratio ($e$): The ratio of the total volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) to the volume of the solid rock mass / mineral skeleton ($V_s$):
    $$e = \frac{V_v}{V_s}$$
    Key Physical Feature: Because $V_s$ is in the denominator, the void ratio is a true dimensionless ratio (not a percentage). It can theoretically exceed $1.0$ (e.g., $e > 1.0$ to $4.0$ in pumice, volcanic tuff, diatomite, and soft bentonitic clay).
  • Porosity ($n$): The ratio of the total volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) to the total bulk volume of the rock specimen ($V$):
    $$n = \frac{V_v}{V} = \frac{V_v}{V_s + V_v}$$
    Key Physical Feature: Usually expressed as a fraction or percentage ($n \times 100\%$). Because the total volume $V$ is strictly greater than the pore volume ($V > V_v$), porosity must strictly lie in the range $0 < n < 1.0$ ($0\% < n < 100\%$).
2. Algebraic Inter-Conversion & Geotechnical Equivalence

Derivation of the Conversion Equations

The relationship between void ratio ($e$) and porosity ($n$) is derived directly from the fundamental volume partition equation $V = V_s + V_v$:

  1. Expressing $n$ in terms of $e$: Divide both numerator and denominator of the porosity definition by $V_s$: $$n = \frac{V_v}{V} = \frac{V_v}{V_s + V_v} = \frac{\frac{V_v}{V_s}}{\frac{V_s}{V_s} + \frac{V_v}{V_s}} = \frac{e}{1 + e}$$
  2. Expressing $e$ in terms of $n$: Rearrange the equation $n(1 + e) = e \implies n + n e = e \implies n = e(1 - n)$: $$e = \frac{n}{1 - n}$$
  3. Total Volume Expansion Factor ($1 + e$): $$\frac{V}{V_s} = \frac{V_s + V_v}{V_s} = 1 + \frac{V_v}{V_s} = 1 + e \implies V = V_s (1 + e)$$ $$1 - n = 1 - \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{1}{1 + e} \implies V_s = V(1 - n)$$
Characteristic Void Ratio ($e$) Porosity ($n$)
Mathematical Definition $e = \frac{V_v}{V_s}$ $n = \frac{V_v}{V} = \frac{V_v}{V_s + V_v}$
Normalizing Base Solid mineral skeleton ($V_s$, unchanging constant under loading) Total volume ($V$, variable under compressive deformation)
Range of Values $0 < e < \infty$ (can readily exceed $1.0$) $0 < n < 1.0$ (strictly bounded between $0\%$ and $100\%$)
Geotechnical Usage Preferred in settlement, consolidation, and compaction calculations because $V_s$ remains constant during volume strain. Preferred in hydrogeology, groundwater flow, reservoir engineering, and geophysical logging.
3. Geological Types of Porosity: Primary, Secondary & Effective Porosity

In engineering geology and hydrogeology, not all pore spaces behave identically:

  • Primary Porosity: Pores formed during initial deposition or crystallization of the rock (e.g., intergranular pores in sandstone, vesicles in basaltic lava).
  • Secondary Porosity: Pores formed after rock consolidation due to tectonic stress, metamorphism, or chemical weathering (e.g., joints, faults, foliation partings, karst solution cavities in limestone).
  • Effective Porosity ($n_e$): The ratio of interconnected pore volume through which fluids can actively flow to the total rock volume ($n_e = V_{\text{interconnected}} / V$). Isolated vugs or microscopic dead-end pores contribute to total porosity but do not participate in fluid transmission.
  • Specific Yield ($S_y$) & Specific Retention ($S_r$): In an unconfined aquifer: $$n = S_y + S_r$$ where $S_y$ is the volume of water drained by gravity per unit total volume, and $S_r$ is the volume of water held by capillary and surface tension forces against gravity.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 123
The ratio of the total volume of the pore spaces to the total volume of the solid rock mass is termed as :
  • (A) Void ratio
  • (B) Porosity
  • (C) Pores ratio
  • (D) Effective porosity
Correct Answer: (A) Void ratio — By exact geotechnical definition, the ratio of the volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) to the volume of the solid rock mass ($V_s$) is designated as the Void Ratio ($e = V_v / V_s$).
Forensic Analysis of Options
Option (A): Void ratio — Fully Verified & Correct

Void ratio ($e$) is defined rigorously in soil mechanics, rock mechanics, and engineering geology textbooks (Bangar, p. 187; Terzaghi & Peck; ISRM) as the ratio of the volume of voids (pores) to the volume of solid rock mass: $$e = \frac{V_v}{V_s}$$ Because the volume of solids $V_s$ does not change during mechanical compression or consolidation (assuming incompressible mineral grains), geotechnical engineers utilize void ratio as the primary state variable for compaction and settlement equations.

Option (B): Porosity — Incorrect Normalization

Porosity ($n$) is defined as the ratio of the volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) to the total volume of the rock specimen ($V = V_s + V_v$): $$n = \frac{V_v}{V}$$ The question explicitly specifies the ratio to the "total volume of the solid rock mass" ($V_s$), which is the mathematical definition of void ratio, not porosity. Confusing total volume with solid volume is a classical examination pitfall.

Option (C): Pores ratio — Fabricated Distractor

"Pores ratio" is a completely fictitious, non-existent term fabricated as an examination distractor to mislead candidates unfamiliar with standard phase-relationship terminology.

Option (D): Effective porosity — Incorrect Definition

Effective porosity ($n_e$) is the ratio of the volume of interconnected, drainable pore spaces ($V_{vi}$) to the total volume ($V$) of the rock. It accounts only for channels that permit fluid migration, excluding isolated, closed vesicles (such as gas bubbles in pumice). Like total porosity, it is normalized to total volume $V$, not solid volume $V_s$.

8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Geotechnical Parameters for Rock and Soil Phases
Parameter Name Symbol Mathematical Formula Units / Format Typical Range in Intact Rocks
Void Ratio $e$ $e = \frac{V_v}{V_s} = \frac{n}{1 - n}$ Dimensionless decimal (e.g. $0.05$) $0.005 - 0.40$ (dense rocks); $> 1.0$ (pumice)
Total Porosity $n$ $n = \frac{V_v}{V} = \frac{e}{1 + e}$ Percentage ($0 - 100\%$) or fraction $0.5\% - 30\%$ (Granite: $<1\%$; Sandstone: $10-25\%$)
Effective Porosity $n_e$ $n_e = \frac{V_{\text{interconnected}}}{V}$ Percentage ($0 - 100\%$) $0.1\% - 22\%$ (always $\le n$)
Degree of Saturation $S_r$ $S_r = \frac{V_w}{V_v} = \frac{w G_s}{e}$ Percentage ($0 - 100\%$) $0\%$ (oven dry) to $100\%$ (fully saturated)
Moisture Content $w$ $w = \frac{M_w}{M_s} \times 100\%$ Percentage $0.1\% - 15\%$ (intact rock)
8 Advanced Practice Problems & Fully Worked Solutions
Problem 1: Exact Conversion from Porosity to Void Ratio
A porous sandstone specimen has a laboratory measured porosity of $n = 20.0\%$ ($0.20$). Calculate its void ratio ($e$).
Solution:
1. Use the fundamental conversion formula: $$e = \frac{n}{1 - n}$$ 2. Substitute $n = 0.20$: $$e = \frac{0.20}{1 - 0.20} = \frac{0.20}{0.80} = 0.25$$ The void ratio of the sandstone is $0.25$.
Problem 2: Conversion from Void Ratio to Porosity
A sample of volcanic pumice has an exceptionally high void ratio of $e = 1.50$ due to abundant vesicular cavities. Calculate its porosity ($n$) expressed as a percentage.
Solution:
1. Use the conversion formula: $$n = \frac{e}{1 + e}$$ 2. Substitute $e = 1.50$: $$n = \frac{1.50}{1 + 1.50} = \frac{1.50}{2.50} = 0.60 = 60.0\%$$ Physical Insight: Even though void ratio exceeds $1.0$ ($e = 1.50$), porosity can never exceed $100\%$ ($n = 60\%$).
Problem 3: Determination of $e$ and $n$ from Laboratory Masses and Volumes
A cylindrical core of limestone has diameter $D = 50\text{ mm}$, length $L = 100\text{ mm}$, and an oven-dry mass of $M_s = 485.0\text{ g}$. The true grain density of the solid calcite minerals is $\rho_s = 2.71\text{ g/cm}^3$. Calculate: (a) total volume $V$, (b) volume of solids $V_s$, (c) volume of voids $V_v$, (d) porosity $n$, and (e) void ratio $e$.
Solution:
1. Total bulk volume $V$: $$V = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 L = \frac{\pi}{4} (5.0\text{ cm})^2 \times (10.0\text{ cm}) = 196.35\text{ cm}^3$$ 2. Volume of solid mineral skeleton $V_s$: $$V_s = \frac{M_s}{\rho_s} = \frac{485.0\text{ g}}{2.71\text{ g/cm}^3} = 178.97\text{ cm}^3$$ 3. Volume of voids $V_v$: $$V_v = V - V_s = 196.35 - 178.97 = 17.38\text{ cm}^3$$ 4. Porosity $n$: $$n = \frac{V_v}{V} = \frac{17.38}{196.35} = 0.0885 = 8.85\%$$ 5. Void ratio $e$: $$e = \frac{V_v}{V_s} = \frac{17.38}{178.97} = 0.0971$$ Check: $e = \frac{n}{1 - n} = \frac{0.0885}{1 - 0.0885} = \frac{0.0885}{0.9115} = 0.0971$ (Verified).
Problem 4: Consolidation Settlement & Void Ratio Reduction
A saturated clay-shale bed of initial thickness $H_0 = 12.0\text{ m}$ has an initial void ratio $e_0 = 0.85$. Under heavy embankment loading, the void ratio decreases to $e_1 = 0.70$. Assuming one-dimensional vertical strain and incompressible solid grains, calculate the total consolidation settlement ($\Delta H$) of the shale layer.
Solution:
1. Use the standard settlement equation: $$\frac{\Delta H}{H_0} = \frac{\Delta e}{1 + e_0}$$ 2. Compute change in void ratio $\Delta e$: $$\Delta e = e_0 - e_1 = 0.85 - 0.70 = 0.15$$ 3. Calculate settlement $\Delta H$: $$\Delta H = H_0 \left(\frac{\Delta e}{1 + e_0}\right) = 12.0\text{ m} \times \left(\frac{0.15}{1 + 0.85}\right) = 12.0 \times \left(\frac{0.15}{1.85}\right) = 12.0 \times 0.08108 = 0.973\text{ m} \approx 97.3\text{ cm}$$
Problem 5: Athy's Law for Compaction with Depth
In a sedimentary basin, the porosity of shale decreases with depth $z$ according to Athy's compaction equation: $n(z) = n_0 e^{-c z}$, where initial surface porosity is $n_0 = 40.0\%$ and compaction coefficient is $c = 0.0004\text{ m}^{-1}$. Calculate the void ratio of the shale at a depth of $z = 1500\text{ m}$.
Solution:
1. Compute porosity at $z = 1500\text{ m}$: $$c z = 0.0004 \times 1500 = 0.60$$ $$n(1500) = 0.40 \times e^{-0.60} = 0.40 \times 0.54881 = 0.2195 = 21.95\%$$ 2. Compute corresponding void ratio $e$: $$e = \frac{n}{1 - n} = \frac{0.2195}{1 - 0.2195} = \frac{0.2195}{0.7805} = 0.281$$
Problem 6: Degree of Saturation from Void Ratio and Water Content
A weathered granite regolith has a void ratio $e = 0.65$, water content $w = 18.0\%$, and specific gravity of solid mineral grains $G_s = 2.68$. Calculate the degree of saturation ($S_r$) of the specimen.
Solution:
1. Use the fundamental phase identity: $$S_r \cdot e = w \cdot G_s$$ 2. Solve for degree of saturation $S_r$: $$S_r = \frac{w \cdot G_s}{e} = \frac{0.18 \times 2.68}{0.65} = \frac{0.4824}{0.65} = 0.7422 = 74.22\%$$ The rock pore spaces are 74.2% filled with water and 25.8% filled with air.
Problem 7: Effective Porosity vs. Total Porosity in Vesicular Basalt
A core of vesicular basalt has a total volume $V = 200\text{ cm}^3$ and total porosity $n = 18.0\%$. In a helium pycnometer test, the volume of interconnected open pores accessible to gas is determined to be $V_{\text{connected}} = 16.0\text{ cm}^3$, while the remaining vesicles are sealed. Calculate: (a) the total pore volume $V_v$, (b) the effective porosity $n_e$, and (c) the percentage of total pore volume that is completely sealed.
Solution:
1. Total pore volume $V_v$: $$V_v = n \times V = 0.18 \times 200\text{ cm}^3 = 36.0\text{ cm}^3$$ 2. Effective porosity $n_e$: $$n_e = \frac{V_{\text{connected}}}{V} = \frac{16.0\text{ cm}^3}{200\text{ cm}^3} = 0.080 = 8.0\%$$ 3. Sealed pore volume and percentage: $$V_{\text{sealed}} = V_v - V_{\text{connected}} = 36.0 - 16.0 = 20.0\text{ cm}^3$$ $$\% \text{ Sealed} = \left(\frac{20.0}{36.0}\right) \times 100\% = 55.56\%$$
Problem 8: Critical Hydraulic Gradient for Quicksand / Piping
An alluvial sandy aquifer underlying a dam foundation has a specific gravity $G_s = 2.65$ and a void ratio $e = 0.65$. Calculate: (a) the critical hydraulic gradient ($i_c$) at which piping / quicksand failure occurs, and (b) re-express $i_c$ directly in terms of porosity $n$.
Solution:
1. Critical hydraulic gradient in terms of void ratio: $$i_c = \frac{G_s - 1}{1 + e} = \frac{2.65 - 1}{1 + 0.65} = \frac{1.65}{1.65} = 1.00$$ 2. Re-express in terms of porosity $n$: Since $\frac{1}{1 + e} = 1 - n$: $$i_c = (G_s - 1)(1 - n)$$ Compute $n$: $$n = \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{0.65}{1.65} = 0.3939$$ $$i_c = (2.65 - 1)(1 - 0.3939) = 1.65 \times 0.6061 = 1.00$$ Geotechnical Criterion: If upward seepage head loss per unit length reaches $i_c = 1.00$, effective vertical stress reduces to zero ($\sigma' = 0$), causing fluidization of the sediment.

GEO - 2/21 • Engineering Geology & Rock Mechanics

Q124: Bulk Density: Mass Per Unit Volume of Rock with Natural Moisture Content

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 124
Authoritative References: K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 10: Engineering Properties of Rocks, pp. 186–188); Bureau of Indian Standards (IS: 13030-1991: Method of Test for Laboratory Determination of Water Content, Porosity, Density and Related Properties of Intact Rock Specimens); ISRM Suggested Methods (1979); ASTM D7263.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Physics & Standardization of Bulk Density

In engineering geology, geotechnics, and rock mechanics, the mass per unit volume of a rock sample in its as-received state containing its natural in-situ moisture content is formally designated as its Bulk Density ($\rho_b$) (Bangar, p. 187; IS: 13030-1991; ISRM, 1979). When expressed as force per unit volume under gravity ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$), it is termed Unit Weight ($\gamma_b = \rho_b \cdot g$).

Figure 124.1 — Bulk Density and Natural Moisture Content: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 187). Highlighting the exact codified definition: "The mass per unit volume of a rock sample with natural moisture content is its bulk density."

The Fundamental Mass-Volume Formulation

Let a rock sample taken directly from drill core or quarry face have a total natural mass $M_{\text{nat}}$ consisting of dry solid mineral mass ($M_s$) and the mass of natural pore water ($M_w$), occupying a total overall bulk volume $V$ (including both solid minerals and void spaces):

$$\text{Bulk Density: } \rho_b = \frac{M_{\text{nat}}}{V} = \frac{M_s + M_w}{V}$$ $$\text{Bulk Unit Weight: } \gamma_b = \rho_b \cdot g = \frac{W_{\text{nat}}}{V}$$
Figure 124.2 — Three-Phase Density and Unit Weight Relationships: Structural diagram showing the partition of total bulk volume $V$ into solid mineral skeleton ($V_s$) and pore spaces ($V_v$), comparing dry density ($\rho_d$), bulk density with natural moisture ($\rho_b$), saturated density ($\rho_{\text{sat}}$), and submerged buoyant density ($\rho'$).
2. The Spectrum of Rock Densities: Rigorous Distinctions

Standard engineering testing codes (IS: 13030; ISRM; ASTM D7263) distinguish between four primary density states based on moisture conditioning:

Density Type Symbol Mathematical Formula Moisture Conditioning State Primary Engineering Application
Bulk Density $\rho_b$ $\rho_b = \frac{M_s + M_w}{V} = \rho_d (1 + w)$ As-received field core with natural in-situ moisture content ($w$). Calculation of in-situ vertical overburden stress ($\sigma_v = \gamma_b z$), dead load of rock in slopes and retaining walls.
Dry Density $\rho_d$ $\rho_d = \frac{M_s}{V} = \frac{\rho_b}{1 + w}$ Specimen oven-dried at $105^\circ\text{C} \pm 3^\circ\text{C}$ to constant mass ($M_w = 0$). Baseline benchmark for compaction control, porosity calculation ($n = 1 - \rho_d / \rho_s$), and quality control.
Saturated Density $\rho_{\text{sat}}$ $\rho_{\text{sat}} = \frac{M_s + V_v \rho_w}{V}$ Specimen subjected to vacuum saturation until all pore voids are 100% water-filled ($S_r = 100\%$). Submerged foundation analysis, submarine rock slope stability, reservoir rim stability.
Grain / True Density $\rho_s$ $\rho_s = \frac{M_s}{V_s}$ Mass of solid minerals divided exclusively by the volume of solid grains (voids excluded). Mineralogical identification, specific gravity of grains ($G_s = \rho_s / \rho_w$), void ratio calculation.
Submerged (Buoyant) Density $\rho'$ $\rho' = \rho_{\text{sat}} - \rho_w = \left(\frac{G_s - 1}{1 + e}\right) \rho_w$ Effective density below groundwater table considering Archimedes buoyant uplift. Effective stress analysis ($\sigma' = \gamma' z$), dam uplift pressure, pore water pressure stability.
Figure 124.3 — Physical Properties Table: Textbook sheet from K.M. Bangar (p. 187) displaying specific gravities, bulk densities ($\text{g/cm}^3$ and $\text{kN/m}^3$), and porosities for Granite, Dolerite, Sandstone, Shale, and Limestone.
3. Laboratory Determination & Practical Significance

Laboratory Determination Techniques (IS: 13030)

  • Caliper Method (Regular Specimens): For machined cylindrical cores or cut prisms, diameter and length are measured with a precision vernier caliper or micrometer to calculate $V = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 L$. Specimen is weighed immediately upon unsealing to determine $M_{\text{nat}}$.
  • Buoyancy / Water Displacement Method (Irregular Lumps): For irregular rock fragments, Archimedes' principle is applied. To prevent water from infiltrating the open pore spaces during submersion, the lump is briefly dipped in molten paraffin wax of known density ($\rho_{\text{wax}} \approx 0.90\text{ g/cm}^3$) to form a thin, impermeable coating before determining buoyant weight.

Practical Significance in Civil Engineering

  • In-Situ Stress Fields: In deep tunnels and underground caverns, vertical in-situ principal stress ($\sigma_v$) is directly equal to the integrated bulk unit weight of overlying rock strata: $\sigma_v = \int_0^z \gamma_b(z) dz \approx \gamma_b z$. An accurate bulk density is required to prevent catastrophic rockbursts.
  • Dam Abutment & Gravity Dam Stability: Concrete and masonry gravity dams rely upon their own self-weight and the rock foundation's weight to resist overturning and sliding under horizontal reservoir hydrostatic thrust.
  • Haulage & Transportation Economics: In commercial quarrying and open-pit mining, bulk density dictates the payload capacity, truck fleet sizing, conveyor belt load ratings, and railway freight costs.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection

Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 124
The mass per unit volume of a rock sample with natural moisture content is its :
  • (A) Dry density
  • (B) Wet density
  • (C) Bulk density
  • (D) Natural density
Correct Answer: (C) Bulk density — By codified standard definition in engineering geology (Bangar, p. 187; IS: 13030; ISRM), the mass per unit volume of a rock sample containing its natural moisture content is designated as Bulk Density ($\rho_b$).
Forensic Analysis of Options
Option (A): Dry density — Incorrect Moisture Condition

Dry density ($\rho_d$) is defined as the mass of oven-dried solid rock material per unit total volume: $$\rho_d = \frac{M_s}{V}$$ It requires driving off all moisture by heating the specimen in an oven at $105^\circ\text{C}$ until constant weight is attained. It excludes all natural moisture ($M_w = 0$), making it incorrect for a sample containing its natural moisture content.

Option (B): Wet density — Colloquial / Non-Standard Engineering Usage

While "wet density" is occasionally used casually in informal parlance, standard Indian testing codes (IS: 13030-1991), ISRM suggested methods, and standard textbooks (Bangar, p. 187) formally codify this property as Bulk Density. Furthermore, in many geotechnical contexts, "wet density" implies an artificially soaked or saturated specimen ($\rho_{\text{sat}}$), whereas "bulk density" specifically designates the intact rock mass with its in-situ natural water content.

Option (C): Bulk density — Fully Verified & Codified Engineering Term

Bulk density ($\rho_b$) is the exact verbatim definition given in K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 187, Section 10.3): "The mass per unit volume of a rock sample with natural moisture content is its bulk density." It incorporates both the solid mineral matrix and whatever moisture resides within the pores under ambient field conditions ($\rho_b = \frac{M_s + M_w}{V}$).

Option (D): Natural density — Non-Codified Synonym

"Natural density" is an unstandardized, descriptive colloquialism. Professional geological and engineering standards universally adopt "bulk density" (or "in-situ bulk density"), not "natural density".

8 Advanced Practice Problems & Fully Worked Solutions
Problem 1: Bulk Density and Unit Weight from Caliper Measurements
A fresh cylindrical rock core of dolerite has a diameter $D = 54.0\text{ mm}$, length $L = 108.0\text{ mm}$, and an as-received natural mass of $M_{\text{nat}} = 712.5\text{ g}$. Taking acceleration due to gravity $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, calculate: (a) the bulk density ($\rho_b$) in $\text{g/cm}^3$ and $\text{kg/m}^3$, and (b) the bulk unit weight ($\gamma_b$) in $\text{kN/m}^3$.
Solution:
1. Calculate specimen volume $V$: $$V = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 L = \frac{\pi}{4} (5.40\text{ cm})^2 \times (10.80\text{ cm}) = 247.34\text{ cm}^3$$ 2. Calculate bulk density $\rho_b$: $$\rho_b = \frac{M_{\text{nat}}}{V} = \frac{712.5\text{ g}}{247.34\text{ cm}^3} = 2.8806\text{ g/cm}^3 \approx 2.88\text{ g/cm}^3 = 2881\text{ kg/m}^3$$ 3. Calculate bulk unit weight $\gamma_b$: $$\gamma_b = \rho_b \cdot g = 2881\text{ kg/m}^3 \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2 = 28,263\text{ N/m}^3 = 28.26\text{ kN/m}^3$$
Problem 2: Relationship Between Bulk Density, Dry Density & Water Content
A sandstone specimen has a bulk density of $\rho_b = 2.30\text{ g/cm}^3$ and a natural gravimetric moisture content of $w = 4.5\%$. Determine: (a) the dry density ($\rho_d$) of the rock, and (b) the mass of water contained in a $1.0\text{ m}^3$ block of this in-situ sandstone.
Solution:
1. Dry density formula: $$\rho_d = \frac{\rho_b}{1 + w} = \frac{2.30\text{ g/cm}^3}{1 + 0.045} = \frac{2.30}{1.045} = 2.201\text{ g/cm}^3 = 2201\text{ kg/m}^3$$ 2. In a $1.0\text{ m}^3$ volume ($V = 1.0\text{ m}^3$): $$\text{Total Natural Mass } M_{\text{nat}} = \rho_b \times V = 2300\text{ kg}$$ $$\text{Mass of Solids } M_s = \rho_d \times V = 2201\text{ kg}$$ $$\text{Mass of Water } M_w = M_{\text{nat}} - M_s = 2300 - 2201 = 99\text{ kg} \text{ (or } 99\text{ litres)}$$
Problem 3: Porosity Derivation from Dry Density and Grain Density
The dry density of an arkosic sandstone is $\rho_d = 2.18\text{ g/cm}^3$. The grain density of the powdered mineral constituents is measured using a gas pycnometer to be $\rho_s = 2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$. Calculate the total porosity ($n$) and the void ratio ($e$) of the sandstone.
Solution:
1. Relate dry density to grain density and porosity: $$\rho_d = \rho_s (1 - n) \implies 1 - n = \frac{\rho_d}{\rho_s}$$ $$n = 1 - \frac{\rho_d}{\rho_s} = 1 - \frac{2.18}{2.65} = 1 - 0.8226 = 0.1774 = 17.74\%$$ 2. Compute void ratio $e$: $$e = \frac{n}{1 - n} = \frac{0.1774}{1 - 0.1774} = \frac{0.1774}{0.8226} = 0.2156$$
Problem 4: Wax-Coated Immersion Method for Irregular Lumps
To determine the bulk density of an irregular lump of porous limestone, the specimen is weighed in air ($M_1 = 340.0\text{ g}$). It is then coated with molten paraffin wax of density $\rho_{\text{wax}} = 0.90\text{ g/cm}^3$. The mass of the waxed specimen in air is $M_2 = 358.0\text{ g}$. When suspended in water ($\rho_w = 1.00\text{ g/cm}^3$), the submerged apparent mass is $M_3 = 205.0\text{ g}$. Calculate the bulk density ($\rho_b$) of the limestone.
Solution:
1. Mass of the wax coating: $$M_{\text{wax}} = M_2 - M_1 = 358.0 - 340.0 = 18.0\text{ g}$$ 2. Volume of the wax coating: $$V_{\text{wax}} = \frac{M_{\text{wax}}}{\rho_{\text{wax}}} = \frac{18.0\text{ g}}{0.90\text{ g/cm}^3} = 20.0\text{ cm}^3$$ 3. Total volume of waxed specimen (by Archimedes' principle, loss of mass in water equals mass of displaced water): $$V_{\text{total}} = \frac{M_2 - M_3}{\rho_w} = \frac{358.0 - 205.0}{1.00} = 153.0\text{ cm}^3$$ 4. Volume of the bare rock specimen $V$: $$V = V_{\text{total}} - V_{\text{wax}} = 153.0 - 20.0 = 133.0\text{ cm}^3$$ 5. Bulk density of rock: $$\rho_b = \frac{M_1}{V} = \frac{340.0\text{ g}}{133.0\text{ cm}^3} = 2.556\text{ g/cm}^3 \approx 2.56\text{ g/cm}^3$$
Problem 5: In-Situ Vertical Stress Calculation Under Stratified Rock Column
A deep exploratory mining shaft intersects three horizontal rock strata: (1) $0 - 50\text{ m}$: Weathered sandstone with bulk unit weight $\gamma_{b1} = 22.0\text{ kN/m}^3$; (2) $50 - 180\text{ m}$: Massive limestone with bulk unit weight $\gamma_{b2} = 26.0\text{ kN/m}^3$; (3) $180 - 400\text{ m}$: Dense basalt with bulk unit weight $\gamma_{b3} = 28.5\text{ kN/m}^3$. Calculate the total vertical overburden stress ($\sigma_v$) at the bottom of the shaft ($z = 400\text{ m}$).
Solution:
1. Sum vertical stresses generated by each layer: $$\sigma_v = \sum \gamma_{bi} \cdot h_i$$ $$\sigma_{v1} = 22.0\text{ kN/m}^3 \times 50\text{ m} = 1100\text{ kPa} = 1.10\text{ MPa}$$ $$\sigma_{v2} = 26.0\text{ kN/m}^3 \times (180 - 50)\text{ m} = 26.0 \times 130 = 3380\text{ kPa} = 3.38\text{ MPa}$$ $$\sigma_{v3} = 28.5\text{ kN/m}^3 \times (400 - 180)\text{ m} = 28.5 \times 220 = 6270\text{ kPa} = 6.27\text{ MPa}$$ 2. Total vertical stress at $400\text{ m}$: $$\sigma_v = 1.10 + 3.38 + 6.27 = 10.75\text{ MPa}$$
Problem 6: Submerged Buoyant Unit Weight in Subsea Tunneling
An undersea railway tunnel is excavated through marine basalt located below the ocean floor. The basalt has specific gravity $G_s = 2.90$ and void ratio $e = 0.05$. Assuming complete saturation ($S_r = 100\%$) by seawater of density $\rho_{\text{sw}} = 1025\text{ kg/m}^3$ ($\gamma_{\text{sw}} = 10.05\text{ kN/m}^3$), determine: (a) the saturated unit weight ($\gamma_{\text{sat}}$), and (b) the effective buoyant submerged unit weight ($\gamma'$).
Solution:
1. Saturated unit weight $\gamma_{\text{sat}}$: $$\gamma_{\text{sat}} = \left(\frac{G_s + e}{1 + e}\right) \gamma_w = \left(\frac{2.90 + 0.05}{1 + 0.05}\right) \times 9.81 = \left(\frac{2.95}{1.05}\right) \times 9.81 = 2.8095 \times 9.81 = 27.56\text{ kN/m}^3$$ 2. Effective submerged unit weight in seawater $\gamma'$: $$\gamma' = \gamma_{\text{sat}} - \gamma_{\text{sw}} = 27.56 - 10.05 = 17.51\text{ kN/m}^3$$ Geotechnical Implication: Submergence reduces the effective confining body weight of the rock mass by $36.5\%$, significantly reducing sliding friction along inclined joint planes.
Problem 7: Water Absorption by Mass and Saturated Density
A limestone block has an oven-dry mass $M_{\text{dry}} = 500.0\text{ g}$ and a bulk volume $V = 200.0\text{ cm}^3$. After 48 hours of immersion under water, its saturated surface-dry mass increases to $M_{\text{sat}} = 515.0\text{ g}$. Calculate: (a) dry density ($\rho_d$), (b) water absorption by mass ($A_w \%$), (c) saturated density ($\rho_{\text{sat}}$), and (d) apparent porosity ($n_a$).
Solution:
1. Dry density: $$\rho_d = \frac{M_{\text{dry}}}{V} = \frac{500.0\text{ g}}{200.0\text{ cm}^3} = 2.50\text{ g/cm}^3$$ 2. Water absorption by mass: $$A_w = \frac{M_{\text{sat}} - M_{\text{dry}}}{M_{\text{dry}}} \times 100\% = \frac{515.0 - 500.0}{500.0} \times 100\% = \frac{15.0}{500.0} \times 100\% = 3.0\%$$ 3. Saturated density: $$\rho_{\text{sat}} = \frac{M_{\text{sat}}}{V} = \frac{515.0\text{ g}}{200.0\text{ cm}^3} = 2.575\text{ g/cm}^3$$ 4. Apparent porosity: $$n_a = \frac{V_w}{V} = \frac{15.0\text{ cm}^3}{200.0\text{ cm}^3} = 0.075 = 7.5\%$$
Problem 8: Commercial Quarry Dimension Stone Haulage Tonnage
A dimension stone quarry extracts granite blocks measuring $2.5\text{ m} \times 1.5\text{ m} \times 1.2\text{ m}$. The granite has a laboratory bulk density of $\rho_b = 2.65\text{ tonnes/m}^3$. If a highway transport trailer has a maximum legal payload limit of $32.0\text{ tonnes}$, determine: (a) the tonnage of a single block, and (b) whether the trailer can legally carry two blocks in a single shipment.
Solution:
1. Volume of one block: $$V = 2.5\text{ m} \times 1.5\text{ m} \times 1.2\text{ m} = 4.50\text{ m}^3$$ 2. Mass of one block: $$M_1 = V \times \rho_b = 4.50\text{ m}^3 \times 2.65\text{ tonnes/m}^3 = 11.925\text{ tonnes}$$ 3. Check two blocks: $$M_2 = 2 \times 11.925 = 23.85\text{ tonnes}$$ $$\text{Since } 23.85\text{ tonnes} < 32.0\text{ tonnes}, \text{ the trailer can legally haul two blocks with } 8.15\text{ tonnes reserve capacity.}$$ (Three blocks would weigh $35.775\text{ tonnes}$, exceeding the legal payload limit).

Q125: Schmidt Rebound Hammer: Working Principle, Empirical Indices vs. Absolute Strength

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 125
Authoritative References: Evert Hoek, Practical Rock Engineering (Ch. 5: Rock Mass Properties, pp. 82–84, Fig. 5.7); ISRM (International Society for Rock Mechanics), Suggested Methods for the Quantitative Description of Discontinuities in Rock Masses (1978); ASTM D5873 (Standard Test Method for Determination of Rock Hardness by Rebound Hammer Method); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (p. 188); D.U. Deere and R.P. Miller (1966), Engineering Classification and Index Properties for Intact Rock.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Working Principle, Mechanical Operation & The Nature of Rebound Value (R)

The Schmidt Rebound Hammer (also known as the sclerometer or Swiss hammer) is a portable, non-destructive mechanical instrument widely employed in civil engineering and engineering geology to assess the surface hardness and estimate the compressive strength of rock faces and concrete structures (ISRM, 1978; ASTM D5873; Hoek, 2007; Bangar, p. 188).

Figure 125.1 — Schmidt Hammer Rebound Testing: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 188). Describes the non-destructive rebound operation, spring-actuated hammer impact, and the empirical nature of the rebound number $R$.

Mechanical Operation of the Instrument

The device operates on the principle of elastic collision and kinetic energy restitution:

  1. A cylindrical steel plunger protruding from the front of the housing is pressed firmly and perpendicularly against the test rock surface.
  2. This action compresses an internal heavy-duty spring connected to an internal steel hammer mass ($m$).
  3. At maximum extension, an internal latch automatically releases the hammer mass, propelling it forward with a fixed, calibrated impact energy ($E_{\text{impact}}$).
  4. The hammer strikes the shoulder of the plunger, which transmits a compressive shock pulse into the rock.
  5. A portion of the kinetic energy is dissipated through localized plastic deformation, micro-crushing of mineral grains, and acoustic radiation, while the remaining elastic strain energy causes the hammer mass to rebound backward along the guide rod.
  6. A lightweight rider slides along a graduated scale, capturing the maximum backward displacement. The reading is designated as the Rebound Number ($R$), expressed on an arbitrary scale from $10$ to $100$.
Figure 125.2 — Influence of Testing Orientation on Rebound Value (R): Authoritative calibration chart from Evert Hoek (Practical Rock Engineering, Ch. 5, Fig. 5.7). Illustrates the essential correction curves required when the hammer is inclined vertically downward ($\alpha = -90^\circ$), horizontal ($\alpha = 0^\circ$), or vertically upward ($\alpha = +90^\circ$) due to gravitational forces acting on the hammer mass.
2. The Crucial Distinction: Empirical Relative Index vs. Absolute Physical Measure

Why Statement (C) is Technically False

The central misconception in non-destructive testing is assuming that the Schmidt hammer gives an "absolute" measurement of rock strength or hardness. It does not:

  • No Direct Physical Units: Rebound value $R$ is a purely arbitrary, dimensionless index (scaled $10 - 100$). It does not measure stress (such as $\text{MPa}$ or $\text{N/mm}^2$), nor does it correspond directly to fundamental physical hardness scales (e.g., Mohs scratch hardness, Vickers diamond pyramid hardness, or Brinell ball indentation).
  • Strictly an Empirical Proxy: The rebound value reflects the near-surface restitution coefficient of the rock. To convert $R$ into an estimated Uniaxial Compressive Strength ($\sigma_c$), one must rely on empirical statistical regression curves (e.g., the Deere-Miller chart or ISRM equations) that incorporate rock unit weight ($\gamma$):
    $$\log_{10} \sigma_c = 0.00088 \gamma R + 1.01 \quad (\text{Deere \& Miller, 1966})$$
  • Dependence on Extraneous Testing Variables: The recorded rebound distance is drastically influenced by external environmental and geometric factors independent of intact material strength:
    • Hammer Inclination ($\theta$): Gravity accelerates the hammer mass when pointing downward (yielding artificially high readings) and decelerates it when firing upward.
    • Surface Roughness & Weathering: A paper-thin weathered rind ($< 1\text{ mm}$) or surface roughness will cause micro-crushing and absorb impact energy, depressing $R$ by $30 - 50\%$ even if the underlying rock mass is exceptionally sound.
    • Specimen Rigidity / Mass: When testing loose core pieces without clamping them rigidly in a heavy steel V-block ($> 20\text{ kg}$), the specimen flexes and vibrates, dissipating energy and giving falsely low $R$ values.
    • Moisture State: Water-saturated rock surfaces yield systematically lower $R$ values than oven-dry or ambient dry surfaces.
3. Hammer Specifications & ISRM Standard Testing Protocols

Type L vs. Type N Schmidt Hammers

Specification Type L Hammer (Rock Mechanics) Type N Hammer (Concrete / Hard Rock)
Impact Energy $0.735\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ ($0.735\text{ J}$) $2.207\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ ($2.207\text{ J}$) ($3\times$ higher energy)
Primary Application Drill cores, thin rock slabs, weak or fragile rocks (ISRM Recommended Standard). Heavy civil concrete structures, massive in-situ rock outcrops, blocky hard rock faces.
Specimen Damage Minimal surface damage; does not shatter fragile cores. Can shatter or induce macro-cracking in drill cores of diameter $< 75\text{ mm}$.

ISRM Standard Data Reduction Protocol

To eliminate outliers caused by local mineral grains, micro-voids, or localized crushing, the ISRM mandates the following test procedure:

  1. Select a smooth, planar, unweathered rock face free from visible micro-cracks.
  2. Perform at least $20$ individual impacts separated by at least one plunger diameter ($> 30\text{ mm}$) to prevent testing pre-shattered rock.
  3. Discard the lowest $50\%$ of the recorded values (which represent local surface crushing or void collapse) and compute the mean of the upper $50\%$ (top 10 values) to establish the representative Rebound Value ($R$).
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 125
Find out the incorrect statement regarding Schmidt Hammer :
  • (A) It is concrete test hammer originally designed for carrying out in-situ tests on the hardness of concrete.
  • (B) The instrument measures the distance of rebound of a controlled impact on a rock surface.
  • (C) The distance of rebound (R) gives an absolute measure of surface hardness or strength.
  • (D) Schmidt hammer rebound values have been found to correlate well with other measures of rock strength, including Young’s Modulus and Uniaxial Strength.
Correct Answer: (C) — Statement (C) is FALSE and therefore the correct selection! The rebound value ($R$) is strictly an empirical, non-destructive relative index, NOT an absolute measure of hardness or compressive strength.
Forensic Analysis of Options
Option (A): Statement is TRUE (Hence Incorrect Choice)

Historical Fact: The Schmidt rebound hammer was invented in 1948 by Swiss civil engineer Ernst Schmidt specifically for the non-destructive in-situ evaluation of concrete hardness and curing uniformity in civil engineering construction. It was only later adopted by geotechnical engineers and formalized by the ISRM (1978) for rock mechanics testing. Because Statement (A) is factually correct, it is not the "incorrect statement" sought by the question.

Option (B): Statement is TRUE (Hence Incorrect Choice)

Physical Operation: The core working mechanism of the Schmidt hammer relies on a spring-propelled internal mass delivering a controlled, standardized impact energy to the plunger. The rider directly measures the distance of rebound ($R$) of this mass along the guide bar. Because Statement (B) accurately describes the mechanical operating principle of the instrument, it is factually true.

Option (C): Statement is FALSE — Fully Verified & Correct Option

Statement (C) claims that $R$ gives an "absolute measure of surface hardness or strength." This is fundamentally false:

  1. The rebound number $R$ is a unitless, arbitrary index on a scale from $10$ to $100$. It has no physical dimensions of stress ($\text{N/m}^2$, $\text{Pa}$) or standard hardness units.
  2. It provides only a relative empirical index. To estimate compressive strength ($\sigma_c$) or Young's modulus ($E$), the rebound number must be calibrated against laboratory crushing tests using empirical correlation charts (Deere-Miller, 1966; Hoek, 2007).
  3. The reading is heavily influenced by non-material factors including hammer orientation (gravity effects), specimen size/mass, and surface roughness.

Therefore, Statement (C) is the incorrect statement and constitutes the correct answer to the question.

Option (D): Statement is TRUE (Hence Incorrect Choice)

Empirical Validity: Extensive peer-reviewed research across decades (Deere & Miller, 1966; ISRM, 1978; Barton & Choubey, 1977; Hoek, 2007) has proven that when properly normalized for orientation and surface roughness, rebound values correlate exceptionally well ($r > 0.85 - 0.92$) with Uniaxial Compressive Strength ($\sigma_c$), Joint Wall Compressive Strength (JCS), and tangent Young's Modulus ($E_t$). Because Statement (D) is true, it is not the target of the question.
