Exam-Standard Permeability Practice Problems (8 Rigorous Exercises)
Problem 1: Constant Head Permeameter Standard Calculation
A constant head permeameter test is performed on a clean sand sample. The cylindrical permeameter has an internal diameter of $D = 10\text{ cm}$ and a length between manometer taps of $L = 15\text{ cm}$. Under a constant head difference of $\Delta h = 30\text{ cm}$, a total volume of $V = 480\text{ cm}^3$ of water is collected in $t = 2.0\text{ minutes}$. Calculate the hydraulic conductivity ($K$) in: (a) $\text{cm/s}$, and (b) $\text{m/day}$.
Solution:
1. Cross-sectional area: $$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times (10)^2}{4} = 78.54\text{ cm}^2$$ 2. Time in seconds: $$t = 2.0\text{ min} = 120\text{ s}$$ 3. Hydraulic conductivity: $$K = \frac{V \cdot L}{A \cdot \Delta h \cdot t} = \frac{480 \times 15}{78.54 \times 30 \times 120} = \frac{7200}{282,744} \approx 0.02546\text{ cm/s}$$ 4. Convert to $\text{m/day}$: $$K = 0.02546\text{ cm/s} \times \left(\frac{1\text{ m}}{100\text{ cm}}\right) \times \left(\frac{86,400\text{ s}}{1\text{ day}}\right) \approx 22.0\text{ m/day}$$
Problem 2: Falling Head Permeability of Fine Silt
A falling head permeameter test is conducted on an undisturbed core of lacustrine silt. The soil sample has length $L = 12\text{ cm}$ and diameter $D = 7.5\text{ cm}$. The standpipe has an internal diameter of $d = 0.8\text{ cm}$. Over an elapsed time of $t = 25\text{ minutes}$, the water level drops from $h_1 = 90\text{ cm}$ to $h_2 = 45\text{ cm}$. Calculate the hydraulic conductivity ($K$) of the silt in $\text{cm/s}$.
Solution:
1. Areas: $$a = \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 0.8^2}{4} = 0.5027\text{ cm}^2$$ $$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 7.5^2}{4} = 44.18\text{ cm}^2$$ 2. Time in seconds: $$t = 25 \times 60 = 1500\text{ s}$$ 3. Falling head formula: $$K = \frac{a L}{A t} \ln\left(\frac{h_1}{h_2}\right) = \frac{0.5027 \times 12}{44.18 \times 1500} \ln\left(\frac{90}{45}\right) = \frac{6.0324}{66,270} \times \ln(2) = (9.1027 \times 10^{-5}) \times 0.69315 \approx 6.31 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm/s}$$
Problem 3: Evaporation Error in Constant Head Testing of Clay
A student mistakenly attempts to test a clay sample ($K = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm/s}$) in a constant head permeameter with $A = 50\text{ cm}^2$, $L = 10\text{ cm}$, and $\Delta h = 20\text{ cm}$ over a test run of $t = 6\text{ hours}$. (a) Calculate the theoretical volume of seepage water $V$ that would exit the sample. (b) If ambient laboratory evaporation from the collection beaker occurs at a rate of $0.15\text{ mL/hr}$, compare the evaporation loss to the seepage volume.
Solution:
1. Time in seconds: $$t = 6 \times 3600 = 21,600\text{ s}$$ 2. Theoretical seepage volume: $$V = \frac{K \cdot A \cdot \Delta h \cdot t}{L} = \frac{(1.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm/s}) \times 50\text{ cm}^2 \times 20\text{ cm} \times 21,600\text{ s}}{10\text{ cm}} = \frac{0.216}{10} = 0.0216\text{ cm}^3 \approx 0.0216\text{ mL}$$ 3. Evaporation loss over 6 hours: $$V_{\text{evap}} = 0.15\text{ mL/hr} \times 6\text{ hr} = 0.90\text{ mL}$$ 4. Comparison: $$\frac{V_{\text{evap}}}{V} = \frac{0.90}{0.0216} \approx 41.7\text{ times}$$ Conclusion: The evaporation loss is nearly 42 times larger than the total volume of water passing through the sample! The beaker would end up completely bone dry, demonstrating why constant head testing of fine-grained soils is impossible.
Problem 4: Temperature & Viscosity Normalization ($K_{20}$)
A laboratory permeability test is conducted at a water temperature of $12^\circ\text{C}$, yielding an uncorrected hydraulic conductivity of $K_{12} = 1.85 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm/s}$. Dynamic viscosities of water are $\mu_{12} = 1.236\text{ cP}$ and $\mu_{20} = 1.002\text{ cP}$. Normalize the hydraulic conductivity to the standard international baseline of $20^\circ\text{C}$ ($K_{20}$).
Solution:
1. Fundamental relationship between hydraulic conductivity and fluid viscosity: $$K \propto \frac{1}{\mu} \implies K_{20} = K_T \cdot \left(\frac{\mu_T}{\mu_{20}}\right)$$ 2. Substitute values: $$K_{20} = (1.85 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm/s}) \times \left(\frac{1.236\text{ cP}}{1.002\text{ cP}}\right) = (1.85 \times 10^{-3}) \times 1.2335 \approx 2.28 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm/s}$$ Failing to normalize for the colder laboratory water temperature would have underestimated the standard permeability by $23.3\%$.
Problem 5: Determination of Intrinsic Permeability ($k$)
For the sand tested in Problem 1 ($K_{20} = 2.546 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$ with water density $\rho_w = 998.2\text{ kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, and dynamic viscosity $\mu = 1.002 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$), calculate the intrinsic permeability of the matrix $k$ in: (a) $\text{m}^2$, and (b) Darcys ($1\text{ Darcy} \approx 9.8692 \times 10^{-13}\text{ m}^2$).
Solution:
1. Formula relating $K$ and $k$: $$K = \frac{k \rho g}{\mu} \implies k = \frac{K \mu}{\rho g}$$ 2. Calculate in $\text{m}^2$: $$k = \frac{(2.546 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}) \times (1.002 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s})}{998.2\text{ kg/m}^3 \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2} = \frac{2.551 \times 10^{-7}}{9792.3} \approx 2.605 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}^2$$ 3. Convert to Darcys: $$k = \frac{2.605 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}^2}{9.8692 \times 10^{-13}\text{ m}^2/\text{Darcy}} \approx 26.39\text{ Darcys}$$
Problem 6: Critical Upward Gradient and Quick Sand Condition
In an upward-flow constant head permeameter cell, sand with specific gravity $G_s = 2.65$ and void ratio $e = 0.65$ is subjected to an upward hydraulic gradient. (a) Calculate the critical hydraulic gradient ($i_c$) at which the effective stress becomes zero and quicksand / boiling occurs. (b) If the sample length is $L = 20\text{ cm}$, what head loss $\Delta h$ will trigger failure?
Solution:
1. Critical hydraulic gradient equation: $$i_c = \frac{G_s - 1}{1 + e} = \frac{2.65 - 1}{1 + 0.65} = \frac{1.65}{1.65} = 1.00$$ 2. Critical head loss: $$i_c = \frac{\Delta h_c}{L} \implies \Delta h_c = i_c \cdot L = 1.00 \times 20\text{ cm} = 20\text{ cm}$$ If the upstream head exceeds the downstream head by more than $20\text{ cm}$, seepage forces completely counteract the buoyant weight of sand grains, causing the sand bed to fluidize ("quicksand" condition).
Problem 7: Discharge Velocity vs True Seepage Velocity
A coarse sand sample tested in a constant head permeameter has hydraulic conductivity $K = 4.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$ and total porosity $n = 0.35$. Under a hydraulic gradient of $i = \Delta h / L = 0.25$, calculate: (a) The Darcian discharge velocity ($v$), and (b) The actual pore seepage velocity ($v_s$).
Solution:
1. Discharge velocity (macroscopic Darcian flux): $$v = K \cdot i = (4.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}) \times 0.25 = 1.125 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} = 0.1125\text{ mm/s}$$ 2. Actual interstitial pore seepage velocity: $$v_s = \frac{v}{n} = \frac{1.125 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}}{0.35} \approx 3.214 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} = 0.3214\text{ mm/s}$$ Observation: Water molecules travel through the tortuous interconnected pore channels at nearly three times the apparent Darcian velocity because water can only move through the open porosity $n$.
Problem 8: Anisotropic Permeability of Layered Permeameter Sample
A composite permeameter specimen is constructed by stacking three equal horizontal layers, each $5\text{ cm}$ thick ($L_1 = L_2 = L_3 = 5\text{ cm}$, total $L = 15\text{ cm}$). The layers have hydraulic conductivities $K_1 = 10^{-2}\text{ cm/s}$, $K_2 = 10^{-3}\text{ cm/s}$, and $K_3 = 10^{-4}\text{ cm/s}$. Calculate: (a) Equivalent hydraulic conductivity for flow perpendicular to layers ($K_{\perp}$), and (b) Equivalent conductivity for flow parallel to layers ($K_{\parallel}$).
Solution:
1. Flow perpendicular to layering (harmonic mean): $$K_{\perp} = \frac{\sum L_i}{\sum (L_i / K_i)} = \frac{5 + 5 + 5}{\frac{5}{10^{-2}} + \frac{5}{10^{-3}} + \frac{5}{10^{-4}}} = \frac{15}{500 + 5000 + 50000} = \frac{15}{55,500} \approx 2.70 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm/s}$$ 2. Flow parallel to layering (arithmetic mean): $$K_{\parallel} = \frac{\sum (K_i \cdot L_i)}{\sum L_i} = \frac{(10^{-2} \times 5) + (10^{-3} \times 5) + (10^{-4} \times 5)}{15} = \frac{0.05 + 0.005 + 0.0005}{15} = \frac{0.0555}{15} \approx 3.70 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm/s}$$ $$\text{Anisotropy Ratio } \frac{K_{\parallel}}{K_{\perp}} = \frac{3.70 \times 10^{-3}}{2.70 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 13.7$$ Flow parallel to bedding is nearly $14\times$ faster, because perpendicular flow is severely throttled by the lowest permeability layer ($K_3$).

Q145: Freshwater-Saline Water Interface Geometry: Glover's Dynamic Parabolic Profile

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 145
Authoritative References: Robert E. Glover, The Pattern of Fresh-Water Flow in a Coastal Aquifer (Journal of Geophysical Research, 1959, Vol. 64, No. 4, pp. 457–459); David K. Todd and Larry W. Mays, Groundwater Hydrology (3rd Ed., Wiley, Ch. 14: Saline Water Intrusion, pp. 555–578); C.W. Fetter, Applied Hydrogeology (4th Ed., Prentice Hall, Ch. 8, pp. 312–322); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 3: Hydrogeology, p. 32).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Ghyben-Herzberg Principle of Coastal Hydrostatic Balance

In coastal aquifers, lighter freshwater ($\rho_f \approx 1.000\text{ g/cm}^3$) floats upon denser saline seawater ($\rho_s \approx 1.025\text{ g/cm}^3$). The fundamental relationship governing this equilibrium was independently formulated by Dutch engineer Willem Badon Ghyben (1888) and German engineer Baurat Alexander Herzberg (1901) (Todd & Mays, 2005; Fetter, 2001; Bangar, p. 32).

Figure 145.1 — Hydrostatic Equilibrium across Coastal Freshwater-Saltwater Systems: Balancing freshwater hydrostatic pressure $\rho_f g (h_f + z)$ against seawater hydrostatic pressure $\rho_s g z$ along the zero-velocity interface line at depth $z$ below mean sea level.

Hydrostatic Derivation of the 40:1 Ratio

At any point along the interface at depth $z$ below mean sea level (MSL), hydrostatic pressure in the freshwater column of total height $(h_f + z)$ must balance the hydrostatic pressure of the saltwater column of depth $z$:

$$\rho_s \cdot g \cdot z = \rho_f \cdot g \cdot (h_f + z)$$

Expanding and solving for interface depth $z$:

$$\rho_s z - \rho_f z = \rho_f h_f \implies z(\rho_s - \rho_f) = \rho_f h_f$$ $$z = \left(\frac{\rho_f}{\rho_s - \rho_f}\right) h_f$$

Substituting standard densities ($\rho_f = 1.000\text{ g/cm}^3$, $\rho_s = 1.025\text{ g/cm}^3$):

$$z = \left(\frac{1.000}{1.025 - 1.000}\right) h_f = \frac{1.000}{0.025} h_f = 40 \cdot h_f$$

Thus, for every $1\text{ meter}$ that the freshwater table stands above mean sea level, the freshwater-saline water interface extends $40\text{ meters}$ below sea level.

2. The Dynamic Hydrodynamic Flow & Glover's Parabolic Interface Solution (1959)
Figure 145.2 — Robert E. Glover's Dynamic Parabolic Interface Model (1959): Incorporating seaward freshwater discharge $Q$ and vertical equipotential convergence. The interface forms a smooth, upward-opening parabola with an offshore submarine discharge gap $x_0$, steepening at the coast and flattening inland.

The Hydrostatic Paradox and the Seepage Gap

While the static Ghyben-Herzberg relation provides a first-order approximation, it suffers from a fatal physical paradox: at the shoreline where the water table intersects sea level ($h_f = 0$), the formula predicts $z = 0$. This would force the interface to intersect the shoreline exactly at the water surface, providing zero cross-sectional area for freshwater to discharge into the ocean, which violates continuity and Darcy's Law.

In reality, freshwater flows continuously seaward toward the ocean. In 1959, Robert E. Glover formulated the exact hydrodynamic solution using complex potential theory for steady 2-dimensional flow in an unconfined coastal aquifer:

$$z^2 = \frac{2 Q}{\Delta \rho \cdot K} x + \left(\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho \cdot K}\right)^2$$

Where:

  • $z$ = Depth of the interface below mean sea level at distance $x$ inland ($\text{m}$).
  • $x$ = Horizontal distance measured inland from the shoreline ($x \ge 0$) ($\text{m}$).
  • $Q$ = Seaward freshwater discharge per unit length of coastline ($\text{m}^3/\text{day per m}$ or $\text{m}^2/\text{s}$).
  • $K$ = Saturated hydraulic conductivity of the coastal aquifer ($\text{m/day}$ or $\text{m/s}$).
  • $\Delta \rho = \frac{\rho_s - \rho_f}{\rho_f} \approx \frac{1.025 - 1.000}{1.000} = 0.025$ (dimensionless relative density difference).
Figure 145.3 — Facsimile from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 3, p. 32): Coastal hydrogeology cross-section showing freshwater flow lines, the parabolic interface, and the upward curvature of the boundary separating fresh groundwater from underlying marine seawater.

Mathematical Proof of the "Concave Upward" Geometry

The algebraic form $z^2 = 2 p x + p^2$ is the canonical equation of a parabola opening along the positive horizontal axis. Let us inspect its geometric curvature:

  1. Express depth $z$ as a function of horizontal distance $x$: $$z(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2 Q}{\Delta \rho K} x + \left(\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K}\right)^2}$$
  2. The first derivative represents the interface slope: $$\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K \cdot z} > 0$$ Because $z$ increases with inland distance $x$, the slope is positive (the interface dips deeper inland).
  3. The second derivative represents the rate of change of slope (curvature): $$\frac{d^2 z}{dx^2} = -\frac{Q^2}{(\Delta \rho K)^2 \cdot z^3} < 0$$
  4. In standard geological and geographical cross-sections, elevation $y$ is plotted vertically upward ($y = -z$). Transforming into vertical Cartesian coordinates: $$\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} = -\frac{d^2 z}{dx^2} = +\frac{Q^2}{(\Delta \rho K)^2 \cdot z^3} > 0$$
Geometric Conclusion:
Because $\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} > 0$, the mathematical curve is strictly CONCAVE UPWARD (it forms a bowl-like profile that curves steeply upward near the shoreline and flattens out gradually inland).
3. Submarine Discharge Gap ($x_0$) and Transition Zone Dynamics

At the sea surface ($z = 0$), Glover's equation reveals that the interface extends seaward beyond the shoreline by an offshore distance $x_0$:

$$0 = \frac{2 Q}{\Delta \rho K} x_0 + \left(\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K}\right)^2 \implies x_0 = -\frac{Q}{2 \Delta \rho K}$$

This offshore distance represents the width of the submarine freshwater seepage gap through which freshwater discharges into the sea floor under the ocean, preventing seawater from choking the coastal aquifer.

Under natural conditions, tidal pulsations, seasonal recharge fluctuations, and molecular diffusion blur the sharp interface into a brackish transition zone (zone of dispersion), but the overarching structural envelope remains strictly concave upward.

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 145: Choose the correct answer regarding the shape and the nature of the fresh water-saline water interface near to a coastal area from the options given below :
(A) Linear and horizontal
(B) Concave upward
(C) Linear and inclined
(D) Convex downward
Correct Answer: (B) Concave upward
Forensic Analysis & Option Refutations
INCORRECT Option (A): Linear and horizontal

Option (A) posits that the interface is completely flat and horizontal. A horizontal interface would require hydrostatic conditions throughout the entire aquifer where the freshwater table is also perfectly flat and horizontal ($h_f = 0$ everywhere). Under such conditions, the hydraulic gradient is zero ($i = dh/dx = 0$), meaning zero groundwater flow towards the sea ($Q = 0$). In active coastal aquifers where precipitation recharges the hinterland and drives seaward discharge, a horizontal interface is physically impossible.

CORRECT Option (B): Concave upward

Option (B) represents the exact, hydrodynamically proven geometric configuration of the freshwater-saline water boundary in coastal aquifers:

  • Under Glover's exact potential flow solution (1959), the interface obeys the parabolic function $z^2 = \frac{2Q}{\Delta \rho K} x + \left(\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K}\right)^2$.
  • In vertical elevation coordinates ($y = -z$), the second derivative is positive ($\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} > 0$), which mathematically defines a concave upward profile.
  • Physically, flow lines converge near the coastal discharge gap, producing high vertical velocity gradients that cause the interface to plunge steeply near the coast and flatten asymptotically inland into a horizontal plateau.

Thus, Option (B) is indisputably the correct hydrogeological answer.

INCORRECT Option (C): Linear and inclined

Option (C) reflects a common elementary misconception that arises from applying the basic Ghyben-Herzberg ratio ($z = 40 h_f$) to an idealized planar water table ($h_f = c \cdot x$), which produces a straight sloping line ($z = 40 c x$). However, this crude model completely ignores the vertical flow components near the shoreline, the existence of the submarine seepage face ($x_0$), and the convergence of flow net equipotentials. Rigorous field measurements and hydrodynamic physics prove that the interface is parabolic and distinctly curved (concave upward), not a straight inclined line.

INCORRECT Option (D): Convex downward

Option (D) claims the interface is "convex downward" (which would mean $\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} < 0$). This inverted curvature would imply that the interface is nearly horizontal at the coastline and curves increasingly steeper as one moves further inland into the continental interior. This is the exact opposite of natural groundwater hydraulics: groundwater flow velocity is highest near the coastal discharge face (causing steep interface dip) and lowest inland where hydraulic gradients flatten. Hence, convex downward violates the fundamental laws of potential flow.

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Coastal Hydrogeology: Interface Models & Governing Equations
Model Formulation Interface Shape Governing Equation Assumptions & Boundary Physics
Ghyben-Herzberg (1888/1901) Linear inclined wedge (approximate) $$z = \left(\frac{\rho_f}{\rho_s - \rho_f}\right) h_f \approx 40 h_f$$ Hydrostatic equilibrium; strictly horizontal flow; zero submarine discharge face ($z=0$ at coast).
Glover Solution (1959) Parabolic (Concave Upward) $$z^2 = \frac{2 Q}{\Delta \rho K} x + \left(\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K}\right)^2$$ Exact hydrodynamic potential flow; steady 2D discharge $Q$; includes submarine seepage face $x_0$.
Henry Problem (1964) Dispersive S-shaped transition zone $$\nabla \cdot (K \nabla h) = 0, \quad \nabla \cdot (D \nabla C) - \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla C = 0$$ Coupled density-dependent fluid flow and hydrodynamic salt solute dispersion; non-sharp interface.
Exam-Standard Coastal Hydrogeology Practice Problems (8 Rigorous Exercises)
Problem 1: Classic Ghyben-Herzberg Interface Depth
In an unconfined coastal sand aquifer, an observation well situated $250\text{ m}$ from the sea records a water table elevation of $h_f = 2.40\text{ m}$ above mean sea level. Assuming freshwater density $\rho_f = 1.000\text{ g/cm}^3$ and seawater density $\rho_s = 1.025\text{ g/cm}^3$: (a) Calculate the depth to the saltwater interface below mean sea level ($z$). (b) What is the total freshwater saturated column thickness ($H$) at this location?
Solution:
1. Interface depth below sea level: $$z = \frac{\rho_f}{\rho_s - \rho_f} h_f = \frac{1.000}{1.025 - 1.000} \times 2.40\text{ m} = 40 \times 2.40\text{ m} = 96.0\text{ meters}$$ 2. Total freshwater column thickness: $$H = h_f + z = 2.40\text{ m} + 96.0\text{ m} = 98.4\text{ meters}$$ The entire column of $98.4\text{ m}$ consists of fresh potable water floating above dense saline seawater.
Problem 2: Glover Submarine Discharge Gap Calculation
A coastal aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of $K = 30\text{ m/day}$ and discharges freshwater into the ocean at a rate of $Q = 3.6\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ per meter length of coastline. Taking relative density difference $\Delta \rho = 0.025$: (a) Calculate the seaward width of the submarine discharge gap ($x_0$). (b) What is the depth of the interface directly at the coastline ($x = 0$)?
Solution:
1. Calculate parameter term: $$\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho \cdot K} = \frac{3.6}{0.025 \times 30} = \frac{3.6}{0.75} = 4.8\text{ meters}$$ 2. Seaward gap width ($x_0$): $$x_0 = \frac{Q}{2 \Delta \rho K} = \frac{4.8}{2} = 2.4\text{ meters}$$ Freshwater discharges through a strip extending $2.4\text{ m}$ offshore along the ocean floor.
3. Interface depth at the shoreline ($x = 0$): $$z(0) = \sqrt{0 + \left(\frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K}\right)^2} = \frac{Q}{\Delta \rho K} = 4.8\text{ meters}$$ Unlike Ghyben-Herzberg which incorrectly predicts $z(0) = 0$, Glover's solution correctly shows the interface lies $4.8\text{ m}$ beneath the shoreline.
Problem 3: Glover Parabolic Profile Depth Inland
Using the coastal aquifer parameters from Problem 2 ($Q/(\Delta \rho K) = 4.8\text{ m}$), calculate the interface depth $z$ at inland distances of: (a) $x = 50\text{ m}$, (b) $x = 200\text{ m}$, and (c) $x = 800\text{ m}$. Demonstrate that the rate of interface deepening flattens inland.
Solution:
1. Formula: $z(x) = \sqrt{2(4.8)x + (4.8)^2} = \sqrt{9.6 x + 23.04}$
2. At $x = 50\text{ m}$: $$z(50) = \sqrt{9.6(50) + 23.04} = \sqrt{480 + 23.04} = \sqrt{503.04} \approx 22.43\text{ m}$$ 3. At $x = 200\text{ m}$: $$z(200) = \sqrt{9.6(200) + 23.04} = \sqrt{1920 + 23.04} = \sqrt{1943.04} \approx 44.08\text{ m}$$ 4. At $x = 800\text{ m}$: $$z(800) = \sqrt{9.6(800) + 23.04} = \sqrt{7680 + 23.04} = \sqrt{7703.04} \approx 87.77\text{ m}$$ 5. Slope evaluation: From $x = 0$ to $50\text{ m}$, $\Delta z / \Delta x = (22.43 - 4.8) / 50 = 0.353\text{ m/m}$ (very steep).
From $x = 200$ to $800\text{ m}$, $\Delta z / \Delta x = (87.77 - 44.08) / 600 = 0.0728\text{ m/m}$ ($5\times$ flatter).
This mathematically proves the concave upward nature of the profile.
Problem 4: Upconing Beneath a Pumping Well (Dagan-Bear Criterion)
A production well in an unconfined coastal aquifer penetrates to a depth leaving a distance of $d = 20\text{ m}$ between the well bottom and the initial flat freshwater-saline interface. If $K = 25\text{ m/day}$ and $\Delta \rho = 0.025$, calculate the critical pumping rate ($Q_c$) above which the saltwater cone becomes unstable and surges directly into the well (upconing threshold $Q_c \approx 0.45 \pi d^2 K \Delta \rho$).
Solution:
1. Dagan & Bear (1968) critical upconing formula: $$Q_c = 0.45 \cdot \pi \cdot d^2 \cdot K \cdot \Delta \rho$$ 2. Substitute values: $$Q_c = 0.45 \times 3.14159 \times (20)^2 \times 25 \times 0.025 = 0.45 \times 3.14159 \times 400 \times 0.625$$ $$Q_c = 565.49 \times 0.625 \approx 353.43\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$$ Pumping at rates exceeding $353\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ will cause the saline cusp to enter the well screen, ruining drinking water quality.
Problem 5: Variable Salinity and Estuarine Water Densities
Calculate the Ghyben-Herzberg depth ratio $\alpha = \rho_f / (\rho_s - \rho_f)$ for three distinct coastal water bodies ($\rho_f = 1.000\text{ g/cm}^3$): (a) Open ocean ($\rho_s = 1.025\text{ g/cm}^3$), (b) Brackish coastal lagoon/estuary ($\rho_s = 1.012\text{ g/cm}^3$), and (c) Hypersaline tidal lagoon ($\rho_s = 1.036\text{ g/cm}^3$).
Solution:
1. Open ocean: $$\alpha_1 = \frac{1.000}{1.025 - 1.000} = \frac{1.000}{0.025} = 40.0$$ 2. Brackish lagoon: $$\alpha_2 = \frac{1.000}{1.012 - 1.000} = \frac{1.000}{0.012} \approx 83.33$$ 3. Hypersaline lagoon: $$\alpha_3 = \frac{1.000}{1.036 - 1.000} = \frac{1.000}{0.036} \approx 27.78$$ Physical Insight: Along brackish estuaries, a $1\text{ m}$ head drop causes over $83\text{ m}$ of saline encroachment, making estuarine groundwater systems twice as sensitive to over-abstraction as open ocean coasts.
Problem 6: Sea Level Rise Impact on Interface Migration
A coastal plain has a Regional water table slope of $i = dh/dx = 0.0015$ inland. Global climate change produces a projected sea level rise of $\Delta h_{\text{sea}} = 0.60\text{ meters}$. Assuming the regional freshwater table elevation remains unchanged, calculate the horizontal inland migration distance of the saltwater interface toe ($\Delta x$).
Solution:
1. Effective loss of freshwater head relative to new sea level: $$\Delta h_f = 0.60\text{ m}$$ 2. Horizontal distance needed to regain $0.60\text{ m}$ of water table head under slope $i = 0.0015$: $$\Delta x = \frac{\Delta h_f}{i} = \frac{0.60\text{ m}}{0.0015} = 400\text{ meters}$$ A seemingly modest $60\text{ cm}$ sea level rise drives the saltwater wedge $400\text{ meters}$ further inland, contaminating coastal shallow wells across the aquifer.
Problem 7: Tidal Mixing & Dispersion Zone Thickness
Instead of a knife-sharp interface, an unconfined coastal aquifer develops a transition zone governed by 1D advective-dispersive transport. If longitudinal dispersivity is $\alpha_L = 2.0\text{ m}$ and average pore velocity is $v = 0.4\text{ m/day}$, calculate: (a) The hydrodynamic dispersion coefficient ($D_L = \alpha_L v$), and (b) Estimate the transition zone width $W \approx 4 \sqrt{D_L t}$ after $t = 30\text{ days}$ of continuous tidal cycling.
Solution:
1. Dispersion coefficient: $$D_L = \alpha_L \cdot v = 2.0\text{ m} \times 0.4\text{ m/day} = 0.8\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$$ 2. Transition zone thickness: $$W \approx 4 \sqrt{D_L t} = 4 \sqrt{0.8 \times 30} = 4 \sqrt{24} = 4 \times 4.899 \approx 19.6\text{ meters}$$ Tidal action transforms the boundary into a $19.6\text{ m}$ wide zone of brackish water (salinity $1,000 - 30,000\text{ mg/L}$).
Problem 8: Engineered Hydraulic Pressure Barrier
To repel an advancing saline wedge, an injection well array is installed along the coast. If the required seaward gradient to halt saltwater movement is $i_{\text{req}} = 0.003$ and the coastal aquifer transmissivity is $T = 600\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$, calculate the continuous freshwater recharge rate ($q_{\text{inj}}$) required per kilometer of coastline.
Solution:
1. Recharge discharge per meter width of coast: $$q' = T \cdot i_{\text{req}} = 600\text{ m}^2/\text{day} \times 0.003 = 1.8\text{ m}^3/\text{day per m}$$ 2. Total injection discharge per kilometer ($L = 1000\text{ m}$): $$Q_{\text{total}} = q' \times L = 1.8\text{ m}^3/\text{day/m} \times 1000\text{ m} = 1,800\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$$ A line of injection wells recharging $1.8\text{ MLD}$ (million liters per day) creates a freshwater hydraulic pressure ridge that repels saltwater seaward.

Q146: Aquifer Hydraulics: Pumping Period vs Post-Pumping Residual Drawdown Recovery

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 146
Authoritative References: Charles V. Theis, The Relation Between the Lowering of the Piezometric Surface and the Rate and Duration of Discharge of a Well Using Ground-Water Storage (Trans. AGU, 1935); David K. Todd and Larry W. Mays, Groundwater Hydrology (3rd Ed., Wiley, Ch. 4: Well Hydraulics, pp. 135–158); C.W. Fetter, Applied Hydrogeology (4th Ed., Prentice Hall, Ch. 5, pp. 175–188); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 3: Hydrogeology, p. 33).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Architecture of an Aquifer Pumping Test: Pumping Phase vs Recovery Phase

In groundwater hydrology, an Aquifer Performance Test (Pumping Test) is the standard field methodology used to quantify the primary hydrodynamic parameters of an aquifer: Transmissivity ($T$) and Storativity ($S$) (Theis, 1935; Todd & Mays, 2005; Fetter, 2001; Bangar, p. 33).

A complete pumping test consists of two distinct, mutually exclusive operational periods:

  1. The Pumping Period: Water is continuously discharged from a production well at a measured rate $Q$ for a predetermined duration $t_p$. Hydraulic head declines throughout the surrounding formation, establishing a dynamic cone of depression.
  2. The Recovery Period: The pump is abruptly shut down at time $t = t_p$. Groundwater flows inward from the outer edges of the cone of depression, causing piezometric levels in the well and surrounding piezometers to rise back toward the pre-pumping static equilibrium level.
Figure 146.1 — Complete Pumping and Recovery Timeline: Evolution of water levels during continuous pumping (duration $t_p$) exhibiting active drawdown $s(t)$, followed by post-pumping recovery (elapsed recovery time $t'$) exhibiting residual drawdown $s'(t')$.

Parameters Gathered During the Active Pumping Period

While the pump is actively operating ($0 \le t \le t_p$), hydrogeologists gather three fundamental datasets:

  • Drawdown ($s$): The instantaneous vertical decline in hydraulic head relative to the initial static water table ($s = h_0 - h$).
  • Time-Drawdown Data: A continuous time series recording the progressive deepening of drawdown $s$ against elapsed pumping time $t$ in individual observation wells.
  • Distance-Drawdown Data: Simultaneous measurements of drawdown $s$ recorded at the same elapsed time across multiple observation wells located at varying radial distances $r_1, r_2, \dots, r_n$ from the pumping center.
2. Theis Recovery Method & Definition of Residual Drawdown ($s'$)
Figure 146.2 — Facsimile from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 3, p. 33): Detailed treatment of well pumping hydraulics, the principle of superposition during recovery, and semilog analysis of residual drawdown $s'$ versus dimensionless time ratio $t/t'$.

Definition of Residual Drawdown ($s'$)

Residual Drawdown ($s'$):
During the recovery period after pumping has ceased, Residual Drawdown is defined as the difference between the original pre-pumping static water level ($h_0$) and the recovering water level ($h$) at elapsed recovery time $t'$: $$s' = h_0 - h(t') \quad [\text{meters}]$$ Residual drawdown exists and is measured exclusively during the recovery period. It cannot exist during the active pumping period.

Theis Superposition Theorem for Recovery

In 1935, C.V. Theis demonstrated that recovery can be modeled mathematically by applying the Principle of Superposition:

  • Assume the pumping well continues to discharge at rate $Q$ indefinitely from $t = 0$.
  • At time $t = t_p$ (when the pump is actually shut off), an imaginary recharge well is introduced at the same location, injecting water into the aquifer at an identical rate $+Q$.

The net residual drawdown $s'$ at any elapsed recovery time $t'$ (where total elapsed time from the start of pumping is $t = t_p + t'$) is the algebraic sum of the continuing drawdown minus the recharge buildup:

$$s' = \frac{Q}{4 \pi T} \left[ W(u) - W(u') \right]$$ $$\text{where } u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} \quad \text{and} \quad u' = \frac{r^2 S'}{4 T t'}$$

For sufficiently long pumping and recovery times ($u, u' \le 0.05$), truncating the well function series yields the famous Theis Recovery Formula:

$$s' = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{t}{t'}\right)$$

A plot of residual drawdown $s'$ on arithmetic scale versus the dimensionless time ratio $t/t'$ on logarithmic scale forms a straight line whose slope $\Delta s'$ yields Transmissivity ($T$):

$$T = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi \Delta s'}$$
3. Why Hydrogeologists Prefer Recovery Analysis

In hydrogeological practice, recovery test data are often considered far more reliable and precise than active pumping test data for determining formation transmissivity:

  1. Absence of Discharge Fluctuations: During pumping, maintaining an exactly constant discharge $Q$ is difficult due to engine speed variations, generator cycling, and falling dynamic water levels. In recovery, $Q = 0$ is absolute and unvarying.
  2. Elimination of Turbulent Well Losses: In an active pumping well, turbulent frictional head loss across the well screen and gravel pack ($s_w = B Q + C Q^2$) distorts water level readings. During recovery, no water is withdrawn, eliminating turbulent wellbore head loss entirely ($C Q^2 = 0$).
  3. No Water Cascading or Entrained Air: Pumping water levels are often disrupted by cascading water from perforated casing sections above the pump inlet. Recovery levels rise smoothly under laminar conditions.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 146: Find out the term which is not related to the pumping period of a well :
(A) Drawdown
(B) Time-drawdown data
(C) Residual drawdown
(D) Distance-drawdown data
Correct Answer: (C) Residual drawdown
Forensic Analysis & Option Refutations
INCORRECT SELECTION Option (A): Drawdown

Drawdown ($s = h_0 - h$) is the primary dependent physical variable measured throughout the active pumping period of a well. It quantifies the instantaneous head drop induced by groundwater extraction. Because drawdown is intimately and directly related to the pumping period, selecting Option (A) is incorrect.

INCORRECT SELECTION Option (B): Time-drawdown data

Time-drawdown data consists of the progressive decline in piezometric head recorded against elapsed pumping time ($t$) from the start of pumping. It forms the empirical basis for the Theis curve-matching and Cooper-Jacob straight-line methods evaluated during the pumping period. Thus, Option (B) is a core pumping-phase parameter.

CORRECT ANSWER Option (C): Residual drawdown

Option (C) is the single parameter that is NOT related to the pumping period:

  • By standard hydrogeological definition (Theis, 1935; Todd & Mays; Fetter), Residual Drawdown ($s'$) is measured exclusively during the recovery period following complete pump shutdown ($t > t_p$).
  • It represents the difference between the original pre-pumping static water level and the rising water level during recovery.
  • While the pump is running, only active drawdown ($s$) exists. Residual drawdown cannot be observed until the pumping phase has fully terminated.

Therefore, Option (C) is the unambiguous correct choice.

INCORRECT SELECTION Option (D): Distance-drawdown data

Distance-drawdown data represents simultaneous measurements of drawdown across multiple observation wells located at various radial distances ($r$) from the pumping well at a specific time $t$ during the active pumping period. It is used to plot the cone of depression and calculate transmissivity and storativity via the Cooper-Jacob distance method ($s$ vs $\log r$). Hence, it belongs strictly to the pumping phase.

Hydrogeologic Synthesis: Pumping Phase vs Recovery Phase Parameters
Hydraulic Parameter Test Period Mathematical Notation Governing Analytical Relationship Physical Meaning
Active Drawdown Pumping Phase ($t \le t_p$) $$s = h_0 - h(t)$$ $$s = \frac{Q}{4 \pi T} W\left(\frac{r^2 S}{4 T t}\right)$$ Total decline of piezometric head below static baseline during pumping.
Time-Drawdown Data Pumping Phase ($t \le t_p$) $$s \text{ vs } t$$ $$s = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{2.25 T t}{r^2 S}\right)$$ Chronological progression of head drop in a single observation well.
Distance-Drawdown Data Pumping Phase ($t \le t_p$) $$s \text{ vs } r$$ $$s = \frac{2.303 Q}{2 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)$$ Radial profile of the cone of depression across multiple piezometers at fixed $t$.
Residual Drawdown Recovery Phase ONLY ($t > t_p$) $$s' = h_0 - h(t')$$ $$s' = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{t}{t'}\right)$$ Residual unrecovered head drop remaining after pump shutdown at recovery time $t'$.
Exam-Standard Well Hydraulics Practice Problems (8 Rigorous Exercises)
Problem 1: Transmissivity Determination from Theis Recovery Plot
A well is pumped at a constant discharge of $Q = 1440\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ for $t_p = 24\text{ hours}$ and then shut down. Measurements of residual drawdown $s'$ are plotted against $\log_{10}(t/t')$, where $t = t_p + t'$. The straight line fitted through the data reveals a drawdown change per log cycle of $\Delta s' = 0.92\text{ m}$. Calculate the Transmissivity ($T$) of the aquifer in: (a) $\text{m}^2/\text{day}$, and (b) $\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.
Solution:
1. Theis recovery transmissivity formula: $$T = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi \Delta s'} = \frac{2.303 \times 1440}{4 \times 3.14159 \times 0.92} = \frac{3316.32}{11.561} \approx 286.85\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$$ 2. Convert to $\text{m}^2/\text{s}$: $$T = \frac{286.85\text{ m}^2/\text{day}}{86,400\text{ s/day}} \approx 3.32 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$$
Problem 2: Calculation of Expected Residual Drawdown
A confined aquifer has $T = 400\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$. A well is pumped at $Q = 1200\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ for $t_p = 10\text{ hours}$ ($600\text{ min}$). Calculate the theoretical residual drawdown $s'$ in an observation well after: (a) $t' = 30\text{ minutes}$ of recovery, and (b) $t' = 300\text{ minutes}$ of recovery.
Solution:
1. Parameter coefficient: $$\frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} = \frac{2.303 \times 1200}{4 \times 3.14159 \times 400} = \frac{2763.6}{5026.55} \approx 0.5498\text{ meters per log cycle}$$ 2. At $t' = 30\text{ min}$, total time $t = 600 + 30 = 630\text{ min}$: $$\frac{t}{t'} = \frac{630}{30} = 21 \implies \log_{10}(21) \approx 1.3222$$ $$s'(30) = 0.5498 \times 1.3222 \approx 0.727\text{ meters}$$ 3. At $t' = 300\text{ min}$, total time $t = 600 + 300 = 900\text{ min}$: $$\frac{t}{t'} = \frac{900}{300} = 3.0 \implies \log_{10}(3.0) \approx 0.4771$$ $$s'(300) = 0.5498 \times 0.4771 \approx 0.262\text{ meters}$$
Problem 3: Hydrogeologic Boundary Diagnostics from Recovery Intercept
In an ideal infinite, homogeneous, isotropic confined aquifer, the theoretical straight line of $s'$ vs $\log(t/t')$ extrapolates to zero residual drawdown ($s' = 0$) at precisely $t/t' = 1.0$. Explain what hydrogeologic conditions are indicated if field data extrapolate to: (a) $t/t' > 1.0$ at $s' = 0$, and (b) $t/t' < 1.0$ at $s' = 0$.
Solution:
1. Case (a) $t/t' > 1.0$ at $s' = 0$: The recovering water level reaches static equilibrium before $t/t' = 1.0$. This signifies that the aquifer received recharge from an external source during the test (e.g., intersection with a recharge boundary such as a perennial river or lake, or downward leakage from an overlying formation).
2. Case (b) $t/t' < 1.0$ at $s' = 0$: The straight line extrapolates to a value of $t/t' < 1.0$, meaning that even after infinite recovery time ($t' \to \infty, t/t' \to 1.0$), some residual drawdown remains unrecovered. This indicates either an impermeable barrier boundary (fault, bedrock pinchout), aquifer depletive overdraft, or that storativity during recovery ($S'$) differs from storativity during pumping ($S$).
Problem 4: Distance-Drawdown Determination of Storativity
During the active pumping period of a test ($Q = 2000\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$, $t = 480\text{ minutes} = 0.333\text{ days}$), simultaneous drawdowns measured in two piezometers are $s_1 = 1.85\text{ m}$ at $r_1 = 20\text{ m}$, and $s_2 = 0.95\text{ m}$ at $r_2 = 80\text{ m}$. Calculate: (a) Aquifer Transmissivity ($T$), and (b) Aquifer Storativity ($S$).
Solution:
1. Distance-drawdown formula: $$s_1 - s_2 = \frac{2.303 Q}{2 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)$$ $$1.85 - 0.95 = 0.90\text{ m} = \frac{2.303 \times 2000}{2 \times 3.14159 \times T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{80}{20}\right) = \frac{4606}{6.2832 T} \log_{10}(4)$$ $$0.90 = \frac{733.06}{T} \times 0.60206 = \frac{441.35}{T} \implies T = \frac{441.35}{0.90} \approx 490.4\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$$ 2. Zero-drawdown radius ($r_0$): $$s_1 = \frac{2.303 Q}{2 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_0}{r_1}\right) \implies 1.85 = \frac{4606}{3081.2} \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_0}{20}\right) = 1.4948 \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_0}{20}\right)$$ $$\log_{10}\left(\frac{r_0}{20}\right) = \frac{1.85}{1.4948} = 1.2376 \implies \frac{r_0}{20} = 10^{1.2376} \approx 17.28 \implies r_0 \approx 345.6\text{ m}$$ 3. Storativity: $$S = \frac{2.25 T t}{r_0^2} = \frac{2.25 \times 490.4 \times 0.333}{(345.6)^2} = \frac{367.43}{119,439} \approx 3.08 \times 10^{-3}$$
Problem 5: Wellbore Storage Distortion at Very Early Recovery Time
In a pumping well of casing radius $r_c = 0.15\text{ m}$, water level recovery is initially dominated by wellbore storage (casing refilling) rather than aquifer inflow. The critical time after which wellbore storage effects become negligible is given by Papadopulos and Cooper (1967) as $t'_c \ge \frac{25 r_c^2}{T}$. For $T = 150\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$, calculate $t'_c$ in seconds.
Solution:
1. Calculate $t'_c$ in days: $$t'_c = \frac{25 \times (0.15)^2}{150} = \frac{25 \times 0.0225}{150} = \frac{0.5625}{150} = 0.00375\text{ days}$$ 2. Convert to minutes and seconds: $$t'_c = 0.00375\text{ days} \times 1440\text{ min/day} = 5.4\text{ minutes} = 324\text{ seconds}$$ Recovery data collected prior to $5.4\text{ minutes}$ reflect water filling the open casing rather than true Darcy flow through the aquifer formation.
Problem 6: Well Efficiency and Turbulent Skin Effect
During pumping at $Q = 1500\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$, the total drawdown measured inside the pumped well is $s_w = 6.80\text{ m}$. Transmissivity computed from recovery analysis is $T = 320\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$, which predicts a theoretical laminar aquifer drawdown of $s_{\text{formation}} = 4.25\text{ m}$. (a) Calculate the well loss component ($s_{\text{well loss}}$). (b) Determine the Well Efficiency ($E_w$).
Solution:
1. Well loss due to screen entrance turbulence and gravel pack head loss: $$s_{\text{well loss}} = s_w - s_{\text{formation}} = 6.80\text{ m} - 4.25\text{ m} = 2.55\text{ meters}$$ 2. Well Efficiency: $$E_w = \left(\frac{s_{\text{formation}}}{s_w}\right) \times 100\% = \left(\frac{4.25}{6.80}\right) \times 100\% \approx 62.5\%$$ Recovery testing uniquely isolated the true aquifer transmissivity without distortion from the $2.55\text{ m}$ well loss.
Problem 7: Residual Drawdown under Step-Drawdown Pumping History
A well is pumped in two consecutive steps before shutdown: Step 1 at $Q_1 = 800\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ for duration $t_1 = 4\text{ hours}$ ($240\text{ min}$), followed immediately by Step 2 at $Q_2 = 1400\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ for duration $t_2 = 4\text{ hours}$ ($240\text{ min}$, total pumping $t_p = 480\text{ min}$). Formulate the generalized superposition recovery equation for residual drawdown $s'$ at recovery time $t'$.
Solution:
1. By generalized multi-rate superposition: $$s'(t') = \frac{2.303}{4 \pi T} \left[ Q_1 \log_{10}\left(\frac{t_1 + t_2 + t'}{t_2 + t'}\right) + Q_2 \log_{10}\left(\frac{t_2 + t'}{t'}\right) \right]$$ 2. For $t' = 60\text{ min}$: $$s'(60) = \frac{2.303}{4 \pi T} \left[ 800 \log_{10}\left(\frac{240 + 240 + 60}{240 + 60}\right) + 1400 \log_{10}\left(\frac{240 + 60}{60}\right) \right]$$ $$s'(60) = \frac{2.303}{4 \pi T} \left[ 800 \log_{10}\left(\frac{540}{300}\right) + 1400 \log_{10}(5) \right] = \frac{2.303}{4 \pi T} [ 800(0.2553) + 1400(0.6990) ]$$ $$s'(60) = \frac{2.303}{4 \pi T} [ 204.24 + 978.60 ] = \frac{2.303 \times 1182.84}{4 \pi T}$$
Problem 8: Comparison Between Pumping and Recovery Data Robustness
A field pump test experiences an unmonitored generator throttle surge at $t = 180\text{ minutes}$ that increases discharge from $1000\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ to $1150\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$. Explain why this generator failure invalidates Cooper-Jacob pumping curve analysis but leaves subsequent post-shutdown Theis recovery analysis unaffected if the final rate is recorded.
Solution:
1. Pumping Period Invalidation: Cooper-Jacob and Theis type-curve methods strictly assume a constant discharge $Q$. The $15\%$ jump in $Q$ creates a secondary pressure wave, causing drawdowns to deviate unpredictably from the standard logarithmic curve and producing erroneous values for $T$ and $S$.
2. Recovery Period Robustness: Once the pump is completely stopped, the discharge is exactly $Q = 0.000\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$ with zero fluctuations. The subsequent recovery curve converges to the late-time average discharge, allowing reliable evaluation of formation transmissivity.

Q147: Cooper-Jacob Straight-Line Method: Mathematical Limits of Validity ($u \le 0.05$)

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 147
Authoritative References: Hilton H. Cooper and C.E. Jacob, A Generalized Graphical Method for Evaluating Formation Constants and Summarizing Well-Field History (Trans. AGU, 1946, Vol. 27, pp. 526–534); David K. Todd and Larry W. Mays, Groundwater Hydrology (3rd Ed., Wiley, Ch. 4: Well Hydraulics, pp. 140–152); C.W. Fetter, Applied Hydrogeology (4th Ed., Prentice Hall, Ch. 5, pp. 170–182); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 3: Hydrogeology, p. 34).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Theis Well Function & The Cooper-Jacob Semilog Simplification

In 1935, Charles V. Theis derived the exact non-equilibrium equation for transient radial groundwater flow to a pumping well in a confined, homogeneous, isotropic aquifer:

$$s = \frac{Q}{4 \pi T} W(u)$$ $$\text{where } u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t}$$

Here, $s$ is drawdown, $Q$ is constant pumping discharge, $T$ is aquifer transmissivity, $S$ is storativity, $r$ is radial distance to the observation well, $t$ is elapsed pumping time, and $W(u)$ is the exponential integral (the Theis Well Function), expandable as an infinite convergent Taylor-Maclaurin series:

$$W(u) = -0.57721566 - \ln(u) + u - \frac{u^2}{2 \cdot 2!} + \frac{u^3}{3 \cdot 3!} - \frac{u^4}{4 \cdot 4!} + \dots$$
Figure 147.1 — Theis Type Curve vs Cooper-Jacob Straight-Line Approximation: Comparison of exact Theis $W(u)$ against Cooper-Jacob semilog straight line. For small $u \le 0.05$ (large $t$ or small $r$), the two models merge seamlessly (error $< 2\%$). For large $u > 0.05$ (short test duration or distant piezometer), the Cooper-Jacob line diverges severely into non-linear deviation.

The Cooper-Jacob Straight-Line Formula (1946)

In 1946, Hilton H. Cooper and C.E. Jacob noted that when the dimensionless argument $u$ is sufficiently small ($u \le 0.05$ or $u \le 0.01$), all higher-order polynomial terms in the expansion ($u - u^2/4 + \dots$) become negligibly small and can be dropped without significant loss of accuracy:

$$W(u) \approx -\ln(u) - 0.5772 = \ln\left(\frac{1}{u}\right) - \ln(1.781) = \ln\left(\frac{1}{1.781 u}\right) = \ln\left(\frac{0.5615}{u}\right) = \ln\left(\frac{2.25}{4 u}\right)$$ $$W(u) \approx \ln\left(\frac{2.25 T t}{r^2 S}\right) = 2.303 \log_{10}\left(\frac{2.25 T t}{r^2 S}\right)$$

Substituting this into the drawdown equation gives the Cooper-Jacob Semilog Equation:

$$s = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{2.25 T t}{r^2 S}\right)$$

Plotting drawdown $s$ on an arithmetic scale against elapsed time $t$ on a logarithmic scale yields a straight line with slope $\Delta s$ (drawdown per log cycle of time):

$$T = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi \Delta s} \quad \text{and} \quad S = \frac{2.25 T t_0}{r^2}$$
2. The Critical Invalidity Criterion ($u > 0.05$): When Cooper-Jacob CANNOT Be Used
Figure 147.2 — Facsimile from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 3, p. 34): Derivation of the Cooper-Jacob modification, explicit definition of the dimensionless variable $u$, and the mathematical threshold condition $u < 0.05$ restricting valid semilog graphical analysis.

The Fundamental Limit of Validity

The Cooper-Jacob straight-line approximation is mathematically valid if and only if:

$$u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} \le 0.05 \quad (\text{or } u \le 0.01 \text{ for } < 1\% \text{ error})$$

Conversely, the Cooper-Jacob method CANNOT BE USED whenever:

$$u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} > 0.05$$

Deconstruction of the Inequality

Examining the algebraic structure of the fraction $u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t}$ reveals exactly what physical test conditions cause $u$ to exceed $0.05$:

  1. Condition (i) — When the pump test is of SHORT duration ($t$ is small):
    Because elapsed pumping time $t$ resides in the denominator, when $t$ is small (during early test stages or short-duration pumping), the quotient $\frac{r^2 S}{4 T t}$ becomes large ($u \gg 0.05$). The higher-order terms in the series cannot be neglected, the semilog plot is non-linear and curved, and applying Cooper-Jacob results in catastrophic errors. (Method cannot be used!)
  2. Condition (iii) — When the observation well is situated FAR AWAY from the main well ($r$ is large):
    Because radial distance $r$ resides in the numerator as a squared term ($r^2$), any increase in $r$ dramatically magnifies $u$. For a distant piezometer, the cone of depression has not sufficiently developed, making $u \gg 0.05$ throughout most or all of the test. (Method cannot be used!)

Why Conditions (ii) and (iv) FAVOR the Cooper-Jacob Method

  • Condition (ii) — When the pump test is of LONG duration ($t$ is large): As $t \to \infty$, the denominator grows enormous, driving $u \to 0$ ($u \ll 0.01$). This makes Cooper-Jacob maximally accurate and fully valid!
  • Condition (iv) — When the observation well is situated NEAR to the main well ($r$ is small): A small radial distance $r$ minimizes the $r^2$ numerator, ensuring that $u \le 0.01$ is achieved almost immediately after pumping begins. This makes Cooper-Jacob ideally suited.
Definitive Exam Conclusion:
The Cooper-Jacob method CANNOT be used under (i) short duration and (iii) distant observation well, because both conditions force $u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} > 0.05$.
3. Quantitative Error Progression as a Function of $u$
Dimensionless Variable $u$ Exact Theis $W(u)$ Cooper-Jacob Approximation $\ln(2.25 / u)$ Truncation Error (%) Applicability Status
$0.001$ $6.3315$ $6.3324$ $+0.01\%$ Perfect
$0.010$ $4.0379$ $4.0395$ $+0.04\%$ Excellent ($< 1\%$ error)
$0.050$ $2.4679$ $2.5157$ $+1.94\%$ Standard Cutoff Limit ($< 2\%$ error)
$0.100$ $1.8229$ $1.9363$ $+6.22\%$ Marginal (Error $> 5\%$)
$0.200$ $1.2227$ $1.3787$ $+12.76\%$ INVALID (Error $> 12\%$)
$0.500$ $0.5598$ $0.7675$ $+37.10\%$ FATALLY INVALID (Error $> 37\%$)
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 147: Conditions under which Jacob-Cooper method cannot be used for analysis of pump test data :
(i) When the pump test is of short duration,
(ii) When the pump test is of long duration,
(iii) When the observation well is situated far away from the main well,
(iv) When the observation well is situated nearer to the main well.
Choose the correct set of answer from the following :
(A) (i) and (iii)
(B) (ii) and (iii)
(C) (ii) and (iv)
(D) (i) and (iv)
Correct Answer: (A) (i) and (iii)
Forensic Analysis & Option Refutations
CORRECT Option (A): (i) and (iii)

Option (A) combines the exact two physical conditions that violate the mathematical validity criterion of the Cooper-Jacob semilog method ($u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} \le 0.05$):

  • Condition (i) — Short Duration ($t$ small): When the pump test has run for only a brief period, $t$ is small, causing the denominator $4 T t$ to be small, driving $u > 0.05$. The drawdown curve on semilog paper is strongly concave and has not yet straightened.
  • Condition (iii) — Distant Observation Well ($r$ large): Because distance enters as $r^2$, locating the piezometer far away magnifies the numerator enormously, forcing $u > 0.05$. For distant wells, hours or days of pumping are needed before the straight-line approximation becomes valid.

Because both (i) and (iii) invalidate the straight-line assumption, Option (A) is the indisputably correct answer.

INCORRECT Option (B): (ii) and (iii)

Option (B) includes Condition (ii) ("When the pump test is of long duration"). Long duration means $t$ is large, which drives $u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} \to 0$ ($u \ll 0.01$). This is precisely the operational condition under which the Cooper-Jacob method is most reliable, accurate, and recommended! Because Condition (ii) is a condition of validity rather than invalidity, Option (B) is incorrect.

INCORRECT Option (C): (ii) and (iv)

Option (C) pairs Condition (ii) (long duration) with Condition (iv) (observation well situated near to the main well). This represents the gold standard, ideal operational domain for applying the Cooper-Jacob method: small $r$ minimizes the numerator while large $t$ maximizes the denominator, producing $u < 0.001$ where truncation error is less than $0.01\%$. Claiming the method cannot be used under these conditions is completely contrary to hydrogeologic science.

INCORRECT Option (D): (i) and (iv)

While Condition (i) is an invalidating condition, Condition (iv) ("When the observation well is situated nearer to the main well") dramatically assists validity because a small $r$ keeps $r^2$ small, helping $u$ drop below $0.05$ very rapidly. Therefore, Condition (iv) is not a condition under which the method cannot be used, refuting Option (D).

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Hydrogeologic Synthesis: Pumping Test Analytical Methods Comparison
Analytical Method Mathematical Formulation Plot Coordinates Validity Limits / Constraints Best Field Domain
Theis Type Curve (1935) $$s = \frac{Q}{4 \pi T} W(u)$$ $\log s$ vs $\log(t / r^2)$ Universal: Valid for all values of $u$ ($0 < u < \infty$); requires curve superposition. Short-duration tests, early pumping data, and distant observation wells ($u > 0.05$).
Cooper-Jacob Semilog (1946) $$s = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{2.25 T t}{r^2 S}\right)$$ $s$ vs $\log t$ or $s$ vs $\log r$ Restricted: Valid ONLY when $u \le 0.05$ (fails when $t$ is small or $r$ is large). Late-time pumping data ($t > t_{\min}$), near observation wells, and single-well production tests.
Chow Method (1952) $$F(u) = \frac{s}{\Delta s}, \quad W(u) = 4 \pi \frac{s \cdot T}{Q}$$ $s$ vs $\log t$ nomograph Valid for all $u$, but avoids curve matching by calculating slope $F(u)$ at any chosen point. Quick parameter estimation without requiring full Theis curve overlay sheets.
Exam-Standard Well Hydraulics Practice Problems (8 Rigorous Exercises)
Problem 1: Minimum Time ($t_{\min}$) Calculation for Cooper-Jacob Validity
A pumping test is conducted in a confined aquifer with Transmissivity $T = 360\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$ and Storativity $S = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$. An observation well is located at distance $r = 60\text{ m}$ from the pumping well. Calculate the minimum elapsed pumping time ($t_{\min}$) in minutes after which the Cooper-Jacob method can be legitimately applied under the standard criterion $u \le 0.05$.
Solution:
1. Validity threshold formula: $$u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} \le 0.05 \implies t \ge \frac{r^2 S}{4 T \times 0.05} = \frac{r^2 S}{0.20 T} = \frac{5 r^2 S}{T}$$ 2. Substitute given values: $$t_{\min} = \frac{5 \times (60\text{ m})^2 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-4})}{360\text{ m}^2/\text{day}} = \frac{5 \times 3600 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-4})}{360} = \frac{3.6}{360} = 0.010\text{ days}$$ 3. Convert to minutes: $$t_{\min} = 0.010\text{ days} \times 1440\text{ min/day} = 14.4\text{ minutes}$$ Conclusion: For the first $14.4\text{ minutes}$ of pumping, $u > 0.05$ and Cooper-Jacob CANNOT be used. Only time-drawdown data collected after $t \ge 14.4\text{ min}$ may be fitted to the straight line.
Problem 2: Maximum Distance ($r_{\max}$) for Short Pumping Duration
Due to mechanical failure, a pump test must be terminated after only $t = 30\text{ minutes} = 0.02083\text{ days}$. The aquifer has $T = 500\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$ and $S = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$. Calculate the maximum radial distance ($r_{\max}$) of an observation well that can be analyzed using the Cooper-Jacob method ($u \le 0.05$).
Solution:
1. Rearrange $u \le 0.05$ for radial distance $r$: $$r^2 \le \frac{0.05 \times 4 T t}{S} = \frac{0.20 T t}{S}$$ $$r_{\max} = \sqrt{\frac{0.20 \times 500\text{ m}^2/\text{day} \times 0.02083\text{ days}}{1.5 \times 10^{-4}}} = \sqrt{\frac{2.083}{1.5 \times 10^{-4}}} = \sqrt{13,886.7} \approx 117.8\text{ meters}$$ Any observation well located beyond $118\text{ meters}$ has $u > 0.05$ and cannot be interpreted via the Cooper-Jacob method for this short test.
Problem 3: Numerical Error Analysis at $u = 0.20$
A hydrogeologist uses the Cooper-Jacob equation to estimate drawdown at a point where $u = 0.20$. Exact Theis well function is $W(0.20) = 1.2227$. (a) Calculate the Cooper-Jacob approximation $W_{\text{CJ}} = \ln(2.25 / 0.20)$. (b) Determine the percentage overestimation error.
Solution:
1. Cooper-Jacob approximation: $$W_{\text{CJ}} = \ln\left(\frac{2.25}{0.20}\right) = \ln(11.25) \approx 2.4204 - 0.5772 = 1.3787$$ 2. Error calculation: $$\text{Absolute Error} = 1.3787 - 1.2227 = +0.1560$$ $$\text{Percentage Error} = \left(\frac{0.1560}{1.2227}\right) \times 100\% \approx +12.76\%$$ Using Cooper-Jacob when $u = 0.20$ overestimates drawdown by nearly $13\%$, leading to severe errors in calculated aquifer transmissivity.
Problem 4: Complete Cooper-Jacob Time-Drawdown Parameter Evaluation
A well is pumped at $Q = 1800\text{ m}^3/\text{day}$. An observation well at $r = 40\text{ m}$ produces a semilog time-drawdown plot whose valid straight-line portion ($u \le 0.05$) yields a drawdown per log cycle of $\Delta s = 1.12\text{ m}$ and intersects the zero-drawdown axis at $t_0 = 1.8\text{ minutes} = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}\text{ days}$. Calculate: (a) Transmissivity ($T$), and (b) Storativity ($S$).
Solution:
1. Transmissivity: $$T = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi \Delta s} = \frac{2.303 \times 1800}{4 \times 3.14159 \times 1.12} = \frac{4145.4}{14.074} \approx 294.54\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$$ 2. Storativity: $$S = \frac{2.25 T t_0}{r^2} = \frac{2.25 \times 294.54 \times (1.25 \times 10^{-3})}{40^2} = \frac{0.8284}{1600} \approx 5.18 \times 10^{-4}$$
Problem 5: Verification of Data Points Excluded by $u \le 0.05$ Rule
For the test in Problem 4 ($T = 294.54\text{ m}^2/\text{day}$, $S = 5.18 \times 10^{-4}$, $r = 40\text{ m}$), verify whether drawdown recorded at $t = 5\text{ minutes}$ ($0.00347\text{ days}$) can be included in the Cooper-Jacob straight line.
Solution:
1. Compute $u$ at $t = 5\text{ minutes}$: $$u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} = \frac{(40)^2 \times (5.18 \times 10^{-4})}{4 \times 294.54 \times 0.00347} = \frac{1600 \times (5.18 \times 10^{-4})}{4.088} = \frac{0.8288}{4.088} \approx 0.2027$$ 2. Evaluate criterion: $$u = 0.2027 > 0.05$$ Conclusion: Because $u > 0.05$, the 5-minute data point MUST BE EXCLUDED from the straight line fit. The minimum valid time is $t_{\min} = \frac{5 r^2 S}{T} = \frac{5 \times 0.8288}{294.54} = 0.01407\text{ days} = 20.3\text{ minutes}$.
Problem 6: Delayed Drainage Plateau in Unconfined Aquifers
Explain why the Cooper-Jacob straight line method fails in unconfined aquifers during intermediate pumping times ($10\text{ min} < t < 4\text{ hours}$), even though $t$ appears sufficiently large.
Solution:
1. The Cooper-Jacob method assumes strictly horizontal, 2-dimensional radial flow with constant storativity $S$.
2. In an unconfined aquifer during intermediate pumping times, delayed gravity drainage occurs as pore water drains vertically down from the descending capillary fringe.
3. This creates strong vertical flow components ($v_z \ne 0$) and a temporary flattening (plateau) in the drawdown curve where drawdown ceases to follow a logarithmic line.
4. Only after late time ($t > 4\text{ hours}$), when vertical gradients vanish and full specific yield ($S_y$) is mobilized, does a second, parallel Cooper-Jacob straight line emerge.
Problem 7: Impermeable Fault Boundary Slope Doubling
During a Cooper-Jacob pumping test, the initial straight line slope is $\Delta s_1 = 0.80\text{ m}$. At $t = 120\text{ minutes}$, the cone of depression intersects a planar impermeable normal fault. (a) What will be the new slope $\Delta s_2$ of the semilog straight line at late time? (b) Explain the mathematical cause using image well theory.
Solution:
1. By Image Well Theory, an impermeable barrier boundary is mathematically equivalent to placing an imaginary discharge well pumping at identical rate $+Q$ located symmetrically across the fault barrier.
2. At late time, both real and image wells contribute equal drawdown to the observation well: $$s_{\text{total}} = s_{\text{real}} + s_{\text{image}} = \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log(t) + \frac{2.303 Q}{4 \pi T} \log(t) = \frac{2.303 (2Q)}{4 \pi T} \log(t)$$ 3. The slope exactly doubles: $$\Delta s_2 = 2 \times \Delta s_1 = 2 \times 0.80\text{ m} = 1.60\text{ meters per log cycle}$$
Problem 8: Recharge Boundary Stabilization
If the cone of depression intersects a fully penetrating perennial river instead of an impermeable fault, describe the behavior of the Cooper-Jacob semilog drawdown curve at late time.
Solution:
1. An open surface water body acts as a constant-head recharge boundary ($s = 0$ along the riverline).
2. By image well theory, this is modeled by an imaginary recharge well injecting water at rate $-Q$.
3. At late time, the recharge cancels all further expansion of the cone of depression. Drawdown stabilizes to a steady-state value ($ds/dt = 0$), and the slope of the semilog curve becomes zero (horizontal straight line).

Q148: Water Well Drilling in the Bhabar Piedmont: Why Cable Tool Percussion is the Proven Standard

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 148
Authoritative References: Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), Manual on Ground Water and Water Well Drilling in Difficult Boulder Formations; David K. Todd and Larry W. Mays, Groundwater Hydrology (3rd Ed., Wiley, Ch. 5: Water Well Drilling & Design, pp. 185–215); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 3: Hydrogeology, p. 35); Fletcher G. Driscoll, Groundwater and Wells (2nd Ed., Johnson Screens, pp. 268–315).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Geological Framework of the Himalayan Bhabar Piedmont Zone

The Bhabar Zone is a continuous, $10\text{ to }25\text{ km}$ wide piedmont alluvial belt situated along the southern foothills of the Siwalik range / Outer Himalayas in northern and eastern India (Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, West Bengal, and Assam) (CGWB, 2018; Bangar, p. 35; Todd & Mays, 2005).

From an engineering and hydrogeological drilling perspective, the Bhabar formation presents one of the most hostile and challenging sub-surface environments in the world:

  • Lithological Chaos: The formation comprises unassorted, coarse torrent deposits including massive quartzite, granite, and sandstone boulders (ranging from $30\text{ cm}$ to over $1.5\text{ meters}$ in diameter), gravels, pebbles, and coarse sands with virtually no binding clay matrix.
  • Extreme Hydraulic Conductivity & Porosity: The boulder matrix possesses cavernous void spaces and enormous hydraulic conductivities ($K > 100 - 300\text{ m/day}$).
  • Deep Water Table: Due to rapid infiltration, the water table in the Bhabar is extraordinarily deep (often lying $50\text{ to }120\text{ meters}$ below ground surface).
  • Zero Borehole Stability: Unconsolidated boulders lack all cohesion; any unsupported vertical borehole wall collapses instantaneously.
Figure 148.1 — Mechanics of Cable Tool Percussion Drilling in Boulder Strata: The massive chisel bit smashes and shatters hard quartzite boulders through reciprocating vertical impacts ($40-60\text{ blows/min}$), while a heavy steel casing is simultaneously driven downward using drive clamps, continuously supporting the collapsible borehole walls without drilling mud.
2. Technological Deconstruction: Why Hydraulic Rotary Methods Fail in Boulder Beds
Figure 148.2 — Facsimile from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 3, p. 35): Classification of water well drilling methods, highlighting the operational necessity of cable tool percussion with concurrent casing drive for boulder-gravel piedmont formations.

1. Catastrophic Failure of Direct Mud Rotary

In direct mud rotary drilling, bentonite mud is pumped down the drill pipe to lubricate the bit and float cuttings upward through the open annulus. In the Bhabar boulder bed:

  1. 100% Circulation Loss ("Blind Drilling"): The drilling fluid disappears instantly into the cavernous voids between boulders. Without returning mud, cuttings cannot be brought to the surface, and the fluid column disappears.
  2. Borehole Collapse: The moment mud hydrostatic pressure is lost, the loose boulder gravels cave in around the drill string, seizing and burying the drill bit and drill collars.
  3. Bit Deflection and Tooth Destruction: Tricone roller cone bits deflect violently off smooth, spherical quartzite boulders, causing crooked holes and shearing off tungsten-carbide teeth.

2. Impossibility of Reverse Circulation Rotary

Reverse rotary requires the annular space to remain filled with fluid to the ground surface. In the Bhabar, maintaining a surface fluid head is physically impossible because water drains into the boulder bed faster than high-capacity pumps can replenish it. Furthermore, boulders larger than the drill pipe diameter ($150\text{ mm}$) cannot pass up the pipe.

3. Failure of Air Rotary (DTH Hammer)

While down-the-hole (DTH) hammers can crush hard rock, compressed air dissipates rapidly into the porous boulder voids, destroying the uphole annular air velocity required to lift heavy cobbles. Furthermore, without a continuous casing, the loose borehole walls collapse over the top of the hammer, trapping thousands of dollars of equipment downhole.

3. Working Principles of the Cable Tool Method in Boulder Formations

The Cable Tool Percussion Method (spudder rig) is the time-tested, Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) mandated method for drilling production wells in Bhabar boulder tracts:

  1. Crushing Heavy Chisel Bit: A heavy drill string—consisting of a wire rope socket, drilling jars, a massive drill stem, and a heavy chisel bit (total string weight $1,500\text{ to }3,500\text{ kg}$)—is raised and dropped $40\text{ to }60\text{ times per minute}$ by a walking beam mechanism. The immense kinetic impact delivers thousands of joules of localized crushing energy, shattering even the hardest quartzite and crystalline boulders into small fragments.
  2. Simultaneous Casing Driving: As the bit pulverizes the formation, a heavy-duty steel well casing equipped with a hardened forged steel drive shoe is driven downward simultaneously using drive clamps attached to the drill stem. The casing advances step-by-step with the hole, permanently supporting the loose borehole walls and preventing any collapse.
  3. No Drilling Mud Required: The method requires only a small volume of water poured into the bottom of the casing to turn pulverized rock into a slurry. Mud chemicals are not required, preserving the natural high permeability of the aquifer.
  4. Bailing Extraction: When slurry accumulates, the tool string is hoisted out, and a cylindrical dart-valve or sand pump bailer is run downhole to scoop out the crushed cuttings.
CGWB Benchmark Conclusion:
Because the Cable Tool Method concurrently crushes massive boulders and drives heavy steel casing to prevent wall collapse without needing circulating fluid, it is the only traditional method suitable for drilling in the Bhabar piedmont zone.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 148: The suitable method of drilling in the Piedmont zone (Bhabar) occurring adjacent to the Himalayan foothills is :
(A) Rotary method
(B) Cable tool method
(C) Reverse rotary method
(D) Air rotary method
Correct Answer: (B) Cable tool method
Forensic Analysis & Option Refutations
INCORRECT Option (A): Rotary method

Direct rotary drilling is entirely unsuited for the Bhabar boulder zone. The high void ratio and cavernous permeability of unconsolidated boulder gravels cause instantaneous and total loss of circulation (100% mud loss into the formation). Without fluid circulation, the open borehole walls collapse instantly, burying and seizing the drill bit and drill pipe. Furthermore, roller cone bits bounce violently off hard quartzite boulders, leading to crooked boreholes and severe mechanical fatigue failure.

CORRECT Option (B): Cable tool method

The Cable Tool (Percussion) Method is the recognized, authoritative standard for the Himalayan Bhabar piedmont belt (CGWB Manual; Bangar, p. 35):

  • Its reciprocating, multi-ton chisel bit delivers high-energy impact shocks that pulverize hard quartzite and crystalline boulders into gravel/sand-sized chips.
  • A heavy steel drive casing fitted with a hardened drive shoe is driven down concurrently with the drilling advance, 100% encasing and supporting the unstable loose boulder walls.
  • It operates without circulating drilling mud, eliminating the hazard of lost circulation and preventing mud caking across the productive aquifer zones.

Therefore, Option (B) is the universally recognized correct engineering and geological choice.

INCORRECT Option (C): Reverse rotary method

Reverse circulation rotary drilling requires a large, continuous hydrostatic water head maintained in an open, un-cased annular space to support the borehole walls. In the porous, unconfined Bhabar boulder bed, water drains away into the gravels immediately, causing violent borehole collapse. Additionally, reverse rotary suction pipes cannot evacuate cobbles and boulders exceeding the drill pipe inner diameter ($150\text{ mm}$), resulting in pipe clogging.

INCORRECT Option (D): Air rotary method

Standard air rotary and down-the-hole (DTH) hammer drilling fail in unconsolidated boulder gravels because the pressurized air stream escapes laterally into the porous boulder voids, destroying the annular velocity needed to lift heavy rock fragments to the surface. Most critically, because the borehole walls remain un-cased during drilling, loose boulders and cobbles dislodge and cave in above the hammer, permanently trapping the drill string downhole.

Exam-Standard Well Engineering Practice Problems (8 Rigorous Exercises)
Problem 1: Kinetic Energy of Cable Tool Chisel Impact
A cable tool rig operates in a Bhabar boulder bed with a tool string (jars, stem, and chisel bit) having a total mass of $M = 1800\text{ kg}$. The spudder mechanism drops the tools through a stroke height of $h = 0.85\text{ m}$ at a frequency of $52\text{ strokes/min}$. Assuming gravitational acceleration $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ and mechanical efficiency $\eta = 88\%$: (a) Calculate the kinetic energy delivered per impact blow. (b) Determine the average crushing power delivered to the rock face in kilowatts ($\text{kW}$).
Solution:
1. Impact energy per blow ($E$): $$E = \eta \cdot M \cdot g \cdot h = 0.88 \times 1800\text{ kg} \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2 \times 0.85\text{ m} = 13,205.8\text{ Joules} \approx 13.21\text{ kJ}$$ 2. Total energy delivered per minute: $$E_{\text{min}} = 13,205.8\text{ J/blow} \times 52\text{ blows/min} = 686,701.6\text{ J/min}$$ 3. Power delivered to the rock face: $$P = \frac{686,701.6\text{ J}}{60\text{ seconds}} \approx 11,445\text{ Watts} \approx 11.45\text{ kW}$$ This continuous delivery of $13.2\text{ kJ}$ per blow shatters tough quartzite boulders that would destroy rotary bits.
Problem 2: Volume of Boulders and Bailing Cycles
A $350\text{ mm}$ diameter borehole is advanced through a Bhabar boulder bed for a depth of $\Delta L = 6.0\text{ m}$. Due to mechanical crushing and fragmentation, the pulverized cuttings exhibit a bulking factor of $B = 1.35$. If the capacity of the bailer is $V_{\text{bailer}} = 0.12\text{ m}^3$ and it fills to $80\%$ capacity on average, calculate the minimum number of bailing runs required.
Solution:
1. In-situ volume of borehole drilled: $$V_{\text{solid}} = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} \cdot \Delta L = \frac{\pi \times (0.35\text{ m})^2}{4} \times 6.0\text{ m} = 0.09621\text{ m}^2 \times 6.0\text{ m} \approx 0.5773\text{ m}^3$$ 2. Bulked volume of pulverized cuttings: $$V_{\text{cuttings}} = V_{\text{solid}} \times B = 0.5773\text{ m}^3 \times 1.35 \approx 0.7794\text{ m}^3$$ 3. Effective volume per bailing run: $$V_{\text{eff}} = 0.12\text{ m}^3 \times 0.80 = 0.096\text{ m}^3/\text{run}$$ 4. Number of bailing runs: $$N = \frac{0.7794}{0.096} \approx 8.12 \implies \mathbf{9\text{ bailing runs}}$$
Problem 3: Fluid Loss Calculation in Direct Rotary Attempt
A contractor mistakenly attempts direct mud rotary drilling in a Bhabar boulder zone. The borehole diameter is $D = 300\text{ mm}$, penetrating a boulder formation of hydraulic conductivity $K = 180\text{ m/day} = 2.083 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m/s}$. The excess hydrostatic pressure head of the drilling mud column over the formation water table is $\Delta h = 15\text{ m}$. Using Thiem's radial flow approximation for cylindrical seepage over an uncased $5\text{ m}$ interval ($r_w = 0.15\text{ m}$, influence radius $R = 3.0\text{ m}$), calculate the rate of mud loss into the formation in $\text{liters/second}$.
Solution:
1. Seepage discharge equation: $$Q = \frac{2 \pi K \cdot b \cdot \Delta h}{\ln(R / r_w)}$$ 2. Substitute values ($b = 5\text{ m}$, $\ln(3.0 / 0.15) = \ln(20) \approx 2.9957$): $$Q = \frac{2 \times 3.14159 \times (2.083 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m/s}) \times 5.0\text{ m} \times 15\text{ m}}{2.9957} = \frac{0.9817}{2.9957} \approx 0.3277\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$$ 3. Convert to liters per second: $$Q = 0.3277\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \times 1000\text{ L/m}^3 \approx 327.7\text{ liters/second}$$ Insight: An entire $10\text{ m}^3$ mud pit would be drained in just 30 seconds, explaining why mud circulation is physically impossible in Bhabar boulders.
Problem 4: Dynamic Casing Drive Resistance (Hiley Formula)
A heavy steel casing of total mass $W_c = 4200\text{ kg}$ is driven into Bhabar gravel using drive clamps on a drill stem of falling weight $W = 1600\text{ kg}$ dropped from height $H = 0.70\text{ m}$. The observed permanent penetration set per blow is $s = 4.0\text{ mm} = 0.004\text{ m}$, and elastic temporary compression is $c = 6.0\text{ mm} = 0.006\text{ m}$. The coefficient of restitution between steel faces is $e = 0.50$. Calculate the ultimate dynamic soil resistance $R_u$ in kilonewtons ($\text{kN}$).
Solution:
1. Hiley dynamic pile formula: $$R_u = \frac{\eta \cdot W \cdot H}{s + \frac{c}{2}} \cdot \left(\frac{W + e^2 W_c}{W + W_c}\right)$$ 2. Impact efficiency factor: $$\frac{W + e^2 W_c}{W + W_c} = \frac{1600 + (0.50)^2 \times 4200}{1600 + 4200} = \frac{1600 + 1050}{5800} = \frac{2650}{5800} \approx 0.4569$$ 3. Denominator: $$s + \frac{c}{2} = 0.004 + 0.003 = 0.007\text{ m}$$ 4. Potential energy of hammer: $$W \cdot H = (1600\text{ kg} \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2) \times 0.70\text{ m} = 15,696\text{ N} \times 0.70\text{ m} = 10,987.2\text{ Joules}$$ 5. Ultimate resistance $R_u$: $$R_u = \frac{10,987.2}{0.007} \times 0.4569 = 1,569,600 \times 0.4569 \approx 717,150\text{ N} \approx 717.2\text{ kN}$$ The casing drive shoe must overcome over $717\text{ kN}$ ($73\text{ tonnes}$) of dynamic friction to advance through the boulder bed.
Problem 5: Bhabar vs Tarai Hydrogeologic Contrast
Contrast the hydrogeological regime of the Bhabar belt with the adjacent southern Tarai belt in terms of: (a) grain size, (b) aquifer boundary condition, (c) water table depth, and (d) well yield characteristics.
Solution:
1. Bhabar Zone (Northern Piedmont): Coarse boulders, cobbles, pebbles; strictly unconfined water table; deep water level ($50-100\text{ m}$); acts as the primary regional recharge zone where mountain rivers lose flow into the subsurface.
2. Tarai Zone (Southern Belt): Alternating permeable sand-gravel lenses interbedded with thick impervious clay beds; highly confined (artesian) conditions; water table at or near surface with self-flowing artesian wells (flowing springs); acts as the primary discharge zone of the Himalayan groundwater system.
Problem 6: Well Screen Selection for Boulder Formations
Explain why continuous slot wire-wound stainless steel screens are often replaced by heavy-duty bridge-slot (or shutter) carbon steel screens in Bhabar production wells.
Solution:
1. In coarse boulder-gravel formations, shifting boulders during seismic tremors or heavy pumping exert massive non-uniform lateral earth pressures and point loads.
2. Continuous wire-wound screens, while hydraulically superior in sand aquifers, have low collapse strength against jagged, shifting boulder points.
3. Bridge-slot screens are stamped from heavy-walled steel pipe ($6-10\text{ mm}$ wall thickness). The bridge design provides enormous structural hoop strength and collapse resistance ($> 15-25\text{ bar}$) capable of withstanding severe point-load stresses from surrounding boulders.
Problem 7: Modern Dual Rotary (DR) Technology
Describe the operational mechanism of the Dual Rotary (DR) drilling system as a modern mechanized replacement for traditional cable tool drilling in boulder beds.
Solution:
1. The Dual Rotary rig utilizes two independent rotary drives: (i) A lower rotary drive chuck rotates and pushes heavy casing downward into the ground using hydraulic feed cylinders. (ii) An upper rotary drive operates a top-drive swivel and drill string with a DTH hammer or button bit that drills inside the casing.
2. The casing rotates and advances concurrently with or slightly ahead of the bit, preventing borehole collapse.
3. Carbide casing teeth cut through boulders on the perimeter while the internal bit pulverizes the center, achieving penetration rates of $15-30\text{ m/day}$ compared to $2-3\text{ m/day}$ for cable tool rigs.
Problem 8: Rate of Penetration and Economic Decision-Making
A water supply project must drill a $120\text{ m}$ deep production well in the Bhabar boulder belt. A cable tool rig achieves an average penetration rate of $2.5\text{ m/day}$ with $100\%$ completion certainty. A direct rotary rig claims $20\text{ m/day}$ in soft alluvium but has a historical $95\%$ probability of total borehole loss and pipe abandonment in Bhabar boulders. Formulate an engineering risk-assessment justifying the rig selection.
Solution:
1. Cable Tool Rig: Duration $T = 120 / 2.5 = 48\text{ days}$. Cost is predictable, zero circulating mud cost, zero loss of drill string, 100% completion success.
2. Direct Rotary Rig: Expected time before catastrophic pipe seizure and borehole collapse is $< 2\text{ days}$ ($< 30\text{ m}$ depth). Abandoning $120\text{ m}$ of drill pipe, collars, and bit results in financial loss exceeding millions of rupees plus project delay.
3. Engineering Recommendation: Cable tool percussion is definitively chosen due to zero risk of circulation loss and absolute borehole wall support via concurrent casing advance.
